The lecture of this chapter (figures built as it is explained)

This chapter continues the vibration of systems with several degrees of freedom. In chapter 10 we wrote the equation of motion with a mass and a stiffness matrix, found the eigenpairs and showed that the response expands in modes of vibration (načini nihanja). In chapters 7 and 12 we built such matrices for bars and beams with finite elements. Such models can have thousands of coordinates, and the full solution is expensive for every new load.

The word reduction means making smaller: we replace the large model by a small one that keeps what interests us. What is large here and what is small is shown in figure 21.1 on the smallest example, bar C from section 10.8: a steel bar with modulus of elasticity \(E = 196\) GPa, length \(L = 1\) m and cross-section \(A = 100\) mm². The left end is clamped in a wall, and a force of \(1\) kN pulls at the free end. We divide the bar into sixteen equal pieces, and the dots are their joints, the nodes. Before loading, the end of the bar is at the grey dashed line, after it the bar is orange and its end has moved by \(FL/(EA) = 51{,}02\) µm, strongly magnified in the figure so that it can be seen. Every node moves, and the displacement of each is one coordinate of the model. We draw them above the axis of position \(x/L\): sixteen dots, from \(q_1\) at the wall to \(q_{16}\) at the end, and the last dot is the same \(51{,}02\) µm. This is the large model: sixteen unknowns here, thousands in a real machine.

The word modal says that the small model is built from modes of vibration, that is, from the shapes in which the system can vibrate (definition 8.140). Every position of the sixteen dots can be written as a sum of these shapes, each multiplied by one number (corollary 10.22): the first shape \(\boldsymbol\varphi_1\) with the number \(c_1\), the second with \(c_2\) and all higher ones together. Why does this work? There are as many shapes as coordinates, sixteen, and none of them can be put together from the others, so the sixteen numbers \(c_{\mathrm{r}}\) say the same as the sixteen displacements \(q_{\mathrm{i}}\), only sorted differently. Solving the eigenproblem (lastni problem) is computing these modes and their frequencies. Each mode we keep is one unknown, one number \(c_{\mathrm{r}}\) instead of all the node displacements, so the computation becomes shorter, but we cut something off and must know how much.

How much we may cut off depends on the load. Two cases are common, a force on the structure and a shaking support, and the figure shows the first. For the bar of the figure, the first mode alone gives \(41{,}39\) µm at the end, which is only \(81{,}12\) % of the static displacement of the end, so it matters to know where the rest goes. In the figure it has not vanished: \(4{,}63\) µm comes from the second mode and \(5{,}00\) µm from all higher ones together, \(41{,}39 + 4{,}63 + 5{,}00 = 51{,}02\).

Why does the first mode carry the most? We draw the answer in figure 21.2. On the axes, the position \(x/L\) is horizontal and the displacement vertical. On them we draw the first shape and the second shape, each multiplied by such a number that the end of the bar moves by the same length \(1\) in both. This is the shape \(\hat{\boldsymbol\varphi}_{\mathrm{r}} = \boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}/\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}(L)\), where \(\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}(L)\) is the last component of the column \(\boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}\), the displacement of the end. The first shape rises all the way from the wall to the end. The second first goes down and turns upwards at \(x \approx L/3\).

Below the two shapes we draw by how much each of the sixteen pieces stretches, as a bar: upwards when the piece lengthens, downwards when it shortens. The elongation of a piece is the difference of the displacements of its two nodes, so the elongations of all pieces from the wall to the end add up to the displacement of the end, which is \(1\) in both shapes. In the first shape all bars point upwards and their sum is \(1\). In the second, the first five pieces shorten, together by \(0{,}995\), and the other eleven lengthen by \(1{,}995\), so that the difference is again \(1\). The second shape therefore stretches and compresses the pieces by \(0{,}995 + 1{,}995 = 2{,}99\) in total, almost three times as much as the first.

A piece that stretches more resists more. By equation (7.5) a piece with elongation \(\Delta\) has the strain energy \(EA\,\Delta^2/(2h)\), where \(h = L/16\) is the length of the piece, so a piece with three times the elongation has nine times the energy. We add the energies of the pieces into the energy of the bar. Twice the energy of the shape with end \(1\) is

\[\hat{\boldsymbol\varphi}_{\mathrm{r}}^{\T}\mat K\hat{\boldsymbol\varphi}_{\mathrm{r}} = \frac{EA}{h}\sum_{\mathrm{e}=1}^{16}\Delta_{\mathrm{e}}^2 ,\]

where \(\Delta_{\mathrm{e}}\) is the elongation of piece \(e\), and it is \(1{,}233\) for the first and \(11{,}02\) for the second shape, in units of \(EA/L\). The ratio is \(8{,}94\), close to \(3^2 = 9\).

The share of mode \(r\) in the displacement of the end under a slow force is \(\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}(L)^2F/\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\) (lemma 10.69, section 10.10). In two steps we write it with the energy of the figure:

\[\frac{\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}(L)^2F}{\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}} = \frac{\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}(L)^2F}{\boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}^{\T}\mat K\boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}} = \frac{F}{\hat{\boldsymbol\varphi}_{\mathrm{r}}^{\T}\mat K\hat{\boldsymbol\varphi}_{\mathrm{r}}} .\]

The first equality holds because the mode is \(\mat M\)-normalized, \(\boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}^{\T}\mat M\boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{r}} = 1\) (theorem 10.21), so \(\boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}^{\T}\mat K\boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{r}} = \lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}^{\T}\mat M\boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{r}} = \lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\). The second holds because \(\boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{r}} = \varphi_{\mathrm{r}}(L)\,\hat{\boldsymbol\varphi}_{\mathrm{r}}\), and so \(\boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}^{\T}\mat K\boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{r}} = \varphi_{\mathrm{r}}(L)^2\,\hat{\boldsymbol\varphi}_{\mathrm{r}}^{\T}\mat K\hat{\boldsymbol\varphi}_{\mathrm{r}}\). Since \(F/(EA/L) = 51{,}02\) µm, the share is the static displacement of the end divided by the number of the figure. On the bars at the bottom right this is \(51{,}02/1{,}233 = 41{,}39\) µm for the first and \(51{,}02/11{,}02 = 4{,}63\) µm for the second mode, the same parts as above. The first mode carries the most because its shape stretches the pieces least and therefore has the least energy.

This split holds for a force that changes slowly compared with the vibration of the bar, that is, with a frequency far below the first natural frequency of the model with sixteen elements, \(f_1 = 1253{,}70\) Hz. Only then does every mode respond with its static part. Under a harmonic force with angular frequency \(\Omega\), the undamped response of mode \(r\) is larger by the factor \(1/(1 - \Omega^2/\omega_{\mathrm{r}}^2)\), where \(\omega_{\mathrm{r}}\) is its natural angular frequency (section 10.10). At \(\Omega = 0{,}5\,\omega_1\) this is \(1/(1 - 0{,}25) = 1{,}333\) for the first mode, and the share grows to \(55{,}19\) µm. For the second, \(\omega_2^2 = 9{,}058\,\omega_1^2\), the factor is \(1/(1 - 0{,}25/9{,}058) = 1{,}028\), and the share grows only to \(4{,}76\) µm. For \(\Omega\) close to \(\omega_1\) the factor grows without bound, and there the response is set by damping. How we correct the cut-off modes under a faster force is told in section 21.1. For a machine on a vibrating support, for example a frame on a floor shaken by an earthquake or a neighbouring machine, we must know how much mass each mode really moves, so that we know which modes we may cut off (section 21.2).

The chapter promises three things. First, we will show how to correct the cut-off modes with a small computation: with accelerations and with an added mass at the support, and how to measure how much mass the modes capture. Then we will shrink the model without modes, by keeping chosen coordinates and by dividing a structure into parts that we then join again. Finally we will show three procedures for computing the modes themselves, from the simplest to the one used by large programs, and how damping changes in a shortened model. For every procedure we will say where it fails.

21.1 The mode-acceleration correction (popravek s pospeški)

Section 10.10.5 of chapter 10 ended with a question left open. Bar C of steel, clamped at one end and loaded at the other by a force of \(1\) kN, has sixteen modes with sixteen finite elements. If we keep only the first, we get \(81{,}12\) % of the static tip displacement, and the remaining \(18{,}88\) % is lost. Where did it go? In a large model we cannot afford to compute the modes we cut off. This section shows that for a slow force we do not have to: most of what they contribute comes from one static solution that the model can already compute. The section answers three questions. What do the cut-off modes contribute when the force is slow? How do we add it without computing one more mode? When does this not work, and what happens then? The next two sections of this chapter complete the picture with the response to support motion and with the additional mass method.

21.1.1 The model and what we know

We treat a system with \(n\) coordinates and the equation of motion \(\mat M\ddot{\vek q} + \mat K\vek q = \vek F\cos\Omega t\) (theorem 10.3), where \(\mat K\) is a symmetric positive definite stiffness matrix, \(\mat M\) a symmetric positive definite mass matrix, \(\vek F\) the column of force amplitudes and \(\Omega\) the angular frequency of the force. There is no damping in the equation, although we treated it in section 10.10.4 and in chapter 20. We leave it out because the idea of the correction we are looking for rests only on the ratio between \(\Omega\) and the natural frequencies. Far below the cut-off modes this hardly changes the result: for bar C with classical damping \(\zeta_{\mathrm{r}} = 0{,}02\) in all modes and \(\Omega = 0{,}5\,\omega_1\) the error of the correction goes from \(0{,}240\) % to \(0{,}249\) %. Near a resonance the assumption fails, since there the damping sets the amplitude (section 21.1.6). The eigenpairs \((\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}, \boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{r}})\) with \(\lambda_1 \le \dots \le \lambda_{\mathrm{n}}\) and \(\mat M\)-normalized columns (theorem 10.21) are known only for \(r = 1, \dots, N\) with \(N < n\). Why only a few of the lowest? Computing modes is expensive: every mode is found by repetition, in which one step is one solution of a system with \(\mat K\), and every mode takes several steps (sections 21.6, 21.7 and 21.8). The static solution \(\mat K^{-1}\vek F\) is not expensive: we factor \(\mat K\) once into \(\mat L\mat D\mat L^{\T}\) and solve every new force by forward and backward substitution (lemma 7.47).

As the example we use bar C: steel (\(E = 196\) GPa, \(\rho = 7800\) kg/m³), \(A = 100\) mm², \(L = 1\) m, \(16\) equal elements with the mass matrix of lemma 10.47, clamped at \(x = 0\), with a force \(\vek F\) of amplitude \(1\) kN along the bar at the free end. The first three natural angular frequencies are \(\omega_{\mathrm{r}} = \sqrt{\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}} = 7877{,}26,\ 23\,707{,}75\) and \(39\,766{,}84\) 1/s, so \(f_1 = 1253{,}70\) Hz. The ratio \(\lambda_2/\lambda_1 = 9{,}058\) will come in handy.

What would the force do if we applied it slowly? We draw it as on a blackboard (figure 21.3). At the top is the bar and on it, with dashed lines, the sixteen elements. The left end is clamped in the wall, on the free end the force \(\vek F\) pulls, starting at the point of application and pointing outward. Below are the axes: \(x/L\) horizontally, the displacement \(u\) of the points of the bar vertically, and the nodes of the bar are the coordinates \(\vek q\). A slow force gives the static shape \(\mat K^{-1}\vek F\). It is a straight line, because by the equilibrium of the cut-off right piece of the bar a normal force \(F\) acts in every cross-section, and by Hooke's law the extension per unit length \(F/(EA)\) is therefore the same everywhere. The displacement of the end is \(FL/(EA) = 51{,}0204\) µm.

The part of this shape that the first mode gives is the blue curve: the mode shape \(\boldsymbol\varphi_1\) multiplied by the number \(\boldsymbol\varphi_1^{\T}\vek F/\lambda_1\), which tells how much of shape \(1\) this force excites statically (expansion by modes, corollary 10.22, and lemma 10.69). At the end it reaches \(41{,}39\) µm, which is \(81{,}12\) % of the static value. Up to the full value \(9{,}63\) µm are missing, and this missing part is the orange curve, the difference between blackwhite and blue. It is not a straight line but a shape that is negative almost up to \(x/L = 0{,}75\) (lowest \(-3{,}94\) µm at \(x/L = 0{,}4375\)) and only then positive at the end. This is the displacement the force would cause statically if the bar had only modes from the second on. The cut-off modes therefore do not vanish: under a slow force they remain as a static shape, and we look for a way to get it without them.

21.1.2 Residual flexibility

The flexibility matrix \(\mat K^{-1}\) gives the displacement caused by a unit force (lemma 10.4, its arrangement by modes is lemma 10.69). When we keep \(N\) modes, we subtract their contribution from it and get what remains.

Definition 21.1 Residual flexibility (preostala podajnost)

Let \(\mat K\) and \(\mat M\) be symmetric positive definite matrices of order \(n\) with eigenpairs \((\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}, \boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{r}})\), \(\mat M\)-normalized (theorem 10.21), and let \(N < n\) be a natural number. The residual flexibility after \(N\) kept modes is the symmetric matrix of order \(n\)

\[\mat R_{\mathrm{N}} = \mat K^{-1} - \sum_{\mathrm{r}=1}^{N}\frac{\boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}\boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}^{\T}}{\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}} = \sum_{\mathrm{r}=\mathrm{N}+1}^{n}\frac{\boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}\boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}^{\T}}{\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}} . \tag{21.1}\]

The column \(\mat R_{\mathrm{N}}\vek F\) is the static displacement due to the force \(\vek F\) that the cut-off modes \(N+1, \dots, n\) give.

Explanation

The second equality follows from lemma 10.69, in which \(\mat K^{-1}\) is the sum over all \(n\) modes. The name comes from flexibility (displacement per force) and from the fact that this is the remainder of the flexibility matrix that the kept modes do not cover (in English residual). The matrix \(\mat R_{\mathrm{N}}\) needs only \(\mat K^{-1}\) and the \(N\) kept modes. For bar C with the force at the end, \((\mat R_{\mathrm{N}}\vek F)_{\text{end}} = 9{,}632,\ 5{,}003,\ 3{,}315\) and \(1{,}892\) µm for \(N = 1, 2, 3\) and \(5\), that is \(18{,}88,\ 9{,}81,\ 6{,}50\) and \(3{,}71\) % of the static displacement (figure 21.4).

Source: The notion is after CK §11.3-11.4 (PDF pp. 360-368) and GR §2.8.2 (PDF p. 115). The form with the sum over modes is from lemma 10.69.

Figure 21.4 shows how these numbers add up. Each row is one choice of the number of modes, \(N = 1\) at the top, and its length is the whole static displacement, \(100\) % on the axis below. The blue part of a row is the share of the kept modes, the orange part the residual flexibility: \(18{,}88\) % for one mode. With two, three and five modes the orange share shrinks (\(9{,}81\), \(6{,}50\) and \(3{,}71\) %), but slowly. Why? The contribution of mode \(r\) at the end is \(\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}(L)^2F/\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\). Every mode has its largest displacement at the free end, so \(\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}(L)^2\) is almost the same for all of them. The natural frequencies of a bar with one clamped end are odd multiples of the first (\(\omega_2/\omega_1 = 3{,}01\), \(\omega_3/\omega_1 = 5{,}05\)), so \(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\) grows as \((2r-1)^2\). The contributions therefore fall as \(1/(2r-1)^2\): \(41{,}39\), \(4{,}63\) and \(1{,}69\) µm for \(r = 1, 2, 3\), roughly in the ratio \(1 : 1/9 : 1/25\) (section 10.10.5). With ten modes the error is still \(1{,}33\) % (section 10.10.5), whereas the residual flexibility takes one forward and backward substitution.

21.1.3 The solution with mode accelerations

How do we use the residual flexibility under a harmonic force? We first write the response of the system to the force \(\vek F\cos\Omega t\) by modes and draw it for bar C (figure 21.5). The horizontal axis is the angular frequency in units of \(\omega_1\). On it are the natural frequencies \(\omega_1, \omega_2, \omega_3\) at \(1\), \(3{,}01\) and \(5{,}05\), and above each stands a column showing how much the mode responds. The grey part of length \(1\) is its static part \(\boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}(\boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}^{\T}\vek F)/\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\), the answer to a slow force, and the orange part above it is the inertial part \(\Omega^2/(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}} - \Omega^2)\). The dashed vertical line is the force frequency \(\Omega = 0{,}5\,\omega_1\). The kept mode has an orange part of \(0{,}333\), the two cut-off modes only \(0{,}028\) and \(0{,}0099\): at a low force frequency the cut-off modes keep almost only their static part.

Lemma 21.2 Undamped response to a harmonic force by modes (odziv na harmonično silo po načinih brez dušenja)

Let \(\mat K\) and \(\mat M\) be symmetric positive definite matrices of order \(n\) with modal matrix \(\mat\Phi\) (definition 10.23), \(\Omega \ge 0\) an angular frequency with \(\Omega^2 \ne \lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\) for all \(r\) and \(\vek F\) a real column. Then, with the force frequency \(\Omega\) and the natural frequencies of figure 21.5:

  1. The column \(\vek q(t) = \vek u\cos\Omega t\) solves the equation \(\mat M\ddot{\vek q} + \mat K\vek q = \vek F\cos\Omega t\) if and only if \((\mat K - \Omega^2\mat M)\vek u = \vek F\).
  2. This equation has exactly one solution, the sum of the terms of all modes,
    \[\vek u = \sum_{\mathrm{r}=1}^{n}\frac{\boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}\,(\boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}^{\T}\vek F)}{\lambda_{\mathrm{r}} - \Omega^2} . \tag{21.2}\]
Proof

We must show that inserting \(\vek u\cos\Omega t\) gives the equation for \(\vek u\), and that the matrix of this equation is invertible with an inverse that is a sum over modes.

  1. From \(\vek q = \vek u\cos\Omega t\) it follows that
    \[\ddot{\vek q} = -\Omega^2\vek u\cos\Omega t ,\]
    and inserting into the left side of the equation gives
    \[\mat M\ddot{\vek q} + \mat K\vek q = (\mat K - \Omega^2\mat M)\vek u\cos\Omega t .\]
    This column equals \(\vek F\cos\Omega t\) for every \(t\) exactly when \((\mat K - \Omega^2\mat M)\vek u = \vek F\) (in one direction insert \(t = 0\), in the other multiply by \(\cos\Omega t\)).
  2. By lemma 10.24, \(\mat\Phi^{\T}\mat M\mat\Phi = \mat I\), hence
    \[\mat\Phi^{-1} = \mat\Phi^{\T}\mat M , \qquad \mat\Phi\mat\Phi^{\T} = \mat M^{-1} , \qquad \mat\Phi^{-\T} = \mat M\mat\Phi .\]
  3. Let \(\mat D = \mathrm{diag}(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}} - \Omega^2)\). By lemma 10.24, \(\mat\Phi^{\T}(\mat K - \Omega^2\mat M)\mat\Phi = \mat D\), and all diagonal elements differ from zero, because the force frequency coincides with no natural frequency (the assumption \(\Omega^2 \ne \lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\)). From step 2 it follows that \(\mat K - \Omega^2\mat M = \mat\Phi^{-\T}\mat D\,\mat\Phi^{-1} = \mat M\mat\Phi\,\mat D\,\mat\Phi^{\T}\mat M\).
  4. Let \(\mat B = \mat\Phi\mat D^{-1}\mat\Phi^{\T}\). By step 3,
    \[(\mat K - \Omega^2\mat M)\mat B = \mat M\mat\Phi\,\mat D\,(\mat\Phi^{\T}\mat M\mat\Phi)\,\mat D^{-1}\mat\Phi^{\T} = \mat M\mat\Phi\mat\Phi^{\T} = \mat M\mat M^{-1} = \mat I ,\]
    \[\mat B(\mat K - \Omega^2\mat M) = \mat\Phi\mat D^{-1}(\mat\Phi^{\T}\mat M\mat\Phi)\,\mat D\,\mat\Phi^{\T}\mat M = \mat\Phi\mat\Phi^{\T}\mat M = \mat M^{-1}\mat M = \mat I .\]
    By definition 1.110, \(\mat B = (\mat K - \Omega^2\mat M)^{-1}\), the only solution is \(\vek u = \mat B\vek F\) and this is the sum (21.2).

Source: The proof is not from a source. It is the same proof as for lemma 10.69 (where \(\Omega = 0\)). The sum over modes for damped systems is CK equation (11.31) (PDF p. 350) and theorem 10.72.

For \(\Omega = 0\) the lemma returns lemma 10.69. For \(N\) kept modes we take the first \(N\) terms of the sum (21.2), that is the kept modes. Craig and Kurdila call this the mode-displacement solution (rešitev z odmiki načinov), since the displacements are computed directly from the kept modes (CK §11.3, PDF pp. 360-362). Bar C shows what it lacks: the cut-off modes still have their static part. At \(\Omega = 0\) its error is \(-18{,}88\) % with one mode, and it stays so for small \(\Omega\) as well: at \(\Omega = 0{,}5\,\omega_1\) it is \(-15{,}06\) %.

Why is this so? Look at a single cut-off mode \(r\) (figure 21.6). At the end of the bar it responds with \(c_{\mathrm{r}}\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}/(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}} - \Omega^2)\), where \(c_{\mathrm{r}} = \varphi_{\mathrm{r}}(L)^2F/\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\) is its static part. The axes show the ratio \(\Omega^2/\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\) horizontally and the factor \(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}/(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}} - \Omega^2)\) vertically. The grey horizontal line at height \(1\) is the static part alone, the curve is the whole response of the mode, and the height of the curve above the line is the inertial part \(\Omega^2/(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}} - \Omega^2)\). At the vertical line \(\Omega^2 = \lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\) the mode is in resonance. At \(\Omega = 0{,}5\,\omega_1\) mode \(2\) has the ratio \(\Omega^2/\lambda_2 = 0{,}25/9{,}058 = 0{,}028\), and its dot lies almost on the line, at height \(1{,}028\). Below, the same is drawn as a bar: the top bar has a grey part of length \(1\), the static part, and a barely visible orange part of length \(0{,}028\), the inertial part. In micrometres at the end of the bar:

mode whole response static part inertial part
\(2\) \(4{,}760\) \(4{,}628\) \(0{,}131\)
\(3\) \(1{,}705\) \(1{,}688\) \(0{,}017\)

Most of the response of a cut-off mode is thus static: for mode \(2\) the inertial part is \(0{,}131/4{,}628 = 0{,}028\) of the static, more than thirty times smaller. The mode-displacement solution cuts off both parts of the bar, the grey and the orange, and loses mainly the large one.

The idea of the correction is therefore to split what we cut off, and not to cut off everything. The smallest example is at the top of figure 21.6: a mass \(m\) on a spring \(k\). Every moment of the motion is a balance of forces if we also think of the inertial force that a mass \(m\) with acceleration \(\ddot q\) has, equal to \(-m\ddot q\) (d'Alembert's principle). The spring force \(kq\) balances the force \(F\cos\Omega t\) and the inertial force \(-m\ddot q\), so the blue arrow is exactly as long as the other two together. Below resonance the inertial force points the way the force does, because for \(q = u\cos\Omega t\) the acceleration \(\ddot q = -\Omega^2 q\) is opposite to the displacement, and for a slow force it is short. With several coordinates the same stands in columns: the spring forces \(\mat K\vek q\) balance the force \(\vek F\cos\Omega t\) and the inertial force \(-\mat M\ddot{\vek q}\), so \(\mat K\vek q = \vek F\cos\Omega t - \mat M\ddot{\vek q}\). This is exact, and when we solve it for \(\vek q\) we have \(\vek q = \mat K^{-1}(\vek F\cos\Omega t - \mat M\ddot{\vek q})\). The inertial force is small for a slow force, so we insert the accelerations \(\ddot{\vek q}\) from the kept modes, and everything else stays statically exact. This is the only assumption of the correction. It is justified as long as \(\Omega^2\) is small compared with \(\lambda_{\mathrm{N}+1}\), when the orange part of the bar is short. It fails near a cut-off mode, as the bottom bar shows. What it costs is said by theorem 21.4: in every cut-off mode we miss the fraction \(\Omega^2/(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}} - \Omega^2)\) of its static part. Lord Rayleigh proposed this idea as early as 1894 (GR §2.8.2, PDF p. 115, which cites his work). The name of this procedure comes from the fact that we use the modes only for the accelerations.

Definition 21.3 Mode-acceleration solution (rešitev s pospeški načinov)

Let \(\mat K\), \(\mat M\), \(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\), \(\boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}\) be as in lemma 21.2, \(\vek F\) the force amplitude, \(\Omega^2 \ne \lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\) and \(N < n\). The mode-displacement solution (rešitev z odmiki načinov) with \(N\) modes is the sum of the kept modes only

\[\vek u_{\mathrm{N}}^{\mathrm{MD}} = \sum_{\mathrm{r}=1}^{N}\frac{\boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}\,(\boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}^{\T}\vek F)}{\lambda_{\mathrm{r}} - \Omega^2} . \tag{21.3}\]

The mode-acceleration solution with \(N\) modes is

\[\vek u_{\mathrm{N}}^{\mathrm{MA}} = \mat K^{-1}\big(\vek F + \Omega^2\mat M\,\vek u_{\mathrm{N}}^{\mathrm{MD}}\big) , \tag{21.4}\]

that is, the static solution with the force \(\vek F - \mat M\vek a_{\mathrm{N}}\), where \(\vek a_{\mathrm{N}} = -\Omega^2\vek u_{\mathrm{N}}^{\mathrm{MD}}\) is the amplitude of the acceleration of the motion from the kept modes. The solution \(\vek u_{\mathrm{N}}^{\mathrm{MA}}\) is a column of amplitudes that we get with one solution with \(\mat K\) and with \(N\) modes.

Explanation

The exact solution \(\vek u\) satisfies \(\mat K\vek u = \vek F + \Omega^2\mat M\vek u\) (lemma 21.2, item 1). Equation (21.4) is this equation, in which we replaced \(\vek u\) on the right by \(\vek u_{\mathrm{N}}^{\mathrm{MD}}\). The names are after CK: in the mode-displacement solution the modes are the only source of displacements, in the mode-acceleration solution only the source of accelerations, and to the cut-off modes we add their static part (CK equation (11.40), PDF p. 361, and (11.49), PDF p. 367).

Source: CK §11.3-11.4 (PDF pp. 360-368), GR §2.8.1-2.8.2 (PDF pp. 114-116). The form with \(\mat K^{-1}(\vek F - \mat M\vek a_{\mathrm{N}})\) is after GR (PDF p. 115), the derivation for a harmonic force and the residual flexibility is from theorem 21.4.

What the correction brings is shown by the next theorem. It proves that \(\vek u_{\mathrm{N}}^{\mathrm{MA}}\) is the same as the mode-displacement solution to which we add the residual flexibility, and that the error of a cut-off mode is a small fraction of its static part.

Theorem 21.4 Mode-acceleration correction (popravek s pospeški)

Let \(\mat K\), \(\mat M\), \(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\), \(\boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}\), \(\vek F\), \(\Omega\) and \(N\) be as in definition 21.3, and \(\vek u\) the exact solution (21.2). Then:

  1. \(\vek u_{\mathrm{N}}^{\mathrm{MA}} = \vek u_{\mathrm{N}}^{\mathrm{MD}} + \mat R_{\mathrm{N}}\vek F\). We add the static parts of the cut-off modes.
  2. The errors are
    \[\vek u - \vek u_{\mathrm{N}}^{\mathrm{MA}} = \sum_{\mathrm{r}=\mathrm{N}+1}^{n}\frac{\Omega^2}{\lambda_{\mathrm{r}} - \Omega^2}\cdot\frac{\boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}(\boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}^{\T}\vek F)}{\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}},\qquad \vek u - \vek u_{\mathrm{N}}^{\mathrm{MD}} = \sum_{\mathrm{r}=\mathrm{N}+1}^{n}\frac{\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}}{\lambda_{\mathrm{r}} - \Omega^2}\cdot\frac{\boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}(\boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}^{\T}\vek F)}{\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}} , \tag{21.5}\]
    the static part \(\boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}(\boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}^{\T}\vek F)/\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\) of every cut-off mode is thus multiplied by \(\Omega^2/(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}} - \Omega^2)\) in the mode-acceleration solution and by \(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}/(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}} - \Omega^2)\) in the mode-displacement solution.
  3. At \(\Omega = 0\), \(\vek u_{\mathrm{N}}^{\mathrm{MA}} = \vek u\) for every \(N\), whereas \(\vek u - \vek u_{\mathrm{N}}^{\mathrm{MD}} = \mat R_{\mathrm{N}}\vek F\).
  4. Let the force act on the coordinate \(i\) only, \(\vek F = F_{\mathrm{i}}\vek e_{\mathrm{i}}\) (a column with a one at place \(i\)) with \(F_{\mathrm{i}} > 0\), and let \(\Omega^2 < \lambda_{\mathrm{N}+1}\): the force frequency is to the left of the first cut-off mode (at \(N = 1\)). Then for the same coordinate \(i\)
    \[0 \le u_{\mathrm{i}} - u_{\mathrm{N},\mathrm{i}}^{\mathrm{MA}} \le \frac{\Omega^2}{\lambda_{\mathrm{N}+1} - \Omega^2}\,(\mat R_{\mathrm{N}})_{\mathrm{ii}}F_{\mathrm{i}} \le \frac{\Omega^2}{\lambda_{\mathrm{N}+1} - \Omega^2}\,\big(u_{\mathrm{i}} - u_{\mathrm{N},\mathrm{i}}^{\mathrm{MD}}\big) . \tag{21.6}\]
Idea

The mode-acceleration solution adds to the mode-displacement solution exactly the static part of the cut-off modes. The exact solution has the term \(1/(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}} - \Omega^2)\) for every cut-off mode, the corrected one \(1/\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\). The difference of the two is the orange part of the bar in figure 21.6, small when \(\Omega^2\) is small compared with \(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\).

Proof

We must show that the first expression for \(\vek u_{\mathrm{N}}^{\mathrm{MA}}\) follows from the definition (21.4), that the difference from the exact solution is a sum over the cut-off modes, and that with one excited place we can bound it term by term.

  1. From \(\mat K\boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{r}} = \lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\mat M\boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}\) (theorem 10.21), multiplying by \(\mat K^{-1}/\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\), it follows that \(\mat K^{-1}\mat M\boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{r}} = \boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}/\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\).
  2. By definition (21.4) and step 1 we have
    \[\vek u_{\mathrm{N}}^{\mathrm{MA}} = \mat K^{-1}\vek F + \Omega^2\sum_{\mathrm{r}=1}^{N}\frac{\boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}^{\T}\vek F}{\lambda_{\mathrm{r}} - \Omega^2}\,\mat K^{-1}\mat M\boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{r}} = \mat K^{-1}\vek F + \sum_{\mathrm{r}=1}^{N}\frac{\Omega^2}{\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}} - \Omega^2)}\,\boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}(\boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}^{\T}\vek F) .\]
  3. By definition 21.1, \(\mat K^{-1}\vek F = \mat R_{\mathrm{N}}\vek F + \sum_{\mathrm{r}=1}^{N}\boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}(\boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}^{\T}\vek F)/\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\). We insert into step 2 and for every \(r \le N\) add the coefficients: \(\frac{1}{\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}} + \frac{\Omega^2}{\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}} - \Omega^2)} = \frac{(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}} - \Omega^2) + \Omega^2}{\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}} - \Omega^2)} = \frac{1}{\lambda_{\mathrm{r}} - \Omega^2}\). In units of \(1/\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\) this is the column of the kept mode: the grey part \(1\) and the orange part \(\Omega^2/(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}} - \Omega^2)\) together give \(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}/(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}} - \Omega^2)\), for bar C \(1 + 0{,}333 = 1{,}333\). We obtain \(\vek u_{\mathrm{N}}^{\mathrm{MA}} = \mat R_{\mathrm{N}}\vek F + \sum_{\mathrm{r}=1}^{N}\boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}(\boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}^{\T}\vek F)/(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}} - \Omega^2)\), and this is item 1.
  4. By lemma 21.2, \(\vek u - \vek u_{\mathrm{N}}^{\mathrm{MD}}\) is the sum of the terms \(\boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}(\boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}^{\T}\vek F)/(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}} - \Omega^2)\) for \(r > N\), which is the second equation (21.5) (we multiply and divide the term by \(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\)). By step 3, \(\vek u - \vek u_{\mathrm{N}}^{\mathrm{MA}} = \vek u - \vek u_{\mathrm{N}}^{\mathrm{MD}} - \mat R_{\mathrm{N}}\vek F\), and with the row \(\mat R_{\mathrm{N}}\vek F = \sum_{\mathrm{r}>\mathrm{N}}\boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}(\boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}^{\T}\vek F)/\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\) from equation (21.1) we get for every \(r > N\) the coefficient \(\frac{1}{\lambda_{\mathrm{r}} - \Omega^2} - \frac1{\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}} = \frac{\Omega^2}{\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}} - \Omega^2)}\), in figure 21.6 the curve minus the horizontal line, measured in units of \(1/\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\). This is the first equation (21.5).
  5. At \(\Omega = 0\) every term in the first equation (21.5) is zero, and in the second \(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}/\lambda_{\mathrm{r}} = 1\), the sum is \(\mat R_{\mathrm{N}}\vek F\). This is item 3.
  1. For \(\vek F = F_{\mathrm{i}}\vek e_{\mathrm{i}}\) the \(i\)-th component of the term \(r\) is \(\varphi_{\mathrm{r},\mathrm{i}}^2F_{\mathrm{i}}/\lambda_{\mathrm{r}} =: c_{\mathrm{r}}\), and \(c_{\mathrm{r}} \ge 0\) because \(F_{\mathrm{i}} > 0\). Since \(c_{\mathrm{r}}\) is not negative, we can draw it as a width (figure 21.7, bar C at \(N = 1\) and \(\Omega = 0{,}5\,\omega_1\)): every cut mode is a column, mode \(2\) \(4{,}628\) µm wide, mode \(3\) \(1{,}688\) µm, the others ever narrower. All widths together are \(\sum_{\mathrm{r}>\mathrm{N}}c_{\mathrm{r}} = (\mat R_{\mathrm{N}})_{\mathrm{ii}}F_{\mathrm{i}} = 9{,}632\) µm by equation (21.1). The height of a column on the upper axes is its factor \(\Omega^2/(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}} - \Omega^2)\), so the area of a column is its term in the first equation (21.5) (\(0{,}131\) µm for mode \(2\)), and the whole orange area is the error \(u_{\mathrm{i}} - u_{\mathrm{N},\mathrm{i}}^{\mathrm{MA}} = 0{,}156\) µm. For \(r > N\) we have \(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}} \ge \lambda_{\mathrm{N}+1} > \Omega^2\) (ordering of eigenvalues, theorem 10.21), so \(0 \le \Omega^2/(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}} - \Omega^2) \le \Omega^2/(\lambda_{\mathrm{N}+1} - \Omega^2)\), since the denominator only grows with \(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\): with a larger \(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\) we move left along the curve of figure 21.6, where less of it lies above the horizontal line. So no column to the right of the first cut one is higher than it. If we raise every column to the height of the first, \(\Omega^2/(\lambda_{\mathrm{N}+1} - \Omega^2) = 0{,}0284\), we get the dashed rectangle, which covers all columns, with the area \(0{,}0284 \cdot 9{,}632 = 0{,}273\) µm. From the first equation (21.5) it therefore follows that \(0 \le u_{\mathrm{i}} - u_{\mathrm{N},\mathrm{i}}^{\mathrm{MA}} \le \frac{\Omega^2}{\lambda_{\mathrm{N}+1} - \Omega^2}\sum_{\mathrm{r}>\mathrm{N}}c_{\mathrm{r}} = \frac{\Omega^2}{\lambda_{\mathrm{N}+1} - \Omega^2}(\mat R_{\mathrm{N}})_{\mathrm{ii}}F_{\mathrm{i}}\).
  2. From the second equation (21.5), \(u_{\mathrm{i}} - u_{\mathrm{N},\mathrm{i}}^{\mathrm{MD}} = \sum_{\mathrm{r}>\mathrm{N}}\frac{\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}}{\lambda_{\mathrm{r}} - \Omega^2}c_{\mathrm{r}} \ge \sum_{\mathrm{r}>\mathrm{N}}c_{\mathrm{r}}\), because \(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}/(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}} - \Omega^2) \ge 1\) for \(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}} > \Omega^2\) (left of the resonance the curve is everywhere above the horizontal line \(1\)). On the middle axes of figure 21.7 these are the same columns with height \(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}/(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}} - \Omega^2) = 1 + \Omega^2/(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}} - \Omega^2)\): the grey part of height \(1\) has the area \(\sum_{\mathrm{r}>\mathrm{N}}c_{\mathrm{r}} = 9{,}632\) µm, and on it sits the orange cap, the same orange area \(0{,}156\) µm as above (step 4), only at a scale where it is barely visible. The whole column is the error of the mode-displacement solution, \(9{,}787\) µm, and it is not smaller than the grey part alone. We multiply the inequality by the positive \(\Omega^2/(\lambda_{\mathrm{N}+1} - \Omega^2)\) and together with step 6 obtain the last inequality in (21.6). The whole chain stands on the number line at the bottom: the mode-acceleration error \(0{,}156\) µm, the bound \(0{,}273\) µm and \(0{,}0284\) times the mode-displacement error \(0{,}278\) µm, each segment longer than the one before.
Explanation

By this theorem the mode-acceleration solution is not a different method but the mode-displacement solution to which we add \(\mat R_{\mathrm{N}}\vek F\), the static part of the cut-off modes. The column \(\mat R_{\mathrm{N}}\vek F\) is entirely independent of \(\Omega\), we compute it once. By step 2 of the proof, \(\vek u_{\mathrm{N}}^{\mathrm{MA}}\) lies in the subspace spanned by \(\boldsymbol\varphi_1, \dots, \boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{N}}\) and \(\mat K^{-1}\vek F\), so by only \(N + 1\) columns. When these columns are linearly independent, they can be the columns of the matrix \(\mat\Psi\) of a Ritz approximation (definition 10.58), and we return to such a choice in section 21.8.

Why does item 4 require a single force and the displacement at its own place? There the contribution of every mode \(\varphi_{\mathrm{r},\mathrm{i}}^2F_{\mathrm{i}}/\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\) is a square times a positive number, so it is not negative, and the terms only add. At another place or with several forces the terms have both signs and partly cancel: the orange curve \(\mat R_1\vek F\) of figure 21.3 is \(+9{,}63\) µm at the end but \(-3{,}94\) µm at \(x/L = 0{,}4375\). The sum can then be small although the single terms are not, and a bound term by term no longer bounds it. The equations (21.5) hold for every force and every coordinate.

Source: The proof is ours. The form of the mode-acceleration solution for an undamped system is CK equation (11.49) (PDF p. 367), item 3 is CK example 11.6 (PDF p. 368, "the exact static solution is produced at \(\Omega = 0\) without any contribution from normal modes").

21.1.4 Bar C and the smallness of the correction

We test the theorem on bar C, on the end amplitude under a force of \(1\) kN (figure 21.8). On the axes the ratio \(\Omega/\omega_1\) is horizontal and the end amplitude in µm vertical. The poles are the resonances \(\omega_1\) and \(\omega_2 = 3{,}010\,\omega_1\), where the exact amplitude (cut off above \(100\) µm) runs off to infinity. The exact amplitude (blackwhite) is the static displacement \(51{,}02\) µm at \(\Omega = 0\), rises up to the first resonance, above it is first negative (the end oscillates in antiphase with the force), passes through zero at \(\Omega \approx 2{,}00\,\omega_1\) (there the end stands still) and then runs off again at the second. The mode-displacement solution with one mode (blue, dashed) has only the pole at \(\omega_1\) and is lower than the exact one by \(9{,}63\) µm at \(\Omega = 0\). The mode-acceleration solution with one mode (orange) is the same curve, shifted up by \(\mat R_1\vek F\), so by theorem 21.4, item 1. We therefore see it almost on the exact curve up to about \(\Omega = \omega_1\) and again after the resonance, but it lacks the pole at \(\omega_2\).

The exact numbers for the dots at \(\Omega = 0{,}5\,\omega_1\) and \(1{,}5\,\omega_1\) are in the table. The error is the ratio \((u_{\text{end},\mathrm{N}} - u_{\text{end}})/u_{\text{end}}\), and the exact value \(u_{\text{end}}\) we compute with NumPy from the equation \((\mat K - \Omega^2\mat M)\vek u = \vek F\).

\(\Omega/\omega_1\) exact (µm) \(N\) mode-displacement mode-acceleration
\(0\) \(51{,}0204\) \(1\) \(-18{,}88\) % \(0{,}00\) %
\(2\) \(-9{,}81\) % \(0{,}00\) %
\(3\) \(-6{,}50\) % \(0{,}00\) %
\(0{,}5\) \(64{,}9724\) \(1\) \(-15{,}06\) % \(-0{,}240\) %
\(2\) \(-7{,}74\) % \(-0{,}037\) %
\(3\) \(-5{,}11\) % \(-0{,}012\) %
\(1{,}5\) \(-21{,}7158\) \(1\) \(+52{,}47\) % \(+8{,}12\) %
\(2\) \(+24{,}12\) % \(+1{,}08\) %
\(3\) \(+15{,}59\) % \(+0{,}32\) %

At \(\Omega = 0\) the correction is exact, as item 3 of the theorem says. At \(\Omega = 0{,}5\,\omega_1\) the mode-acceleration solution with one mode (\(-0{,}24\) %) is more accurate than the mode-displacement solution with three modes (\(-5{,}11\) %). Item 4 tells how large the error is. For \(N = 1\), \(\Omega^2/(\lambda_2 - \Omega^2) = 0{,}25/(9{,}058 - 0{,}25) = 0{,}0284\) (we measure \(\Omega^2\) in units of \(\lambda_1\), as \(\lambda_2/\lambda_1 = 9{,}058\)). The upper bound from equation (21.6) is \(0{,}0284 \cdot 9{,}632 = 0{,}273\) µm, and the actual error is \(0{,}156\) µm, that is \(0{,}240\) % of \(64{,}97\) µm (figure 21.7 in the proof). The ratio of the error of the mode-acceleration solution to the error of the mode-displacement solution is \(0{,}156/9{,}787 = 0{,}016\), below the bound \(0{,}0284\). The correction reduces the error \(63\) times here.

The smallness on which this stands needs a number. The condition \(\Omega^2 \ll \lambda_{\mathrm{N}+1}\) is needed so that the inertial part of a cut-off mode is small compared with its static part, in figure 21.6 the orange part of the bar short compared with the grey. The mode-acceleration solution misses the orange part in mode \(r\) (equation (21.5)), the mode-displacement solution both parts. For the lowest cut-off mode, in units of its static part:

\(\Omega^2/\lambda_{\mathrm{N}+1}\) mode-acceleration misses \(\dfrac{\Omega^2}{\lambda_{\mathrm{N}+1} - \Omega^2}\) mode-displacement misses \(\dfrac{\lambda_{\mathrm{N}+1}}{\lambda_{\mathrm{N}+1} - \Omega^2}\) ratio of the errors
\(0{,}01\) \(0{,}0101\) \(1{,}0101\) \(0{,}01\)
\(0{,}1\) \(0{,}111\) \(1{,}111\) \(0{,}1\)
\(0{,}81\) \(4{,}263\) \(5{,}263\) \(0{,}81\)

The ratio of the two errors is always \(\Omega^2/\lambda_{\mathrm{N}+1}\). The middle row is the limit we use from here on: the mode-acceleration solution misses a ninth of the static part and ten times less than the mode-displacement solution. The last row is the example of the next section, where the correction fails. For bar C and \(N = 1\), \(\Omega^2 = 0{,}1\lambda_2\) at \(\Omega = 0{,}316\,\omega_2 = 0{,}952\,\omega_1\), just below the first resonance. For \(0 \le \Omega \le 0{,}95\,\omega_1\) the mode-acceleration solution is thus within this bound. At \(\Omega = 1{,}5\,\omega_1\) we have crossed it: \(\Omega^2 = 0{,}25\,\lambda_2\), the ratio is \(0{,}33\) and the error \(+8{,}12\) %, more than thirty times the \(0{,}24\) % at \(0{,}5\,\omega_1\).

21.1.5 When the force is near a cut-off mode

The theorem requires only \(\Omega^2 < \lambda_{\mathrm{N}+1}\), but the correction is good only for \(\Omega^2 \ll \lambda_{\mathrm{N}+1}\). Let us see what happens just below the edge of the theorem's condition. Take \(N = 1\) and the force frequency \(\Omega = 0{,}9\,\omega_2 = 21\,337\) 1/s (\(3396\) Hz), so \(2{,}71\,\omega_1\) and a little below the second pole (figure 21.9).

The axes have \(\omega_2\) as the unit, the pole \(\omega_2\) is at \(1\). The exact curve (blackwhite) runs off at \(\omega_2\) and the dot at \(0{,}9\) is its value \(23{,}764\) µm. The mode-displacement solution with one mode (blue) passes calmly through this region and gives \(-6{,}531\) µm. The mode-acceleration solution with one mode (orange) is the same curve, shifted by \(9{,}632\) µm, and gives \(3{,}100\) µm, so an error of \(-86{,}95\) %. The dot on the orange curve lies \(20{,}66\) µm below the dot on the blackwhite: the static correction does not suffice here.

Why? The cut-off mode \(2\) at \(\Omega = 0{,}9\,\omega_2\) has the ratio \(\lambda_2/(\lambda_2 - \Omega^2) = 1/(1 - 0{,}81) = 5{,}263\), the upper dot on the curve of figure 21.6: it does not respond statically but \(5{,}263\) times more strongly than its static value, because it is near its resonance. Its response at the end is \(24{,}360\) µm and not \(4{,}628\) µm, which is what the static part brings. The mode-acceleration solution adds only the static part, so the error in mode \(2\) is \(\Omega^2/(\lambda_2 - \Omega^2) = 4{,}263\) of its static part (the long orange bar), that is \(4{,}263 \cdot 4{,}628 = 19{,}73\) µm of the total error \(20{,}66\) µm, which in figure 21.9 is the distance between the dots, the remaining \(0{,}93\) µm is contributed by modes from the third on. The error of the mode-acceleration solution is \(0{,}682\) of the error of the mode-displacement solution and no longer \(0{,}016\) as at \(\Omega = 0{,}5\,\omega_1\). The bound from item 4 of the theorem still holds, \(20{,}66 \le 4{,}263 \cdot 9{,}632 = 41{,}06\) µm, but it says only that the error is not larger than \(4{,}263\) times the displacement \((\mat R_1\vek F)_{\text{end}} = 9{,}632\) µm that the residual flexibility gives.

The theorem is not wrong here, but the condition \(\Omega^2 \ll \lambda_{\mathrm{N}+1}\) that the correction needs does not hold: the force frequency must be far below the first cut-off mode, and here the error is large. The dependence of the error on the ratio \(\varrho = \Omega/\omega_{\mathrm{N}+1}\) for \(N = 1\) is:

\(\varrho = \Omega/\omega_2\) \(\varrho^2/(1 - \varrho^2)\) exact (µm) mode-acceleration mode-displacement
\(0{,}25\) \(0{,}0667\) \(105{,}39\) \(-0{,}35\) % \(-9{,}49\) %
\(0{,}5\) \(0{,}3333\) \(-21{,}32\) \(+8{,}34\) % \(+53{,}51\) %
\(0{,}75\) \(1{,}2857\) \(6{,}06\) \(-107{,}84\) % \(-266{,}66\) %
\(0{,}9\) \(4{,}2632\) \(23{,}76\) \(-86{,}95\) % \(-127{,}48\) %
\(0{,}99\) \(49{,}25\) \(233{,}55\) \(-98{,}13\) % \(-102{,}25\) %

The correction is good as long as \(\varrho^2\) is below about \(0{,}1\) (\(\varrho \le 0{,}32\)), for bar C with the first mode thus up to \(\Omega = 0{,}95\,\omega_1\). The limit \(0{,}1\) is a convention and not a theorem: it means that in the lowest cut-off mode we miss at most a ninth of its static part (the middle bar of figure 21.6), and whoever needs a smaller error takes a lower limit. At \(\varrho = 0{,}5\) the error is already \(8\) %, and at \(\varrho = 0{,}75\) the mode-acceleration solution (\(-0{,}48\) µm) even has the wrong sign. A cut-off mode that has its own frequency near the force frequency must be kept. With \(N = 2\) at the same force \(\Omega = 0{,}9\,\omega_2\) the mode-acceleration solution gives \(22{,}832\) µm and an error of \(-3{,}92\) % (figure 21.9, grey), since now the first cut-off mode is \(3\) with \(\Omega/\omega_3 = 0{,}537\), \(\Omega^2/(\lambda_3 - \Omega^2) = 0{,}404\) and its static part only \(1{,}688\) µm. We therefore tie the number of kept modes to the force frequency: we keep all modes below \(\Omega\) and as many above it as make \(\varrho^2 = \Omega^2/\lambda_{\mathrm{N}+1}\) of the lowest cut-off mode lie below about \(0{,}1\). For \(N = 2\), \(\varrho^2 = 0{,}537^2 = 0{,}288\) is still above this limit and the error is \(-3{,}92\) %, for \(N = 3\), \(\varrho^2 = \Omega^2/\lambda_4 = 0{,}144\) and the error is \(-1{,}05\) %.

21.1.6 What the correction does not cover

The theorem holds for an undamped system under a harmonic force, and three limitations matter. First, \(\mat K\) must be positive definite so that \(\mat K^{-1}\) exists. A structure in free space (above) has zero eigenvalues and a singular \(\mat K\) by theorem 10.34. A rigid-body mode has no static part, since \(1/\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\) does not exist at \(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}} = 0\): on the axes of displacement against time a free body under a constant force does not stop at some displacement, it accelerates, while the clamped bar stops at the static displacement. So the correction cannot be used in this form. Craig and Kurdila treat this with inertia relief (razbremenitev vztrajnosti, CK §11.6, PDF pp. 371-376), which is only named here. Second, with classical damping the denominator contains \(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}} - \Omega^2 + 2\mathrm{i}\zeta_{\mathrm{r}}\omega_{\mathrm{r}}\Omega\) (theorem 10.72), and the difference \(1/(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}} - \Omega^2 + 2\mathrm{i}\zeta_{\mathrm{r}}\omega_{\mathrm{r}}\Omega) - 1/\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\) is still small compared with \(1/\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\) when \(\Omega^2 \ll \lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\) (there the curve is near the horizontal line), and the static part \(1/\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\) stays the same. For bar C with \(\zeta_{\mathrm{r}} = 0{,}02\) in all modes, \(N = 1\) and \(\Omega = 0{,}5\,\omega_1\) the size of the error of the mode-acceleration solution is \(0{,}249\) % of the amplitude instead of \(0{,}240\) % without damping, and \(0{,}295\) % with \(\zeta_{\mathrm{r}} = 0{,}05\). Damping is treated by chapter 20. Third, for a general time dependence of the force the correction has the same idea, the static solution with the force \(\vek F(t)\) and the accelerations from the modes. The formula is CK equation (11.40) (PDF p. 361) and is not proved here.

The rule of the section in one line: we keep all modes below \(\Omega\) and as many above it as bring \(\Omega^2/\lambda_{\mathrm{N}+1}\) below about \(0{,}1\), and to all the cut-off ones we add their static part \(\mat R_{\mathrm{N}}\vek F\). Section 21.2 poses the same question, how much the cut-off modes contribute, for support motion instead of a force on a coordinate.

21.2 Effective modal mass (efektivna modalna masa)

Section 21.1 answered how much of the response to a force acting on one coordinate is lost when modes are cut off. Here we ask the same question for a load that is not a force on a coordinate but a motion of the support: an earthquake that shakes a building, ground vibration that reaches a machine. Such a load acts on every mass at once, so the answer is different. Which modes receive anything from it at all, and how many modes must we keep to describe the structure under this load? The section shows that every mode receives a "share of mass", that all the shares together give the mass of the structure (theorem 21.9), and that this share is the measure for the number of modes to keep (GR section 2.9.5, PDF p. 128). The measure is proved only for slow motion of the support. At the end of the section two examples show where it stops holding and why. The section runs in order: first the equation of motion in coordinates relative to the support (theorem 21.5), then the participation factor (definition 21.6), the effective modal mass (definition 21.8) with its sum (theorem 21.9), the force on the support (corollary 21.10) and the limits of the measure. The additional mass method, which solves the same task without partitioning the coordinates, is the subject of section 21.3.

21.2.1 The support moves (podlaga se giblje)

The first model is the frame with three floors of chapter 10: each floor has mass \(m = 500\) kg, each storey stiffness \(k = 501\,760\) N/m, the floors move only horizontally and there is no damping. The natural frequencies of the frame with a fixed support are \(f_{\mathrm{r}} = 2{,}2438\), \(6{,}2870\) and \(9{,}0850\) Hz, the natural circular frequencies \(\omega_{\mathrm{r}} = 14{,}098\), \(39{,}502\) and \(57{,}082\) 1/s. The second model is bar C of section 21.1 (steel, \(A = 100\) mm², \(L = 1\) m, sixteen equal elements, clamped at \(x = 0\)), whose mass is \(m_{\mathrm{T}} = \rho A L = 0{,}78\) kg and whose first natural circular frequency is \(\omega_1 = 7877{,}26\) 1/s. The support is the ground for the frame and the clamped node for the bar. Both supports move as a rigid body with prescribed displacement \(u_{\mathrm{g}}(t)\) and acceleration \(\ddot u_{\mathrm{g}}(t)\). The frame has three floors and stands on the ground, which is the support.

We build the figure part by part. The frame stands on the ground, which the support moves to the right by the displacement \(u_{\mathrm{g}}\) and gives the acceleration \(\ddot u_{\mathrm{g}}\). The original position of the axis of the ground is dashed, the motion is measured by the distance \(u_{\mathrm{g}}\). If the frame were completely rigid, all floors would move by the same \(u_{\mathrm{g}}\) and the frame would stand as the grey dashed frame, with the axis that moves with the support. The frame is flexible, so in reality it is the orange one: the columns bend and the floors lag behind the grey frame, the first by \(y_1\), the second by \(y_2\), the third by \(y_3\). Why do they lag? The ground holds only the lower ends of the columns. A floor has mass and by Newton's second law needs a force to accelerate, and only a bent column can give it that force. So the column must bend first, and by that much the floor lags. At a slow ground acceleration of \(1\) m/s² the lags would be \(y_1 = -2{,}99\) mm, \(y_2 = -4{,}98\) mm and \(y_3 = -5{,}98\) mm, in the ratio \(3 : 5 : 6\) in which the figure is drawn: the lowest storey carries the force of three floors, \(3m/k = 2{,}99\) mm per unit acceleration, the middle one of two, the top one of one (num-02-teach.py). The displacement of the third floor relative to the ground is \(y_3\), its displacement from the original axis is \(q_3\), and \(q_3 = u_{\mathrm{g}} + y_3\). Since \(y_3\) is negative, \(q_3\) is smaller than \(u_{\mathrm{g}}\). What pushes the floors? For an observer at rest with respect to the ground, each floor seems to carry an inertia force \(-m\,\ddot u_{\mathrm{g}}\) against the acceleration of the ground, equal on all floors because they have equal masses.

Now the same with matrices. The support displacement \(q_2\) is the displacement of the ground and the components of \(\boldsymbol q_1\) are the displacements of the floors from the original axis. We split the coordinates into a column \(\boldsymbol q_1\) of structure coordinates (three floor displacements for the frame, the displacements of the sixteen free nodes for the bar) and one support displacement \(q_2\) (the ground for the frame, the clamped node for the bar). The index of \(q_2\) counts blocks of coordinates, not floors: \(q_2\) is the support, while the displacement of the third floor in the figure, \(q_3\), is the third component of the column \(\vek q_1\). Section 21.3 will use the same partition. The mass and stiffness matrices are

\[\mat M = \begin{bmatrix} \mat M_{11} & \mat M_{12} \\ \mat M_{21} & M_{22} \end{bmatrix} , \qquad \mat K = \begin{bmatrix} \mat K_{11} & \mat K_{12} \\ \mat K_{21} & K_{22} \end{bmatrix} , \tag{21.7}\]

with \(\mat M_{21} = \mat M_{12}^\T\) and \(\mat K_{21} = \mat K_{12}^\T\). The frame has \(\mat M_{11} = m\,\mat I\), \(\mat M_{12} = \vek 0\), \(M_{22} = 0\) (we do not count the mass of the ground in the structure), \(\mat K_{12} = (-k, 0, 0)^\T\) and \(K_{22} = k\), with

\[\mat K_{11} = k\begin{pmatrix} 2 & -1 & 0 \\ -1 & 2 & -1 \\ 0 & -1 & 1 \end{pmatrix} . \tag{21.8}\]

For the bar \(M_{22} = m_{\mathrm{T}}/48\) (the diagonal entry \(\rho A h_{\mathrm{e}}/3\) of the consistent mass matrix of the element at the wall, with the element length \(h_{\mathrm{e}} = L/16\)) and \(\mat M_{12}\) has the single nonzero entry \(m_{\mathrm{T}}/96\) in the row of the first free node, because the consistent mass matrix (lemma 10.47) couples neighbouring nodes. This coupling will matter: for the frame \(\mat M_{12} = \vek 0\), for the bar it is not.

The motion of the support is a rigid motion. Such a motion is the grey dashed frame: all floors move by the same ground displacement. A displacement of the support by \(1\) moves all structure coordinates by a column \(\vek s\), and the whole column \(\vek r = (\vek s,\ 1)\) has no strain, hence no elastic forces: \(\mat K\,\vek r = \vek 0\), that is

\[\mat K_{11}\,\vek s + \mat K_{12} = \vek 0 , \qquad \mat K_{21}\,\vek s + K_{22} = 0 . \tag{21.9}\]

The frame has \(\vek s = (1, 1, 1)^\T\), the bar \(\vek s = (1, \dots, 1)^\T\), and we check both conditions with the matrices (frame: \(k\,(2 - 1,\ -1 + 2 - 1,\ -1 + 1) + (-k, 0, 0) = \vek 0\), bar: num-02.py, largest deviation \(0\)). In every system where the support holds the structure with a prescribed rigid motion, condition (21.9) holds, because a rigid motion creates no strain energy, \(\vek r^\T\mat K\,\vek r = 0\), and \(\mat K\) is positive semidefinite (lemma 7.16).

Theorem 21.5 Equation of motion relative to the support (gibalna enačba glede na podlago)

Let \(\mat M\) and \(\mat K\) be symmetric matrices, partitioned as in (21.7), with \(\mat M_{11}\) and \(\mat K_{11}\) positive definite (definition 6.27), and let (21.9) hold. Let \(q_2(t) = u_{\mathrm{g}}(t)\) be a twice continuously differentiable prescribed displacement of the support and \(\vek q_1(t)\) a twice differentiable column of structure displacements. Let no other load act on the structure, that is \(\vek F = (\vek 0,\ F_2)\) in the system \(\mat M\ddot{\vek q} + \mat K\,\vek q = \vek F\) (theorem 10.3 without damping) with \(\vek q = (\vek q_1,\ q_2)\). Put

\[\vek h = \mat M_{11}\,\vek s + \mat M_{12} , \qquad \boldsymbol y = \vek q_1 - \vek s\,u_{\mathrm{g}} . \tag{21.10}\]

We call \(\vek h\) the inertia column (vztrajnostni stolpec), and \(\boldsymbol y\) is the displacement of the structure relative to the support. Then \(\vek q\) satisfies the structure rows of this system exactly when \(\boldsymbol y\) satisfies

\[\mat M_{11}\,\ddot{\boldsymbol y} + \mat K_{11}\,\boldsymbol y = -\vek h\,\ddot u_{\mathrm{g}} . \tag{21.11}\]

For the frame \(\vek h = m\,\vek s = (m, m, m)^\T\), so each floor carries the load \(-m\,\ddot u_{\mathrm{g}}\), as in figure 21.11.

Proof

We must show that the first row of the system turns into (21.11) under the substitution \(\vek q_1 = \boldsymbol y + \vek s\,u_{\mathrm{g}}\). The substitution is invertible, so the converse holds too.

  1. The first row of the system, without load, is \(\mat M_{11}\ddot{\vek q}_1 + \mat M_{12}\,\ddot q_2 + \mat K_{11}\vek q_1 + \mat K_{12}\,q_2 = \vek 0\).
  2. Insert \(\vek q_1 = \boldsymbol y + \vek s\,u_{\mathrm{g}}\), that is the displacement from the original axis as the sum of the displacement of the ground and the lag, and \(q_2 = u_{\mathrm{g}}\) (the column \(\vek s\) is constant, so \(\ddot{\vek q}_1 = \ddot{\boldsymbol y} + \vek s\,\ddot u_{\mathrm{g}}\)): \(\mat M_{11}\ddot{\boldsymbol y} + \mat K_{11}\boldsymbol y + (\mat M_{11}\vek s + \mat M_{12})\,\ddot u_{\mathrm{g}} + (\mat K_{11}\vek s + \mat K_{12})\,u_{\mathrm{g}} = \vek 0\).
  3. By the first condition (21.9) the last term is zero (the grey frame is moved without bending the columns, so without elastic forces), and \(\mat M_{11}\vek s + \mat M_{12} = \vek h\) is (21.10). What remains is (21.11).
  4. For the frame \(\mat M_{12} = \vek 0\) and \(\mat M_{11} = m\,\mat I\), so \(\vek h = m\,\vek s\), the same force on every floor.

Source: The partition into structure and support and the load by inertia forces follow GR section 2.9.4 (PDF p. 126, text read, equations (2.179)-(2.183) are images). The theorem and the proof are ours, the derivation is a direct consequence of theorem 10.3.

The column \(\vek h\) has an interpretation that we need later. If the whole system moves with a rigid acceleration \(1\) (the column \(\vek r\)), the forces that cause this acceleration are \(\mat M\,\vek r\), and the inertia forces are \(-\mat M\,\vek r\). The upper block of the column \(\mat M\,\vek r\), the rows of the structure, is \(\mat M_{11}\vek s + \mat M_{12} = \vek h\). So \(\vek h\) is the column of forces with which we would have to hold the structure if we moved it rigidly with acceleration \(1\). For bar C, \(h_{\mathrm{i}}\) is therefore the sum of row \(i\) of the full mass matrix, which is \(\rho A h_{\mathrm{e}}\) at every node except the last, where it is \(\rho A h_{\mathrm{e}}/2\). Motion of the support is thus, for the structure, the same as the load \(-\vek h\,\ddot u_{\mathrm{g}}\) with a fixed support. For the frame these are the forces on the floors, each of size \(m\) per unit acceleration.

The theorem rests on three assumptions, and each leaves a trace in the result.

  1. The support is rigid: all points where the structure is held have the same displacement \(u_{\mathrm{g}}\), like one line of ground. For the frame and bar C this holds because there is a single place of attachment (one foundation slab, one clamped node). It does not hold for a structure with distant supports that each move in their own way, for example a long bridge or a pipeline. Then \(q_2\) is a column and \(\vek s\) a matrix (GR section 2.9.4, PDF p. 126). Effect of the assumption: the load is a single column \(-\vek h\,\ddot u_{\mathrm{g}}\) and each mode will get one number, not one for every support. What this leaves out is shown by bar C if it were clamped at its other end too: ends that move \(0{,}1\) mm apart stretch the bar of length \(1\) m by \(\varepsilon = 10^{-4}\) without any acceleration, which is the stress \(E\varepsilon = 19{,}6\) MPa for \(E = 196\) GPa, and the single column \(\vek h\) knows nothing of this load.
  2. There is no damping. For the question of this section this is right, because the shares of mass will depend only on \(\mat K_{11}\), \(\mat M_{11}\) and \(\vek h\), not on damping. Viscous damping would add a term \(\mat C_{11}\dot{\boldsymbol y}\) if \(\mat C\,\vek r = \vek 0\), that is if the dampers do not feel the rigid motion (theorem 10.3). The assumption fails right at a natural frequency, where the undamped support force grows beyond all bounds. The effect with a number is in section 21.2.4: at a damping ratio of \(0{,}02\) the support force changes by at most \(1{,}03\) % at the frequencies \(0{,}5\,\omega_1\), \(1{,}5\,\omega_1\) and \(0{,}9\,\omega_2\), while at \(0{,}99\,\omega_1\) it drops from \(69\,046\) to \(31\,033\) kg. Damping itself is the subject of chapter 20. In figure 21.15 this is at the vertical lines of the natural frequencies, where the curve of the undamped force runs off to infinity.
  3. The displacements are small and the structure is linear (theorem 10.3). So we may split the motion into the rigid motion and the lag, and later add up modes. The linear model leaves out that a floor also drops when the columns bend: a column of length \(\ell = 1\) m (chapter 10) with the lag \(v\) at its top shortens its vertical projection by \(\tfrac35\,v^2/\ell\), for a slow ground acceleration of \(1\) m/s² and \(v = 2{,}99\) mm by \(0{,}0054\) mm, which is \(0{,}18\) % of the lag and grows in proportion to it. For a frame that an earthquake damages permanently linearity no longer holds, and the section says nothing about it.

21.2.2 The participation factor (faktor udeležbe)

Equation (21.11) is the equation of theorem 10.3 with the load \(-\vek h\,\ddot u_{\mathrm{g}}\), so we decouple it with the modes of the pair \((\mat K_{11}, \mat M_{11})\) (modal matrix \(\mat\Phi\), definition 10.23). The load on mode \(r\) is its projection on that mode. For the frame the load is the same force on every floor, which we project on the shape of each mode.

Definition 21.6 Participation factor (faktor udeležbe)

Let \(\mat K_{11}\), \(\mat M_{11}\) and \(\vek h\) be as in theorem 21.5 and let \(\boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}\), \(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}} = \omega_{\mathrm{r}}^2\) (\(r = 1, \dots, n_1\)) be the eigenpairs of the pair \((\mat K_{11}, \mat M_{11})\), \(\mat M_{11}\)-normalized (theorem 10.21). Figure 21.12 shows the mode shape and the load \(\vek h\) as two rows of numbers on the floors. The participation factor of mode \(r\) is the number

\[\Gamma_{\mathrm{r}} = \boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}^\T\,\vek h . \tag{21.12}\]

Source: GR (2.186), PDF p. 127, the equation is an image. The name is GR's ("modal participation factors", PDF p. 127). The choice of \(\vek h\) instead of \(\mat M_{11}\vek s\) and the symbol \(\Gamma_{\mathrm{r}}\) for our partition are ours.

The name is literal: \(\Gamma_{\mathrm{r}}\) tells how strongly the support motion excites mode \(r\). In the first mode all displacements are on the same side and \(\Gamma_1\) is large, in the second and third they partly cancel, so \(\Gamma_2\) and \(\Gamma_3\) are small. Since \(\boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}\) is normalized by \(\boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}^\T\mat M_{11}\boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{r}} = 1\) and \(\vek h\) is in kg, \(\Gamma_{\mathrm{r}}\) has the unit kg\(^{1/2}\). Its sign depends on the sign we chose for the mode, since \(-\boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}\) serves equally well. The symbol \(\Gamma\) here means the participation factor and has nothing to do with the broken line \(\Gamma\) of chapter 4, and \(\boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}\) is a mode here, not the nodal rotation \(\varphi_{\mathrm{i}}\) of chapter 12.

Lemma 21.7 Modal equation under support motion (modalna enačba pri gibanju podlage)

Let the hypotheses of theorem 21.5 hold, \(\mat\Phi\) the modal matrix of the pair \((\mat K_{11}, \mat M_{11})\), \(\boldsymbol\eta = \mat\Phi^\T\mat M_{11}\,\boldsymbol y\) the modal coordinates relative to the support (definition 10.27) and \(\Gamma_{\mathrm{r}}\) as in (21.12). Each equation is one pendulum on the common ground. Then for \(r = 1, \dots, n_1\)

\[\ddot\eta_{\mathrm{r}} + \lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\,\eta_{\mathrm{r}} = -\Gamma_{\mathrm{r}}\,\ddot u_{\mathrm{g}} , \qquad \boldsymbol y = \sum_{\mathrm{r}=1}^{n_1}\boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}\,\eta_{\mathrm{r}} . \tag{21.13}\]
Proof

We must show that the decoupling of theorem 10.3 also holds for the load \(-\vek h\,\ddot u_{\mathrm{g}}\) and that the right-hand side of the \(r\)-th equation is \(-\Gamma_{\mathrm{r}}\,\ddot u_{\mathrm{g}}\).

  1. By lemma 10.24, \(\mat\Phi^{-1} = \mat\Phi^\T\mat M_{11}\), so \(\boldsymbol y = \mat\Phi\,\boldsymbol\eta\) (expansion theorem, corollary 10.22).
  2. Insert \(\boldsymbol y = \mat\Phi\,\boldsymbol\eta\) in (21.11) and multiply from the left by \(\mat\Phi^\T\): \(\mat\Phi^\T\mat M_{11}\mat\Phi\,\ddot{\boldsymbol\eta} + \mat\Phi^\T\mat K_{11}\mat\Phi\,\boldsymbol\eta = -\mat\Phi^\T\vek h\,\ddot u_{\mathrm{g}}\).
  3. By lemma 10.24, \(\mat\Phi^\T\mat M_{11}\mat\Phi = \mat I\) and \(\mat\Phi^\T\mat K_{11}\mat\Phi = \mathrm{diag}(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}})\), and the \(r\)-th component of the column \(\mat\Phi^\T\vek h\) is \(\boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}^\T\vek h = \Gamma_{\mathrm{r}}\). Row \(r\) is (21.13).

Source: The proof is not from a source. It is the same step as in the proof of the decoupling theorem (theorem 10.3 and lemma 10.24), with the load \(-\vek h\,\ddot u_{\mathrm{g}}\).

So each mode is a one-degree-of-freedom equation driven by the ground acceleration multiplied by \(\Gamma_{\mathrm{r}}\). In figure 21.12 this is one pendulum for each mode. A mode with \(\Gamma_{\mathrm{r}} = 0\) does not feel the support motion at all. For the frame the modes, normalized by \(\boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}^\T\mat M_{11}\boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{r}} = 1\), are in kg\(^{-1/2}\):

\(r\) \(\varphi_{\mathrm{r},1}\) \(\varphi_{\mathrm{r},2}\) \(\varphi_{\mathrm{r},3}\) \(\Gamma_{\mathrm{r}}\) (kg\(^{1/2}\))
1 \(0{,}014668\) \(0{,}026431\) \(0{,}032959\) \(37{,}0286\)
2 \(-0{,}032959\) \(-0{,}014668\) \(0{,}026431\) \(-10{,}5979\)
3 \(-0{,}026431\) \(0{,}032959\) \(-0{,}014668\) \(-4{,}0700\)

We draw the table in the top row of the figure. For each mode the grey dashed vertical line is the frame at rest with its three floors, and the orange line is the mode shape, in which every floor is displaced by its component \(\varphi_{\mathrm{r},\mathrm{i}}\). The displacements are measured by the blue distances, written in \(10^{-3}\) kg\(^{-1/2}\), positive to the right. The blackwhite arrows are the column \(\vek h = (m, m, m)^\T\): the load is equal and equally directed on all floors. By (21.12) the participation factor is the sum of the products of arrow and displacement, \(\Gamma_{\mathrm{r}} = m\,(\varphi_{\mathrm{r},1} + \varphi_{\mathrm{r},2} + \varphi_{\mathrm{r},3})\) with \(m = 500\) kg:

\[\begin{aligned} \Gamma_1 &= 500\,(14{,}668 + 26{,}431 + 32{,}959)\cdot 10^{-3} = 37{,}03 , \\ \Gamma_2 &= 500\,(-32{,}959 - 14{,}668 + 26{,}431)\cdot 10^{-3} = -10{,}60 , \\ \Gamma_3 &= 500\,(-26{,}431 + 32{,}959 - 14{,}668)\cdot 10^{-3} = -4{,}07 . \end{aligned}\]

In the first mode all three displacements are on the same side, so they add up to \(37{,}03\). In the second the two lower floors are displaced to the left and the top one to the right, in the third the sides alternate, so the displacements mostly cancel and what remains is \(-10{,}60\) and \(-4{,}07\). A uniform load thus excites above all the shape that leans to one side as a whole. The bottom row of the figure, the three oscillators on the common ground with the sum of the masses, is explained in section 21.2.4. The computation is in num-02.py.

21.2.3 The effective modal mass

How much of the mass of the structure does a single mode cover? To answer we need a number with the unit of mass that does not depend on the choice of sign and scale of the mode. The participation factor \(\Gamma_{\mathrm{r}}\) has the unit kg\(^{1/2}\) and depends on the sign, but its square has the unit kg. The square of the participation factor is the height of a column in figure 21.13, measured in percent of the total mass.

Definition 21.8 Effective modal mass (efektivna modalna masa)

Let \(\Gamma_{\mathrm{r}}\) be the participation factors (definition 21.6). In figure 21.13 this is the column of the mode. The effective modal mass of mode \(r\) is

\[m_{\mathrm{r}}^{\mathrm{ef}} = \Gamma_{\mathrm{r}}^2 = \big(\boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}^\T\vek h\big)^2 . \tag{21.14}\]

Source: GR (2.187)-(2.191), PDF pp. 127-128, the notion is GR's ("effective modal mass", Imbert 1984, Preumont 1994). The expression \(\Gamma_{\mathrm{r}}^2\) is our definition, GR writes the sum over modes.

The name is so because \(m_{\mathrm{r}}^{\mathrm{ef}}\) tells how much mass mode \(r\) actually contributes ("effectively") to the reaction of the support in slow motion. This is shown by corollary 21.10 (item 3): the support force per unit ground acceleration, computed with modes \(1\) to \(N\) only, tends to the sum \(\sum_{\mathrm{r} \le \mathrm{N}} m_{\mathrm{r}}^{\mathrm{ef}}\) as the support oscillates more and more slowly, and for some structures the mass felt by the support itself is added to it (theorem 21.9). The sign of the mode disappears, since \(\Gamma_{\mathrm{r}}^2 \ge 0\) and does not change under \(-\boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}\). If the mode is not normalized by \(\boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}^\T\mat M_{11}\boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{r}} = 1\), the mass stays the same in the form \((\boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}^\T\vek h)^2/(\boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}^\T\mat M_{11}\boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{r}})\). For the frame \(m_{\mathrm{r}}^{\mathrm{ef}} = 1371{,}12\), \(112{,}32\) and \(16{,}57\) kg, that is \(91{,}41\), \(7{,}49\) and \(1{,}10\) % of the mass \(m_\Sigma = 3m = 1500\) kg (figure 21.13, bars on the left). The same three masses are the squares of the three oscillators in figure 21.12, and section 21.2.4 shows that these are more than a figure of speech.

Why would the sum of these numbers give the mass of the structure? By the expansion in modes every displacement of the structure is a sum of modes, and if none is cut off, no mass can stay unaccounted for. The exact statement is the next theorem, in which one more quantity appears, the one felt by the support itself. In figure 21.13 this is seen on the cumulative sum, which for the frame reaches \(100\) %.

Theorem 21.9 Sum of effective modal masses (vsota efektivnih modalnih mas)

Let the hypotheses of theorem 21.5 hold and \(\mat M\) be positive semidefinite. Figure 21.13 shows where we are heading: the sum of the shares reaches \(100\) % for the frame and stays below it for the bar, where the gap is the mass at the support. Put the total mass \(m_\Sigma = \vek r^\T\mat M\,\vek r\) and the mass at the support (the part of the structure's mass attached to the support, which moves with it)

\[m_{\mathrm{S}} = M_{22} - \mat M_{21}\,\mat M_{11}^{-1}\mat M_{12} . \tag{21.15}\]

Then:

  1. \(m_{\mathrm{S}} \ge 0\), and \(m_{\mathrm{S}} = 0\) when \(\mat M_{12} = \vek 0\) and \(M_{22} = 0\). For the frame the mass at the support is zero, for bar C the gap to \(100\) % is larger than zero.
  2. The sum over all modes (cumulative sum) is
    \[\sum_{\mathrm{r}=1}^{n_1} m_{\mathrm{r}}^{\mathrm{ef}} = \vek h^\T\mat M_{11}^{-1}\vek h = m_\Sigma - m_{\mathrm{S}} . \tag{21.16}\]
Proof

We must show that the sum of the squares of the participation factors equals \(\vek h^\T\mat M_{11}^{-1}\vek h\) and that this expression can be written with \(m_\Sigma\) and \(m_{\mathrm{S}}\).

  1. By lemma 10.24, \(\mat\Phi^{-1} = \mat\Phi^\T\mat M_{11}\), so \(\mat\Phi\,\mat\Phi^\T\mat M_{11} = \mat I\) and \(\mat\Phi\,\mat\Phi^\T = \mat M_{11}^{-1}\) (multiply by \(\mat M_{11}^{-1}\) from the right).
  2. The sum is \(\sum_{\mathrm{r}} \Gamma_{\mathrm{r}}^2 = \sum_{\mathrm{r}}\vek h^\T\boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}\,\boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}^\T\vek h = \vek h^\T\,\mat\Phi\mat\Phi^\T\,\vek h = \vek h^\T\mat M_{11}^{-1}\vek h\) by step 1.
  3. Insert \(\vek h = \mat M_{11}\vek s + \mat M_{12}\) into \(\mat M_{11}^{-1}\vek h = \vek s + \mat M_{11}^{-1}\mat M_{12}\). So \(\vek h^\T\mat M_{11}^{-1}\vek h = \vek h^\T\vek s + \vek h^\T\mat M_{11}^{-1}\mat M_{12}\), and the last term is \((\vek s^\T\mat M_{11} + \mat M_{21})\,\mat M_{11}^{-1}\mat M_{12} = \vek s^\T\mat M_{12} + \mat M_{21}\mat M_{11}^{-1}\mat M_{12}\).
  4. The total mass is \(m_\Sigma = \vek r^\T\mat M\,\vek r = \vek s^\T\mat M_{11}\vek s + \vek s^\T\mat M_{12} + \mat M_{21}\vek s + M_{22} = \vek s^\T\vek h + \mat M_{21}\vek s + M_{22}\), so \(\vek s^\T\vek h = m_\Sigma - \mat M_{21}\vek s - M_{22}\).
  5. Insert step 4 in step 3 and use \(\vek s^\T\mat M_{12} = \mat M_{21}\vek s\) (symmetry): \(\vek h^\T\mat M_{11}^{-1}\vek h = m_\Sigma - \mat M_{21}\vek s - M_{22} + \mat M_{21}\vek s + \mat M_{21}\mat M_{11}^{-1}\mat M_{12} = m_\Sigma - m_{\mathrm{S}}\). This is item 2.
  6. Let \(\vek v = (-\mat M_{11}^{-1}\mat M_{12},\ 1)\). Expanding, \(\vek v^\T\mat M\,\vek v = \mat M_{21}\mat M_{11}^{-1}\mat M_{12} - 2\,\mat M_{21}\mat M_{11}^{-1}\mat M_{12} + M_{22} = m_{\mathrm{S}}\). Since \(\mat M\) is positive semidefinite, \(m_{\mathrm{S}} \ge 0\). For \(\mat M_{12} = \vek 0\) and \(M_{22} = 0\) equation (21.15) gives \(m_{\mathrm{S}} = 0\). This is item 1.

Source: The sum over modes and the notion \(m_{\mathrm{S}}\) ("the part of the structural mass attached to the support") follow GR section 2.9.5 (PDF pp. 127-128, text read, (2.188)-(2.193) are images). GR neglects the last term of its equation (2.189) as second order in \(\mat M_{12}\). Here that term is kept and the sum is exact. The proof is ours.

The sum (21.16) is simple: if all modes are kept, the effective masses add up to the mass of the structure, except the mass at the support. For the frame \(\mat M_{12} = \vek 0\) and \(M_{22} = 0\), so \(m_{\mathrm{S}} = 0\) and the sum is exactly \(m_\Sigma = 1500\) kg: \(1371{,}1192 + 112{,}3155 + 16{,}5653 = 1500{,}0000\) kg (num-02.py). In figure 21.13 this is the cumulative sum of the frame, which reaches \(100\) %.

We read the figure from the left. The vertical axis shows percent of the total mass, one grey horizontal line is at \(90\) %, the other at \(100\) %. On the left is the frame, its horizontal axis counts the modes \(r = 1, 2, 3\). The three bars are the shares \(91{,}4\), \(7{,}5\) and \(1{,}1\) %, and the cumulative sum (\(91{,}4\), \(98{,}9\), \(100{,}0\) %) reaches \(100\) % at the third mode. One mode already covers \(91{,}4\) %, which exceeds the lower limit of the measure (\(90\) %), on the measure at the end of the section. On the right is bar C with modes \(1\) to \(16\) on its own horizontal axis. Its sixteen bars fall quickly: the first mode \(81{,}06\) % of the mass \(m_{\mathrm{T}}\), the second \(9{,}01\), the third \(3{,}24\), the fourth \(1{,}65\) and the fifth \(0{,}99\) %, cumulatively \(81{,}06\), \(90{,}06\), \(93{,}30\), \(94{,}95\) and \(95{,}95\) %. The first ten modes give \(97{,}85\) %. The sum of all sixteen is \(98{,}20\) %, the orange dashed line, and the cumulative sum does not exceed this line however many modes we take.

Why does the bar not stop at \(100\) %? This is the first near miss of the theorem. The bar has a consistent mass matrix, in which the clamped node has the diagonal entry \(M_{22} = m_{\mathrm{T}}/48 = 2{,}08\) % of the mass and is coupled with the mass element of the first free node. The computation by (21.15) gives \(m_{\mathrm{S}}/m_{\mathrm{T}} = 0{,}018042\), which by theorem 21.9 is exactly the difference \(100 - 98{,}196 = 1{,}804\) %, the gap between the orange dashed line and the \(100\) % line. This much mass is felt by the support itself: the support has a prescribed acceleration \(\ddot u_{\mathrm{g}}\) whatever the structure does, and this part of the mass enters no modal equation (21.13). What would we get if we left out \(\mat M_{12}\)? With \(\vek h' = \mat M_{11}\vek s\) (inertia forces from the motion of the structure only, without the coupling to the support) we would get \(80{,}80\) % for the first mode (instead of \(81{,}06\) %) and the sum \(95{,}83\) % (instead of \(98{,}20\) %). Step 2 of the proof of the theorem explains the difference: the sum is then \(\vek h'^\T\mat M_{11}^{-1}\vek h' = \vek s^\T\mat M_{11}\vek s = 0{,}9583\,m_{\mathrm{T}}\), the mass of the free nodes without the coupling to the support, and not \(m_\Sigma - m_{\mathrm{S}} = 0{,}9820\,m_{\mathrm{T}}\). For the frame with point masses there is no such error, since \(\mat M_{12} = \vek 0\).

We can compare the values for bar C with the continuous bar (theorem 13.24, case (b)) in figure 21.14. On each of the three axes the bar lies from the clamp at \(x = 0\) to the free end at \(x = L\). Its modes are \(\sin k_{\mathrm{r}} x\) with \(k_{\mathrm{r}} = (2r - 1)\pi/(2L)\), drawn above the axes for \(r = 1, 2, 3\): they are zero at the clamp and have a crest at the free end. Since \(\rho A\int_0^L \sin^2 k_{\mathrm{r}} x\,\mathrm dx = \rho A L/2\), the normalized mode is \(\sqrt{2/(\rho A L)}\,\sin k_{\mathrm{r}} x\). The inertia load of the continuous bar is uniform, \(\rho A\) per unit length, just as the arrows of the frame are equal on all floors. So the analogous participation factor is \(\rho A\) times the area under the graph of the normalized mode, \(\Gamma_{\mathrm{r}} = \rho A\int_0^L\sqrt{2/(\rho AL)}\sin k_{\mathrm{r}} x\,\mathrm dx\).

Areas above the axis count positive, areas below it negative. Pairs of equal areas of opposite sign cancel, and exactly one quarter wave of width \(L/(2r - 1)\) is left, whose area is \(1/k_{\mathrm{r}}\). The computation confirms it: \(\int_0^L \sin k_{\mathrm{r}} x\,\mathrm dx = (1 - \cos k_{\mathrm{r}} L)/k_{\mathrm{r}} = 1/k_{\mathrm{r}}\), since \(\cos k_{\mathrm{r}} L = 0\). So \(\Gamma_{\mathrm{r}} = \sqrt{2\rho A/L}\,/k_{\mathrm{r}}\) and the effective mass is

\[\Gamma_{\mathrm{r}}^2 = \frac{2\rho A}{L\,k_{\mathrm{r}}^2} = \frac{8\rho A L}{(2r-1)^2\pi^2} .\]

The factor \((2r - 1)^2\) in the denominator is the square of the number of quarter waves on the bar: a higher mode has more areas that cancel and a narrower quarter that is left.

For \(r = 1, \dots, 5\) the formula gives \(0{,}81057\), \(0{,}09006\), \(0{,}03242\), \(0{,}01654\) and \(0{,}01001\) of the mass \(m_{\mathrm{T}}\), and bar C has \(0{,}81057\), \(0{,}09006\), \(0{,}03240\), \(0{,}01650\) and \(0{,}00994\). The first three pairs are the numbers to the right of the axes. The first two agree to five decimal places, then the difference grows: \(0{,}06\) % for the third, \(0{,}23\) % for the fourth and \(0{,}64\) % for the fifth mode. It grows as fewer and fewer elements fall on one half wave of the mode: the sixteen elements of bar C cover \(2r - 1\) quarter waves, that is \(32/(2r - 1)\) elements per half wave, from \(32\) for the first to \(3{,}6\) for the fifth mode, and a line that is straight between the nodes follows the sine the worse, the fewer pieces it has. This is a comparison of two computations and not a proof that the discrete value converges to the continuous one.

21.2.4 The force on the support (sila na podlago)

The effective mass tells how much mass the kept modes cover when the support moves slowly. What about faster motion? The answer is in the force that the structure demands from the support. This force matters in itself, since by Newton's third law it is the opposite of the force with which the structure loads the support (for a building, the foundation). Let \(F\) be the force that the support must give to the structure, that is the support row of the system \(\mat M\ddot{\vek q} + \mat K\,\vek q = \vek F\), so \(F = \mat M_{21}\ddot{\vek q}_1 + M_{22}\,\ddot q_2 + \mat K_{21}\vek q_1 + K_{22}\,q_2\).
