For a harmonic ground acceleration \(\ddot u_{\mathrm{g}} = \mathrm{Re}(A\,\mathrm e^{\mathrm i\Omega t})\) this force in the harmonic response is \(\mathrm{Re}\big(R(\Omega)\,A\,\mathrm e^{\mathrm i\Omega t}\big)\) with a number \(R(\Omega)\) in kg, which we get as follows. For the frame this is the blackwhite curve in figure 21.15.

Corollary 21.10 Support force by modes (sila na podlago po načinih)

Let the hypotheses of theorem 21.5 hold, \(\mat M\) positive semidefinite, \(\ddot u_{\mathrm{g}} = \mathrm{Re}(A\,\mathrm e^{\mathrm i\Omega t})\), \(\Omega > 0\) and \(\Omega^2 \ne \lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\) for all \(r\). Such a response is the exact curve in figure 21.15, which has poles at the natural frequencies. Let \(\vek q_1 = \mathrm{Re}(\boldsymbol Q_1\,\mathrm e^{\mathrm i\Omega t})\) be the harmonic solution for \(u_{\mathrm{g}} = \mathrm{Re}(-A\,\mathrm e^{\mathrm i\Omega t}/\Omega^2)\) (without free vibration, which does not decay without damping, and without the part \(a + bt\) of the support displacement that the acceleration leaves open: it is a rigid motion, which does not change the force) and \(F = \mathrm{Re}(R\,A\,\mathrm e^{\mathrm i\Omega t})\) the support force. Then:

  1. The support force (blackwhite curve) is
    \[R(\Omega) = m_\Sigma + \sum_{\mathrm{r}=1}^{n_1} m_{\mathrm{r}}^{\mathrm{ef}}\,\frac{\Omega^2}{\lambda_{\mathrm{r}} - \Omega^2} = m_{\mathrm{S}} + \sum_{\mathrm{r}=1}^{n_1} m_{\mathrm{r}}^{\mathrm{ef}}\,\frac{\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}}{\lambda_{\mathrm{r}} - \Omega^2} . \tag{21.17}\]
  2. Let \(N < n_1\). If we keep only modes \(1\) to \(N\), the two approximations (the dashed orange and the blue curve) are
    \[R_{\mathrm{N}}^{\mathrm{nač}} = m_{\mathrm{S}} + \sum_{\mathrm{r}=1}^{N} m_{\mathrm{r}}^{\mathrm{ef}}\,\frac{\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}}{\lambda_{\mathrm{r}} - \Omega^2} , \qquad R_{\mathrm{N}}^{\mathrm{pop}} = m_\Sigma + \sum_{\mathrm{r}=1}^{N} m_{\mathrm{r}}^{\mathrm{ef}}\,\frac{\Omega^2}{\lambda_{\mathrm{r}} - \Omega^2} , \tag{21.18}\]
    the first with the modes (and the mass at the support), the second with the modes and a static remainder, which we get with the total mass.
  3. As \(\Omega \to 0\), \(R \to m_\Sigma\) and \(R_{\mathrm{N}}^{\mathrm{pop}} \to m_\Sigma\), while \(R_{\mathrm{N}}^{\mathrm{nač}} \to m_{\mathrm{S}} + \sum_{\mathrm{r} \le \mathrm{N}} m_{\mathrm{r}}^{\mathrm{ef}} = m_\Sigma - \mu_{\mathrm{N}}\) with the missing mass \(\mu_{\mathrm{N}} = \sum_{\mathrm{r} > \mathrm{N}} m_{\mathrm{r}}^{\mathrm{ef}}\). In figure 21.15 at the left edge the exact curve and the blue one meet the static value, while the orange one stays below it.
  4. If \(\Omega^2 < \lambda_{\mathrm{N}+1}\) (to the left of the next natural frequency), then
    \[0 \le R - R_{\mathrm{N}}^{\mathrm{pop}} \le \frac{\Omega^2}{\lambda_{\mathrm{N}+1} - \Omega^2}\,\mu_{\mathrm{N}} , \qquad R - R_{\mathrm{N}}^{\mathrm{nač}} = \sum_{\mathrm{r} > \mathrm{N}} m_{\mathrm{r}}^{\mathrm{ef}}\,\frac{\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}}{\lambda_{\mathrm{r}} - \Omega^2} \ge \mu_{\mathrm{N}} . \tag{21.19}\]
Proof

We must show that computing the force in the harmonic response gives (21.17), then truncate only the sum and estimate the remainder.

  1. The harmonic solution has \(q_2 = u_{\mathrm{g}}\), so the amplitude of the support displacement is \(U = -A/\Omega^2\), and \(\boldsymbol Q_1 = \boldsymbol Y + \vek s\,U\) with \(\boldsymbol Y\) the amplitude of the vector \(\boldsymbol y\). From (21.11), \((\mat K_{11} - \Omega^2\mat M_{11})\,\boldsymbol Y = -\vek h\,A\). The matrix \(\mat K_{11} - \Omega^2\mat M_{11}\) is invertible because \(\Omega^2\) is not an eigenvalue, so \(\boldsymbol Y = -\mat H\,\vek h\,A\) with \(\mat H = (\mat K_{11} - \Omega^2\mat M_{11})^{-1}\).
  2. By the support row, the amplitude of the force is \(R\,A = (\mat K_{21} - \Omega^2\mat M_{21})\boldsymbol Q_1 + (K_{22} - \Omega^2 M_{22})\,U\). Insert \(\boldsymbol Q_1\) and use \(\mat K_{21}\vek s + K_{22} = 0\) from (21.9): \(R\,A = (\mat K_{21} - \Omega^2\mat M_{21})\boldsymbol Y - \Omega^2\,(\mat M_{21}\vek s + M_{22})\,U\).
  3. By symmetry and the first condition (21.9), \(\mat K_{21} = -\vek s^\T\mat K_{11}\), and by (21.10), \(\mat M_{21} = \vek h^\T - \vek s^\T\mat M_{11}\). So \(\mat K_{21} - \Omega^2\mat M_{21} = -\vek s^\T(\mat K_{11} - \Omega^2\mat M_{11}) - \Omega^2\vek h^\T\).
  4. By steps 1 and 3, \((\mat K_{21} - \Omega^2\mat M_{21})\boldsymbol Y = \vek s^\T\vek h\,A + \Omega^2\,\vek h^\T\mat H\,\vek h\,A\).
  5. With \(U = -A/\Omega^2\) and steps 2 and 4, \(R = \vek s^\T\vek h + \mat M_{21}\vek s + M_{22} + \Omega^2\vek h^\T\mat H\,\vek h\). We expressed the first three terms by \(m_\Sigma\) in step 4 of the proof of theorem 21.9, so \(R = m_\Sigma + \Omega^2\vek h^\T\mat H\,\vek h\).
  6. By lemma 10.24, \(\mat K_{11} - \Omega^2\mat M_{11} = \mat M_{11}\mat\Phi\,(\mat\Lambda - \Omega^2\mat I)\,\mat\Phi^\T\mat M_{11}\) (as in step 2 of the proof of lemma 10.69), the diagonal entries \(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}} - \Omega^2\) are nonzero and \(\mat H = \mat\Phi\,(\mat\Lambda - \Omega^2\mat I)^{-1}\mat\Phi^\T\). Hence \(\vek h^\T\mat H\,\vek h = \sum_{\mathrm{r}}\Gamma_{\mathrm{r}}^2/(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}} - \Omega^2)\) and the first expression of (21.17) follows.
  7. The second expression: \(\Omega^2/(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}} - \Omega^2) = \lambda_{\mathrm{r}}/(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}} - \Omega^2) - 1\) and \(m_\Sigma - \sum_{\mathrm{r}} m_{\mathrm{r}}^{\mathrm{ef}} = m_{\mathrm{S}}\) (theorem 21.9). This is item 1.
  8. As \(\Omega \to 0\) every term \(\Omega^2/(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}} - \Omega^2)\) of the sum in (21.17) tends to \(0\), so \(R \to m_\Sigma\) and \(R_{\mathrm{N}}^{\mathrm{pop}} \to m_\Sigma\). The term \(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}/(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}} - \Omega^2) \to 1\), so \(R_{\mathrm{N}}^{\mathrm{nač}} \to m_{\mathrm{S}} + \sum_{\mathrm{r}\le \mathrm{N}} m_{\mathrm{r}}^{\mathrm{ef}} = m_\Sigma - \mu_{\mathrm{N}}\) by theorem 21.9. This is item 3.
  9. By (21.17) and (21.18) the difference \(R - R_{\mathrm{N}}^{\mathrm{pop}}\) is the sum \(\sum_{\mathrm{r}>\mathrm{N}} m_{\mathrm{r}}^{\mathrm{ef}}\,\Omega^2/(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}} - \Omega^2)\), and for \(r > N\) we have \(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}} \ge \lambda_{\mathrm{N}+1} > \Omega^2\), so \(0 \le \Omega^2/(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}} - \Omega^2) \le \Omega^2/(\lambda_{\mathrm{N}+1} - \Omega^2)\). Multiplying by \(m_{\mathrm{r}}^{\mathrm{ef}} \ge 0\) and summing gives the first inequality of (21.19). The difference \(R - R_{\mathrm{N}}^{\mathrm{nač}}\) is the sum \(\sum_{\mathrm{r}>\mathrm{N}} m_{\mathrm{r}}^{\mathrm{ef}}\,\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}/(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}} - \Omega^2)\), and \(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}/(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}} - \Omega^2) \ge 1\) for \(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}} > \Omega^2\). This is item 4, and item 2 is a definition. In figure 21.15 this is the gap between the exact and the blue curve.

Source: The proof is ours. The form of the sum with the mass \(m_{\mathrm{S}}\) and with the mass completed to \(m_\Sigma\) follows GR section 2.9.4-2.9.5 (reactions on the support, PDF pp. 126-128, equations are images). The approximation \(R_{\mathrm{N}}^{\mathrm{pop}}\) is the same idea as the correction in theorem 21.4.

The approximation \(R_{\mathrm{N}}^{\mathrm{pop}}\) is nothing new: it is the same correction, with the dynamic part of the cut-off modes neglected, as in theorem 21.4, only that the static part of the cut-off modes is now simply the whole remaining mass \(\mu_{\mathrm{N}}\). The first approximation, \(R_{\mathrm{N}}^{\mathrm{nač}}\), needs the modes and \(m_{\mathrm{S}}\), the second only the modes and \(m_\Sigma\) (the total mass can be read from the mass matrix). In figure 21.15 the blue curve is this approximation, which agrees with the exact curve at the static value.

The second expression in (21.17) has a picture that explains the name effective mass directly. Take a single oscillator: a mass \(\mu\) on a spring of stiffness \(\mu\lambda\), standing on the same ground. For it, theorem 21.5 has \(n_1 = 1\), \(\mat M_{11} = \mu\), \(\mat K_{11} = \mu\lambda\), \(\vek s = 1\) and \(\vek h = \mu\). The only mode is \(\varphi = 1/\sqrt{\mu}\) (so that \(\varphi\,\mu\,\varphi = 1\)), the participation factor is \(\Gamma = \sqrt{\mu}\), the effective mass \(\Gamma^2 = \mu\), the mass at the support \(m_{\mathrm{S}} = 0\), and corollary 21.10 gives

\[R_{\mathrm{nih}}(\Omega) = \mu\,\frac{\lambda}{\lambda - \Omega^2} . \tag{21.20}\]

Term \(r\) of the second sum in (21.17) is exactly this expression with \(\mu = m_{\mathrm{r}}^{\mathrm{ef}}\) and \(\lambda = \lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\). So the ground cannot tell the frame from three oscillators standing side by side on the same ground, each with the mass \(m_{\mathrm{r}}^{\mathrm{ef}}\) and the natural frequency of its mode: \(1371\) kg at \(2{,}24\) Hz, \(112\) kg at \(6{,}29\) Hz and \(17\) kg at \(9{,}09\) Hz. For a structure with \(m_{\mathrm{S}} > 0\) a mass \(m_{\mathrm{S}}\) is in addition fixed rigidly to the ground. The equality holds for the support force, in harmonic motion without damping, as the corollary does. It does not hold for the displacements of the floors: oscillator \(r\) does not say where in the frame the mass moves.

From this picture we read the claims of the corollary without computing. In slow motion the accelerations are small, the springs hardly stretch, all oscillators move with the ground as a rigid load and the ground feels the sum of the masses, \(1500\) kg (item 3). To cut off modes is to remove oscillators: with one mode the first oscillator with \(1371\) kg remains, the second and third are missing, together \(\mu_1 = 128{,}88\) kg. The approximation \(R_{\mathrm{N}}^{\mathrm{pop}}\) does not throw the removed oscillators away but fixes them rigidly to the ground, since \(m_\Sigma = m_{\mathrm{S}} + \mu_{\mathrm{N}} + \sum_{\mathrm{r} \le \mathrm{N}} m_{\mathrm{r}}^{\mathrm{ef}}\) and so by (21.18)

\[R_{\mathrm{N}}^{\mathrm{pop}} = m_{\mathrm{S}} + \mu_{\mathrm{N}} + \sum_{\mathrm{r}=1}^{N} m_{\mathrm{r}}^{\mathrm{ef}}\,\frac{\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}}{\lambda_{\mathrm{r}} - \Omega^2} . \tag{21.21}\]

This is good as long as the frequency of the ground is far below the natural frequency of the fixed oscillators, and bad when it comes close, because a small oscillator near resonance pulls on the ground harder than a large one far from it. The contributions of the three oscillators by (21.20) are, at \(\Omega = 0{,}5\,\omega_1\),

\[R = 1828{,}16 + 116{,}01 + 16{,}82 = 1960{,}99\ \mathrm{kg} ,\]

and at \(\Omega = 0{,}9\,\omega_2\)

\[R = -255{,}84 + 591{,}13 + 27{,}06 = 362{,}35\ \mathrm{kg} .\]

The second oscillator with \(112\) kg gives the force \(591\) kg at \(\Omega = 0{,}9\,\omega_2\), more than twice as much as the first with \(1371\) kg. The first is then above its resonance, its mass moves against the ground, so its contribution is negative (num-02-teach.py).

In the figure the horizontal axis is the ratio \(\Omega/\omega_1\) of the ground frequency to the first natural frequency, and the vertical axis is the support force per unit ground acceleration divided by the total mass, \(R/m_\Sigma\). The grey horizontal line is at \(R = m_\Sigma\), the value towards which the exact force and \(R_1^{\mathrm{pop}}\) tend as \(\Omega \to 0\) (item 3). The vertical lines mark the natural frequencies \(\omega_1\) and \(\omega_2\), at which the exact force has a pole. The blackwhite curve is the exact \(R(\Omega)\) from the sum (21.17). The orange dashed curve is \(R_1^{\mathrm{nač}}\) and starts at small \(\Omega\) below the value \(m_\Sigma\): \(1371{,}12\) kg (\(m_{\mathrm{S}} = 0\)) is \(8{,}59\) % less, that is, less by the missing mass \(\mu_1 = 128{,}88\) kg. The blue curve is \(R_1^{\mathrm{pop}}\) and tends exactly to \(m_\Sigma\) as \(\Omega \to 0\). It then runs close to the blackwhite one up to about \(1{,}5\,\omega_1\) (error \(5{,}19\) %, table below), and towards \(\omega_2\) it moves further and further away from it (at \(2\,\omega_1\) the error is already \(59\) %), because the ground frequency approaches the natural frequency of the cut-off second mode.

The numbers for the frame, \(R\) in kg (equal to N per m/s²):

\(0{,}5\,\omega_1\) \(1960{,}990\) \(1828{,}159\) (\(-6{,}77\) %) \(1957{,}040\) (\(-0{,}20\) %) \(1960{,}734\) (\(-0{,}01\) %)
\(1{,}5\,\omega_1\) \(-920{,}260\) \(-1096{,}895\) (\(+19{,}19\) %) \(-968{,}015\) (\(+5{,}19\) %) \(-922{,}895\) (\(+0{,}29\) %)
\(0{,}9\,\omega_2\) \(362{,}353\) \(-255{,}844\) (\(-170{,}61\) %) \(-126{,}964\) (\(-135{,}04\) %) \(351{,}855\) (\(-2{,}90\) %)

The bound (21.19) for \(N = 1\) (\(\mu_1 = 128{,}88\) kg, \(\lambda_2 = 7{,}8509\,\lambda_1\)) is in figure 21.16. On the horizontal axis is the ratio \(\Omega^2/\lambda_2\), which tells how close the ground frequency is to the natural frequency of the first cut-off mode, the grey vertical line is \(\Omega = \omega_2\), and on the vertical axis is the factor. The blue curve is the factor \(\Omega^2/(\lambda_2 - \Omega^2)\) by which the bound multiplies the missing mass \(\mu_1\): near zero it is small, at the vertical line it runs off to infinity. At \(\Omega = 0{,}5\,\omega_1\) we have \(\Omega^2/\lambda_2 = 0{,}0318\), the factor \(0{,}0329\) and the bound \(0{,}0329 \cdot 128{,}88 = 4{,}24\) kg. The actual error is \(1960{,}990 - 1957{,}040 = 3{,}95\) kg, the gap between the blackwhite and the blue curve of figure 21.15, and in figure 21.16 the blackwhite dot just below the blue one. At \(\Omega = 1{,}5\,\omega_1\) the factor is \(0{,}4017\), the bound \(51{,}8\) kg, the error \(47{,}8\) kg. At both frequencies the bound is \(7\) and \(8\) % above the error, because the term \(r = 2\) dominates over \(r = 3\) (\(112{,}32\) against \(16{,}57\) kg) and the bound uses \(\lambda_2\) for both.

For bar C the same holds. With the first mode and \(\Omega = 0{,}5\,\omega_1\) the exact value is \(R/m_{\mathrm{T}} = 1{,}273203\), \(R_1^{\mathrm{pop}}/m_{\mathrm{T}} = 1{,}270190\) (\(-0{,}24\) %) and \(R_1^{\mathrm{nač}}/m_{\mathrm{T}} = 1{,}098801\) (\(-13{,}70\) %). At \(\Omega = 1{,}5\,\omega_1\) the exact value is \(-0{,}424861\), \(R_1^{\mathrm{pop}}/m_{\mathrm{T}} = -0{,}459024\) (error \(8{,}04\) % of the value) and \(R_1^{\mathrm{nač}}/m_{\mathrm{T}} = -0{,}630413\) (\(48{,}38\) %). The curves are in figure 21.17.

We build the figure like figure 21.15. On the horizontal axis is the ratio \(\Omega/\omega_1\), on the vertical one \(R/m_{\mathrm{T}}\), the grey horizontal line is the static value \(1\) and the grey vertical line the first natural frequency. The blackwhite curve is the exact force, the blue one is \(R_1^{\mathrm{pop}}\) and the dashed orange one is \(R_1^{\mathrm{nač}}\). At \(\Omega = 0{,}5\,\omega_1\) the blue point is only \(0{,}24\) % below the blackwhite one, the orange one \(13{,}70\) %. At \(\Omega = 1{,}5\,\omega_1\), already beyond the first natural frequency, the blue one is \(8{,}04\) % of the value away from the blackwhite one, the orange one \(48{,}38\) %.

How much does damping add to this, the second assumption of section 21.2.1? Let every oscillator get a damper with damping ratio \(\zeta\) (this is modal damping, definition 10.64). Figure 21.18 (a) shows one such oscillator: the mass \(\mu\) is linked to the ground by a spring of stiffness \(\mu\lambda\) and by a damper with \(c = 2\zeta\omega\mu\), where \(\omega = \sqrt\lambda\). The force an oscillator asks of the ground is its mass times the absolute acceleration of the mass, because the spring force and the damper force are the only horizontal forces on the mass and both come from the ground, and the absolute displacement is given by theorem 9.80. Term \(r\) becomes \(m_{\mathrm{r}}^{\mathrm{ef}}\,(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}} + 2\mathrm i\zeta\omega_{\mathrm{r}}\Omega)/(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}} - \Omega^2 + 2\mathrm i\zeta\omega_{\mathrm{r}}\Omega)\). That this is also the frame's force follows from the proof of corollary 21.10 with \(\mat K - \Omega^2\mat M\) replaced by \(\mat K + \mathrm i\Omega\mat C - \Omega^2\mat M\): for modal damping with \(\mat C\,\vek r = \vek 0\) every step goes through and \(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}} - \Omega^2\) becomes \(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}} - \Omega^2 + 2\mathrm i\zeta\omega_{\mathrm{r}}\Omega\). The magnitude \(|R|\) for the frame in kg (num-02-teach.py):

\(\Omega\) no damping \(\zeta = 0{,}02\) \(\zeta = 0{,}05\)
\(0{,}5\,\omega_1\) \(1960{,}99\) \(1960{,}70\) (\(-0{,}01\) %) \(1959{,}20\) (\(-0{,}09\) %)
\(1{,}5\,\omega_1\) \(920{,}26\) \(922{,}41\) (\(+0{,}23\) %) \(933{,}47\) (\(+1{,}44\) %)
\(0{,}9\,\omega_2\) \(362{,}35\) \(366{,}07\) (\(+1{,}03\) %) \(382{,}54\) (\(+5{,}57\) %)
\(0{,}99\,\omega_1\) \(69\,046\) \(31\,033\) \(13\,689\)

In figure 21.18 (b) these values lie on three curves above the axis \(\Omega/\omega_1\), with the vertical axis on a logarithmic scale, so that forces from a hundredth to a hundred times the total mass show at once. At the first three frequencies of the table the curves nearly coincide: damping hardly changes the force and the conclusions about the number of modes stand. Right at a natural frequency, at the vertical lines, damping sets the force, at \(0{,}99\,\omega_1\) it drops from \(69\,046\) to \(31\,033\) and \(13\,689\) kg, and the undamped formula says nothing useful there. The percentage of change also misleads where the undamped force crosses zero, at \(\Omega = 2{,}247\,\omega_1\): the undamped force is zero there, the damped one \(56{,}22\) kg at \(\zeta = 0{,}02\) and \(138{,}54\) kg at \(\zeta = 0{,}05\). There damping changes the force by more than \(100\) %, but the force stays small, \(3{,}7\) % of the total mass \(m_\Sigma\).

Now the second near miss, this time of the measure: the frame with one mode covers more than \(90\) % of the mass, yet with one mode the support force at a ground frequency near \(\omega_2\) is badly wrong. At \(0{,}9\,\omega_2\), just before the second vertical line, the error of the approximation \(R_1^{\mathrm{pop}}\) is \(-135\) %, that of the approximation \(R_1^{\mathrm{nač}}\) is \(-171\) %, and even with two modes (\(R_2^{\mathrm{pop}}\)) it is still \(-2{,}90\) %. The cause is the factor \(\Omega^2/(\lambda_2 - \Omega^2) = 0{,}81/0{,}19 = 4{,}263\), which with one mode is far from small: the bound of the corollary (item 4) is \(4{,}263\cdot 128{,}88 = 549{,}4\) kg, the error \(489{,}3\) kg. The bound of corollary 21.10 holds here, since \(\Omega^2 < \lambda_2\), but it is small only when the ratio \(\Omega^2/\lambda_{\mathrm{N}+1}\) is well below \(1\) (\(0{,}032\) at \(0{,}5\,\omega_1\), \(0{,}81\) at \(0{,}9\,\omega_2\)). At \(\Omega^2/\lambda_{\mathrm{N}+1} = 0{,}81\) the denominator \(\lambda_{\mathrm{N}+1} - \Omega^2\) drops to \(0{,}19\,\lambda_{\mathrm{N}+1}\), about a fifth, and the term \(\lambda_{\mathrm{N}+1}/(\lambda_{\mathrm{N}+1} - \Omega^2) = 5{,}26\) of the cut-off mode is more than five times as large as in slow motion, where it is close to \(1\).

21.2.5 What the measure says and what it does not

From the sum (21.16) GR derives a measure for the number of modes: keep so many modes that their share of the total mass is at least \(P\), usually \(90\) to \(95\) % (GR section 2.9.5, PDF p. 128, equation (2.194) is an image). The measure is sensible because the missing mass \(\mu_{\mathrm{N}}\) is, by item 3 of corollary 21.10, exactly the error of the support force in slow motion if we only add up the modes. For the frame one mode suffices for \(91{,}41\) %, for bar C two give \(90{,}06\) % and five give \(95{,}95\) %. For bar C we can never reach \(99\) %, since \(m_{\mathrm{S}}/m_{\mathrm{T}} = 1{,}80\) % (theorem 21.9): the limit \(P\) must lie below \(98{,}20\) %. In figure 21.13 this is the horizontal line at \(90\) %, which the frame reaches with one column, while bar C stops below \(100\) %.

The measure has two further restrictions. First, it holds for the direction of support motion for which it was computed (GR says so explicitly, PDF p. 128: for several directions the measure is applied in each). Second, it vouches only for slow motion, which the second near miss of this section shows: the frame with one mode meets \(90\) %, but at \(\Omega = 0{,}9\,\omega_2\) the error of the support force with \(R_1^{\mathrm{pop}}\) is \(-135\) % (figure 21.15), because the second oscillator is small but close to its resonance. The measure answers the question of how much mass moves together with the support. It does not answer whether the frequencies of the load come close to the natural frequency of the first cut-off mode, since that requires comparing \(\Omega^2\) with \(\lambda_{\mathrm{N}+1}\) (bound (21.19)). So we check both.

The picture that stays: for the ground the structure is a row of oscillators with masses \(\Gamma_{\mathrm{r}}^2\), which add up to the mass of the structure without the mass at the support, and to cut off modes is to remove oscillators (\(R_{\mathrm{N}}^{\mathrm{nač}}\)) or to fix them to the ground (\(R_{\mathrm{N}}^{\mathrm{pop}}\)). What we have not proved is an error estimate for arbitrary time dependence \(u_{\mathrm{g}}(t)\), which would need a Fourier decomposition, and the response for several support coordinates at once (GR takes a matrix instead of a number). The additional mass method of section 21.3 solves the same task without partitioning the coordinates, and later we pose the same question of which coordinates to keep for the coordinates of the structure itself (section 21.4).

21.3 The additional mass method (metoda dodatne mase)

In section 21.2 we solved base motion with relative coordinates: from the displacement of the structure we subtracted the rigid displacement carried by the support, and obtained an equation with the right-hand side \(-\vek h\,\ddot u_{\mathrm{g}}\) (theorem 21.5). That requires us to separate the support node from the other coordinates, to partition the matrices and to impose the motion on the support. Can we do without? The additional mass method takes the model as it is, adds a large mass to the support node and pushes it with a force known from the ground acceleration. One system of equations for all coordinates is then solved at once, without partitioning (GR section 2.9.6, PDF p. 129). This section shows how the method works, why it is only approximate, how large the error is and what the large mass costs.

The model is the frame with three floors from chapter 10. Each floor has mass \(m = 500\) kg, each storey has stiffness \(k = 501\,760\) N/m, the floors move only horizontally and there is no damping. The natural frequencies of the frame with a fixed support are \(f_{\mathrm{r}} = 2{,}2438\), \(6{,}2870\) and \(9{,}0850\) Hz. Here the support is a single node with horizontal displacement \(q_2\), on which the columns of the first storey stand. The ground moves with acceleration \(\ddot u_{\mathrm{g}}(t)\) and the support node moves with it. In a real building a foundation carries the ground motion into the structure, and here we idealize it as a rigid node, since the flexibility of the foundation and the soil would change the model. In figure 21.19 the frame is drawn on the left.

The frame consists of three floors of mass \(m\), joined to each other and to the support by columns, as in chapter 10. The columns of the first storey stand on the support block, which is a node with horizontal displacement \(q_2\) and can roll on the ground, as a foundation moves together with the ground. If we wanted to move the block with acceleration \(\ddot u_{\mathrm{g}}\) by prescription, we would have to partition the matrices and impose the displacement. Instead we load the block with an additional mass \(M_0\), which the structure does not have, and push it with the horizontal force \(M_0\,\ddot u_{\mathrm{g}}\). The force has this value by Newton's law: a body of mass \(M_0\) with acceleration \(\ddot u_{\mathrm{g}}\) needs a force equal to the product of the two. Since we push the block, the arrow ends at its edge. The name "additional mass" is therefore literal: the mass is added, it is not a mass of the structure, and its purpose is to force the acceleration of the block to the value \(\ddot u_{\mathrm{g}}\).

Why should the block really have an acceleration close to \(\ddot u_{\mathrm{g}}\)? The free-body diagram of the block answers (figure 21.19, right), where we cut the structure just above the body of the block. Two horizontal forces act on the body: the push \(M_0\,\ddot u_{\mathrm{g}}\) from the left and the reaction \(R\) of the structure, which pulls the block back when the columns hold it. It is called a reaction because it is the structure's answer to the force with which the block moves it (Newton's third law: the force of the block on the structure and the force of the structure on the block are equal and opposite). By Newton's second law \(M_0\,\ddot q_2 = M_0\,\ddot u_{\mathrm{g}} - R\), so

\[\ddot q_2 = \ddot u_{\mathrm{g}} - \frac{R}{M_0} . \tag{21.22}\]

The acceleration of the block differs from the ground acceleration by \(R/M_0\). In slow motion, far below the first natural frequency \(2{,}2438\) Hz, the frame moves almost as a rigid body and the reaction has to accelerate the whole structure, so by Newton \(R \approx 3m\,\ddot u_{\mathrm{g}} = 1500\ \mathrm{kg}\cdot\ddot u_{\mathrm{g}}\), and the difference is small when \(M_0\) is much larger than this mass. How much larger is shown by theorem 21.14, and here is the plan of its proof: equation (21.22) holds at every time, and the theorem solves it for harmonic ground motion.

Now we write the method in matrices. We split the coordinates into a column \(\vek q_1\) of structure coordinates (for the frame the three floor displacements) and one support displacement \(q_2\), and split the mass and stiffness matrices accordingly,

\[\mat M = \begin{bmatrix} \mat M_{11} & \mat M_{12} \\ \mat M_{21} & M_{22} \end{bmatrix} , \qquad \mat K = \begin{bmatrix} \mat K_{11} & \mat K_{12} \\ \mat K_{21} & K_{22} \end{bmatrix} , \tag{21.23}\]

with \(\mat M_{21} = \mat M_{12}^\T\) and \(\mat K_{21} = \mat K_{12}^\T\). Index \(1\) means the structure, index \(2\) the support, as in GR section 2.9. For the frame \(\mat M_{11} = m\,\mat I\), \(\mat M_{12} = \vek 0\) and \(M_{22} = 0\), since we do not count the mass of the support in the structure.

Definition 21.11 Additional mass method (metoda dodatne mase)

Let \(\mat M\) be a symmetric positive semidefinite and \(\mat K\) a symmetric matrix, split as in (21.23), with \(\mat M_{11}\) and \(\mat K_{11}\) positive definite (definition 6.27). Let \(\vek s\) be a column with \(\mat K\,\vek r = \vek 0\) for \(\vek r = (\vek s,\ 1)\), that is

\[\mat K_{11}\,\vek s + \mat K_{12} = \vek 0 , \qquad \mat K_{21}\,\vek s + K_{22} = 0 . \tag{21.24}\]

The column \(\vek r\) is the rigid motion of the structure caused by a displacement of the support by \(1\) (frame: \(\vek s = (1, 1, 1)\)). Let \(\ddot u_{\mathrm{g}}(t)\) be the prescribed acceleration of the support. We write

\[\vek h = \mat M_{11}\,\vek s + \mat M_{12} , \qquad m_\Sigma = \vek r^\T\mat M\,\vek r . \tag{21.25}\]

The column \(\vek h\) is the inertia column of theorem 21.5 and \(m_\Sigma\) the total mass of the structure and the support without the added mass, as in section 21.2. The prescribed problem is to find the motion of the structure for \(q_2(t) = u_{\mathrm{g}}(t)\). The additional mass method (metoda dodatne mase) with an added mass (dodana masa) \(M_0 > 0\) instead solves

\[\mat M^{0}\,\ddot{\vek q} + \mat K\,\vek q = \begin{bmatrix} \vek 0 \\ M_0\,\ddot u_{\mathrm{g}} \end{bmatrix} , \qquad \mat M^{0} = \mat M + M_0\begin{bmatrix} \mat 0 & \vek 0 \\ \vek 0^\T & 1 \end{bmatrix} , \tag{21.26}\]

that is, the equation with the same stiffness matrix and a mass matrix to which \(M_0\) is added in the row of the support, and with the force \(M_0\,\ddot u_{\mathrm{g}}\) on the support. The matrix \(\mat M^0\) is positive definite.

Source: GR section 2.9.6, (2.195) to (2.197) (PDF pp. 128-129, read): the same model with a matrix \(\mat M^0_{22}\) for several support coordinates, we take one. Condition (21.24) and the symbols \(m_\Sigma\) and \(\vek h\) are ours.

The matrix \(\mat M^{0}\) is positive definite: if \(\vek v^\T\mat M^0\vek v = 0\), both nonnegative terms \(\vek v^\T\mat M\,\vek v\) and \(M_0\,v_2^2\) are zero, so \(v_2 = 0\) and \(\vek v_1^\T\mat M_{11}\vek v_1 = 0\), and since \(\mat M_{11}\) is positive definite, \(\vek v = \vek 0\). System (21.26) is the equation of theorem 10.3 without damping and with the force \((\vek 0,\ M_0\,\ddot u_{\mathrm{g}})\).

How is the added mass related to the penalty method of chapter 12? The second row of system (21.26) is exactly equation (21.22), if we write \(R = \mat M_{21}\ddot{\vek q}_1 + M_{22}\,\ddot q_2 + \mat K_{21}\vek q_1 + K_{22}\,q_2\) for what the structure demands of the support (for the frame the sum of the column forces of the first storey, figure 21.19, reaction): \(R = -M_0\,(\ddot q_2 - \ddot u_{\mathrm{g}})\). In definition 12.27 the constraint \(\mat C\,\vek d = \vek g\) is penalized by the system \((\mat K + \alpha\,\mat C^\T\mat C)\,\vek d = \vek f + \alpha\,\mat C^\T\vek g\) and the penalty forces are \(\vek\lambda_\alpha = -\alpha\,(\mat C\,\vek d_\alpha - \vek g)\). Now the constraint is \(\ddot q_2 = \ddot u_{\mathrm{g}}\), not a constraint on displacement, the penalty number is the added mass, \(\alpha = M_0\), and the "penalty" is the force \(-M_0\,(\ddot q_2 - \ddot u_{\mathrm{g}})\), which grows with how much the acceleration of the support differs from the prescribed one. The name is penalty because a mismatch costs a force, and the size \(M_0\) of the penalty decides how expensive the mismatch is. GR remarks that a penalty is usual for constraints on displacements, but not for constraints on accelerations (PDF p. 128). An exact constraint would be a Lagrange multiplier, which GR treats in chapter 1, section 1.6, and this section does not use it.

How large \(R/M_0\) is in (21.22) depends on the frequency of the motion. What force must the support give the structure if we move it with a harmonic acceleration of amplitude \(a\) and there is no other load? In slow motion the force is \(m_\Sigma\,a\), as for a rigid body (the paragraph at (21.22)). In faster motion the floors no longer move together with the support and the force is different.

How different, we draw for our frame at \(4\) Hz and a ground acceleration of amplitude \(1\) m/s², at the instant of largest displacement (figure 21.20, left). The displacements are drawn strongly enlarged, \(1\) mm of displacement is \(1{,}2\) cm of the figure. The grey dashed axis and the grey outline of the block show the position at rest. The support block is displaced to the left by \(|U| = 1{,}583\) mm, where \(U = -a/\Omega^2\) is the amplitude of the ground displacement. In harmonic motion the acceleration is \(-\Omega^2\) times the displacement, so the ground acceleration points to the right at this instant, opposite to the displacement. If the frame were rigid, all three floors would move as the block does and would lie on the vertical dashed line above the block. This is the rigid shift \(\vek s\,U\). In fact the floors lie to the right of it, and the blue dimension lines measure by how much: \(0{,}8376\), \(2{,}1445\) and \(3{,}0980\) mm. This offset from the rigid shift is the relative displacement, and it alone bends the columns. The columns of the first storey are bent by \(0{,}8376\) mm and pull the block to the right with the force \(k \cdot 0{,}8376\ \mathrm{mm} = 420{,}3\) N. The block itself has no mass (\(M_{22} = 0\)), so the support must hold it with a force \(F\) of the same size to the left, otherwise it would not move as prescribed. The force points against the acceleration. A rigid body of mass \(1500\) kg would at the acceleration \(1\) m/s² demand \(1500\) N to the right, while here the ratio of force to acceleration is \(-420{,}3\) kg. The ratio of the amplitude of the force to the amplitude of the acceleration will be called the dynamic mass.

Definition 21.12 Dynamic mass at the support (dinamična masa na podlagi)

Let \(\mat M\), \(\mat K\), \(\vek s\), \(\vek h\) and \(m_\Sigma\) be as in definition 21.11, \(\Omega \ge 0\), and \(\Omega^2\) not an eigenvalue of the pair \((\mat K_{11}, \mat M_{11})\). Write \(\mat H(\Omega) = (\mat K_{11} - \Omega^2\mat M_{11})^{-1}\). The dynamic mass at the support (dinamična masa na podlagi) is the number

\[m_{\mathrm{d}}(\Omega) = M_{22} + \mat M_{21}\,\vek s - \big(\mat K_{21} - \Omega^2\mat M_{21}\big)\,\mat H(\Omega)\,\vek h . \tag{21.27}\]

It is the ratio of the support force to the ground acceleration in harmonic motion (lemma 21.13, item 1).

Source: The name is ours. The notion is GR's support impedance \(\mat Z^*_{22}\) (2.164) (PDF p. 122): for a rigid motion \(\vek u_{2(\mathrm{i})}\) of the support, \(\vek u_{2(\mathrm{i})}^\T\mat Z^*_{22}(\Omega^2)\,\vek u_{2(\mathrm{i})} = -\Omega^2\,m_{\mathrm{d}}(\Omega)\). At \(\Omega = 0\) the result is the total mass, in GR \(m_\mathrm{T}\) of (2.192) (PDF p. 128), computed from the mass matrix \(\mat M^*_{22}\) (2.158b) condensed on the support. The mass \(m_\mathrm{S}\) of (2.193) is from the block \(\mat M_{22}\) without condensation.

The name has its reason in two words. "Mass", because the ratio of force to acceleration is a mass by Newton's second law, as item 1 of lemma 21.13 shows. "Dynamic", because the number depends on the frequency \(\Omega\), and at \(\Omega = 0\) it is the total mass \(m_\Sigma\) (item 3).

Lemma 21.13 Properties of the dynamic mass (lastnosti dinamične mase)

Let the hypotheses of definition 21.12 hold. Let the support oscillate harmonically, \(q_2 = \mathrm{Re}\big(Q_2\,\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\Omega t}\big)\), and let no force load the structure otherwise. Then:

  1. The displacements of the structure are \(\vek q_1 = \mathrm{Re}\big((\vek s\,Q_2 + \vek Y)\,\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\Omega t}\big)\) with the relative part \(\vek Y = \Omega^2\,\mat H(\Omega)\,\vek h\,Q_2\), and the force that the support must give has amplitude \(-\Omega^2\,m_{\mathrm{d}}(\Omega)\,Q_2\), that is, \(m_{\mathrm{d}}(\Omega)\) times the amplitude \(-\Omega^2 Q_2\) of the support acceleration.
  2. \(m_{\mathrm{d}}(\Omega)\) \(= m_\Sigma + \Omega^2\,\vek h^\T\mat H(\Omega)\,\vek h\).
  3. Let \(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}} = \omega_{\mathrm{r}}^2\) and \(\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}\) be the eigenvalues and modes of the pair \((\mat K_{11}, \mat M_{11})\) and \(\Gamma_{\mathrm{r}} = \vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}^\T\vek h\). Then the dynamic mass is
    \[m_{\mathrm{d}}(\Omega) = m_\Sigma + \sum_{\mathrm{r}=1}^{n_1}\Gamma_{\mathrm{r}}^2\,\frac{\Omega^2}{\omega_{\mathrm{r}}^2 - \Omega^2} , \tag{21.28}\]
    \(m_{\mathrm{d}}(0) = m_\Sigma\), and \(m_{\mathrm{d}}\) has a pole at every \(\omega_{\mathrm{r}}\) with \(\Gamma_{\mathrm{r}} \ne 0\).
Proof

We must show that the structure follows the support with the offset \(\vek Y\) (steps 1 and 2), that the force on the support really is \(-\Omega^2 m_{\mathrm{d}} Q_2\) (step 3), rewrite \(m_{\mathrm{d}}\) with condition (21.24) (steps 4 and 5) and finally insert the modal sum (step 6). We write \(\vek q_1 = \mathrm{Re}(\vek Q_1\,\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\Omega t})\) and \(\vek Y = \vek Q_1 - \vek s\,Q_2\).

  1. The rows of the structure (the floors) without load are \(\mat M_{11}\ddot{\vek q}_1 + \mat M_{12}\ddot q_2 + \mat K_{11}\vek q_1 + \mat K_{12}q_2 = \vek 0\). With \(\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\Omega t}\), \(\ddot{\vek q}_1 \to -\Omega^2\vek Q_1\) (as in step 1 of the proof of theorem 10.72), so \((\mat K_{11} - \Omega^2\mat M_{11})\vek Q_1 + (\mat K_{12} - \Omega^2\mat M_{12})\,Q_2 = \vek 0\).

  2. We insert \(\vek Q_1 = \vek Y + \vek s\,Q_2\), that is the rigid shift and the relative part, and use the first condition (21.24), \(\mat K_{11}\vek s = -\mat K_{12}\), and the definition of \(\vek h\) from (21.25): \((\mat K_{11} - \Omega^2\mat M_{11})\,\vek Y = \Omega^2\,\vek h\,Q_2\). Since \(\mat H\) exists, \(\vek Y = \Omega^2\mat H\,\vek h\,Q_2\). This is the first part of item 1.

  3. The row of the support without the added mass gives the force \(F = (\mat K_{21} - \Omega^2\mat M_{21})\,\vek Q_1 + (K_{22} - \Omega^2 M_{22})\,Q_2\). With \(\vek Q_1 = \vek Y + \vek s\,Q_2\) and the second condition (21.24), \(\mat K_{21}\vek s + K_{22} = 0\), we get \(F = (\mat K_{21} - \Omega^2\mat M_{21})\,\vek Y - \Omega^2\,(\mat M_{21}\vek s + M_{22})\,Q_2\). With \(\vek Y\) from step 2, \(F = -\Omega^2\big[M_{22} + \mat M_{21}\vek s - (\mat K_{21} - \Omega^2\mat M_{21})\mat H\,\vek h\big]Q_2 = -\Omega^2\,m_{\mathrm{d}}\,Q_2\). This is item 1.

  4. Algebra only, one operation at a time. From symmetry and the first condition (21.24)

    \[\mat K_{21} = \mat K_{12}^\T = -\vek s^\T\mat K_{11} .\]

    From (21.25), \(\vek h^\T = \vek s^\T\mat M_{11} + \mat M_{21}\), so

    \[\mat M_{21} = \vek h^\T - \vek s^\T\mat M_{11} .\]

    We insert both into the difference:

    \[\mat K_{21} - \Omega^2\mat M_{21} = -\vek s^\T(\mat K_{11} - \Omega^2\mat M_{11}) - \Omega^2\vek h^\T .\]

    We multiply on the right by \(\mat H\,\vek h\), where \((\mat K_{11} - \Omega^2\mat M_{11})\,\mat H = \mat I\):

    \[(\mat K_{21} - \Omega^2\mat M_{21})\,\mat H\,\vek h = -\vek s^\T\vek h - \Omega^2\vek h^\T\mat H\,\vek h .\]

  5. The total mass is \(m_\Sigma = \vek r^\T\mat M\,\vek r = \vek s^\T\mat M_{11}\vek s + \vek s^\T\mat M_{12} + \mat M_{21}\vek s + M_{22} = \vek s^\T\vek h + \mat M_{21}\vek s + M_{22}\). From (21.27) and step 4, \(m_{\mathrm{d}} = M_{22} + \mat M_{21}\vek s + \vek s^\T\vek h + \Omega^2\vek h^\T\mat H\,\vek h = m_\Sigma + \Omega^2\vek h^\T\mat H\,\vek h\). This is item 2.

  6. Let \(\mat\Phi\) be the modal matrix of the pair \((\mat K_{11}, \mat M_{11})\) (definition 10.23) and \(\mat\Lambda = \mathrm{diag}(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}})\). By lemma 10.24, \(\mat K_{11} - \Omega^2\mat M_{11} = \mat\Phi^{-\T}(\mat\Lambda - \Omega^2\mat I)\mat\Phi^{-1} = \mat M_{11}\mat\Phi\,(\mat\Lambda - \Omega^2\mat I)\,\mat\Phi^\T\mat M_{11}\) (as in step 2 of the proof of lemma 10.69), the diagonal elements \(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}} - \Omega^2\) are nonzero, and with \(\mat\Phi^\T\mat M_{11}\mat\Phi = \mat I\) we get \(\mat H = \mat\Phi\,(\mat\Lambda - \Omega^2\mat I)^{-1}\mat\Phi^\T\). Hence \(\vek h^\T\mat H\,\vek h = \sum_{\mathrm{r}} \Gamma_{\mathrm{r}}^2/(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}} - \Omega^2)\) and item 2 gives (21.28). At \(\Omega = 0\) the sum is zero, \(m_{\mathrm{d}}(0) = m_\Sigma\). As \(\Omega \to \omega_{\mathrm{r}}\) the terms with \(\omega_{\mathrm{s}} \ne \omega_{\mathrm{r}}\) stay bounded. The terms with \(\omega_{\mathrm{s}} = \omega_{\mathrm{r}}\) all have the same sign, since \(\Gamma_{\mathrm{s}}^2 \ge 0\), and if \(\Gamma_{\mathrm{r}} \ne 0\) is among them, the absolute value of their sum grows beyond every bound. This is the pole (the dashed verticals in figure 21.21).

Source: The proof is not from the sources. For a rigid motion of the support, item 3 is GR (2.164) (PDF p. 122) divided by \(-\Omega^2\), and the same modal expansion as in lemma 10.69, with \(\vek h\) in place of a force. Sum (21.28) is the same as the support force per unit acceleration (21.17) in corollary 21.10.

The lemma says that \(m_{\mathrm{d}}\) at \(\Omega = 0\) is the total mass, as Newton demands for a rigid body, and that its absolute value grows beyond every bound when \(\Omega\) approaches a frequency of the structure with fixed support. Figure 21.21 shows this for the frame: the curve of the dynamic mass over the frequency axis starts at \(m_\Sigma = 1500\) kg, and at each of the three natural frequencies \(f_1\), \(f_2\), \(f_3\) of the frame with fixed support (the dashed verticals) it runs off upwards and returns from below. The figure adds an overview to the formula: the method will be accurate where the curve is close to the axis compared with \(M_0\), and it will fail at the verticals. For the frame \(\mat M_{12} = \vek 0\) and \(\vek h = m\,\vek s\), so the \(\Gamma_{\mathrm{r}}^2\) are the effective modal masses of section 21.2 (definition 21.8): \(1371{,}12\), \(112{,}32\) and \(16{,}57\) kg, together \(1500\) kg \(= m_\Sigma\). At \(f = 4\) Hz, that is \(\Omega = 25{,}133\) 1/s, with \(\omega_{\mathrm{r}} = 14{,}098\), \(39{,}502\) and \(57{,}082\) 1/s, the terms of sum (21.28) are \(-2000{,}65\), \(76{,}38\) and \(3{,}98\) kg, and

\[m_{\mathrm{d}}(2\pi\cdot 4\ \mathrm{Hz}) = 1500 - 2000{,}65 + 76{,}38 + 3{,}98 = -420{,}29\ \mathrm{kg} = -0{,}8406\,m . \tag{21.29}\]

The first term is negative because \(\Omega > \omega_1\): above the first natural frequency the first mode oscillates in antiphase with the support and demands a force opposite to the acceleration. This is the dot at \(4\) Hz, slightly below the axis. Why antiphase? A weight on a spring whose free end we shake faster than the weight oscillates by itself cannot follow the hand: when the hand is at its leftmost position, the weight is displaced to the right relative to the hand (section 9.6). The left part of figure 21.20 shows exactly this: the block is on the left, the floors are displaced to the right relative to it. The computation is in num-03.py.

Now we have everything to say what motion the method gives. The theorem holds for harmonic ground motion, because that is the case where the dynamic mass can be computed.

Theorem 21.14 Accuracy of the additional mass method (natančnost metode dodatne mase)

Let the hypotheses of definition 21.11 hold, \(\ddot u_{\mathrm{g}}(t) = \mathrm{Re}\big(A\,\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\Omega t}\big)\) with \(\Omega > 0\), let \(\Omega^2\) not be an eigenvalue of the pair \((\mat K_{11}, \mat M_{11})\), and \(M_0 + m_{\mathrm{d}}(\Omega) \ne 0\). Let \(U = -A/\Omega^2\) be the amplitude of the prescribed support displacement \(u_{\mathrm{g}}\) and \(\vek Y_{\mathrm{t}} = \Omega^2\mat H\,\vek h\,U\) the amplitude of the relative displacement \(\vek q_1 - \vek s\,u_{\mathrm{g}}\) of the prescribed problem. Then:

  1. System (21.26) has one harmonic solution \(\vek q = \mathrm{Re}(\vek Q\,\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\Omega t})\) of this frequency, and with the factor \(\beta = M_0/(M_0 + m_{\mathrm{d}}(\Omega))\) the orange block and the floors differ from the prescribed motion as follows:
    \[Q_2 = \beta\,U , \qquad \vek Q_1 - \vek s\,Q_2 = \beta\,\vek Y_{\mathrm{t}} . \tag{21.30}\]
  2. The relative error \(\varepsilon = \beta - 1 = -m_{\mathrm{d}}/(M_0 + m_{\mathrm{d}})\) is the same for all coordinates of the relative displacement (blue differences). For \(M_0 \ge 2\,|m_{\mathrm{d}}|\), \(|\varepsilon| \le 2\,|m_{\mathrm{d}}|/M_0\), and \(M_0\,\varepsilon \to -m_{\mathrm{d}}\) as \(M_0 \to \infty\).
  3. The natural circular frequencies \(\omega > 0\) of system (21.26) with \(\omega^2\) different from the eigenvalues of the pair \((\mat K_{11}, \mat M_{11})\) are exactly the solutions of \(M_0 + m_{\mathrm{d}}(\omega) = 0\), that is, the intersections of the curve with the horizontal line \(-M_0\).
Proof

We must show that the rows of system (21.26) with a harmonic ansatz give the same relative offset as in lemma 21.13 and an equation for \(Q_2\) in which \(M_0\) is only added to \(m_{\mathrm{d}}\). The first row does not contain \(M_0\), the second contains \(M_0\) on both sides.

  1. We insert \(\vek q = \mathrm{Re}(\vek Q\,\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\Omega t})\), \(\ddot{\vek q} \to -\Omega^2\vek Q\). The rows of the structure (floors) are the same as in step 1 of lemma 21.13. With \(\vek Y = \vek Q_1 - \vek s\,Q_2\), step 2 of the lemma gives \(\vek Y = \Omega^2\mat H\,\vek h\,Q_2\).
  2. The row of the support (Newton's law for the block with the push of amplitude \(M_0\,A\)) is \((\mat K_{21} - \Omega^2\mat M_{21})\,\vek Q_1 + (K_{22} - \Omega^2 M_{22})\,Q_2 - \Omega^2 M_0\,Q_2 = M_0\,A\). The first two terms together are, by step 3 of lemma 21.13, equal to \(-\Omega^2 m_{\mathrm{d}}\,Q_2\), because we computed \(\vek Y\) in step 1. Hence \(-\Omega^2\,(M_0 + m_{\mathrm{d}})\,Q_2 = M_0\,A\).
  3. Since \(M_0 + m_{\mathrm{d}} \ne 0\), \(Q_2 = M_0 A/\big(-\Omega^2 (M_0 + m_{\mathrm{d}})\big) = \beta\,U\) with \(U = -A/\Omega^2\) (the orange block in the right part of figure 21.20), and \(\vek Y\) is determined uniquely by step 1. So the solution is unique.
  4. In the prescribed problem \(q_2 = u_{\mathrm{g}}\), so \(Q_2 = U\) (the shift of the block in the left part of figure 21.20), and by step 1 (without the added mass) \(\vek Y_{\mathrm{t}} = \Omega^2\mat H\,\vek h\,U\). Then by steps 1 and 3, \(\vek Y = \Omega^2\mat H\,\vek h\,\beta\,U = \beta\,\vek Y_{\mathrm{t}}\). This proves item 1.
  5. From step 4, \(\vek Y - \vek Y_{\mathrm{t}} = (\beta - 1)\,\vek Y_{\mathrm{t}}\) and \(\beta - 1 = -m_{\mathrm{d}}/(M_0 + m_{\mathrm{d}})\), the same factor for every coordinate (the two blue differences in the right part of figure 21.20). For \(M_0 \ge 2\,|m_{\mathrm{d}}|\), \(|M_0 + m_{\mathrm{d}}| \ge M_0 - |m_{\mathrm{d}}| \ge M_0/2\) and \(|\varepsilon| \le 2\,|m_{\mathrm{d}}|/M_0\). Also \(M_0\,\varepsilon = -m_{\mathrm{d}}\,M_0/(M_0 + m_{\mathrm{d}}) \to -m_{\mathrm{d}}\). This is item 2.
  6. Free vibration is a solution of (21.26) with \(A = 0\). Steps 1 and 2 give \(-\omega^2\,(M_0 + m_{\mathrm{d}}(\omega))\,Q_2 = 0\) and \(\vek Y = \omega^2\mat H\,\vek h\,Q_2\). For \(Q_2 = 0\) also \(\vek Y = \vek 0\) and \(\vek Q = \vek 0\), which is not a mode. So \(Q_2 \ne 0\) and \(M_0 + m_{\mathrm{d}}(\omega) = 0\). Conversely, if \(M_0 + m_{\mathrm{d}}(\omega) = 0\), we take \(Q_2 = 1\), \(\vek Y\) from step 1 and \(\vek Q_1 = \vek Y + \vek s\), and step 2 gives the row of the support. This is item 3. In figure 21.21 these frequencies are the crossings of the curve with the horizontal line \(-M_0\).

Source: GR section 2.9.6 (PDF p. 129): the method and the criterion that \(M_0\) should be large. Formula (21.30) and its proof are ours, GR does not compute the error. The theorem is proved only for harmonic ground motion, GR states the method for any motion.

What does the theorem say? Because of the added mass the support moves by the factor \(\beta\) of the prescribed displacement, and the structure follows the support with the same factor, so only the overall size of the motion is wrong, not its shape. The right part of figure 21.20 shows this for \(M_0 = 10\,m\), where \(\beta = 1{,}0918\): the grey dashed frame is the prescribed motion from the left part, the orange block and the orange floors are the motion the method gives. The block moves by \(\beta\,U\) \(= -1{,}728\) mm instead of \(U = -1{,}583\) mm, and the relative displacement of the top floor is \(3{,}382\) mm instead of \(3{,}098\) mm. The two differences are \(0{,}145\) mm and \(0{,}284\) mm, both \(9{,}18\) % of the true value. Since the elastic forces of the structure depend only on the relative displacement \(\vek q_1 - \vek s\,q_2\) (a rigid motion produces none, \(\mat K\,\vek r = \vek 0\)), the forces in the columns have the same relative error \(\varepsilon\). The error is \(-m_{\mathrm{d}}/(M_0 + m_{\mathrm{d}})\), about \(-m_{\mathrm{d}}/M_0\), so it is not "a small mass against a large mass" in general, but the dynamic mass at this frequency against \(M_0\). This is the measure that figure 21.22 shows.

Example 21.15 The frame at 4 Hz with masses \(M_0 = 10\,m\) to \(10^4\,m\)

The ground moves with acceleration of amplitude \(1\) m/s² at \(4\) Hz, so \(\Omega = 25{,}133\) 1/s and \(U = -1/\Omega^2 = -1{,}583\) mm. The prescribed problem (theorem 21.14, step 4) has amplitudes of relative displacements of the floors \(\vek Y_{\mathrm{t}}\) that for unit acceleration are \(0{,}8376\), \(2{,}1445\) and \(3{,}0980\) mm. The dynamic mass is, by (21.29), \(m_{\mathrm{d}} = -420{,}29\) kg. We solve system (21.26) for four values of \(M_0\) and in each case compute \(\beta\) from the theorem (column \(Q_2/U\)) and the error \(100\,\varepsilon\):

\(M_0/m\) \(M_0\) (kg) \(Q_2/U = \beta\) \(100\,\varepsilon\) (%) \(-100\,m_{\mathrm{d}}/M_0\) (%) first nonzero \(f\) (Hz) \(\kappa(\mat M^0)\)
10 5000 1,091771 9,177 8,406 2,5248 10
100 50 000 1,008477 0,8477 0,8406 2,2743 100
1000 500 000 1,000841 0,0841 0,0841 2,2469 1000
10 000 5 000 000 1,000084 0,0084 0,0084 2,2441 10 000

For all four \(M_0\) the ratio \(\vek Y/\vek Y_{\mathrm{t}}\) is the same for all three floors and equal to \(\beta\) to six digits (\(1{,}091771\) at \(M_0 = 10\,m\)), as item 1 says. The error falls to a tenth for every tenfold \(M_0\), because \(\varepsilon \approx -m_{\mathrm{d}}/M_0\) (\(|m_{\mathrm{d}}| = 0{,}84\,m\)). As \(M_0\) grows, the nonzero natural frequencies approach the natural frequencies \(2{,}2438\), \(6{,}2870\) and \(9{,}0850\) Hz of the frame with fixed support (at \(M_0 = 10\,m\) they are \(2{,}5248\), \(6{,}3596\) and \(9{,}1006\) Hz), and one frequency is zero, because the frame with the added mass is still a free body (theorem 10.34). In figure 21.21 the three nonzero frequencies are the open circles where the horizontal line \(-M_0 = -5000\) kg crosses the curve, each slightly to the right of its pole. A larger \(M_0\) lowers the line, and since the curve is steep at the poles, the crossings move towards the poles. This is why the frequencies approach those of the frame with fixed support. The squares of the circular frequencies are the eigenvalues of the pair \((\mat K, \mat M^0)\), that is, of system (21.26) without the force. Inserted into \(M_0 + m_{\mathrm{d}}\) they give zero, as item 3 requires: at \(M_0 = 10\,m\), \(M_0 + m_{\mathrm{d}}\) at the computed frequency \(2{,}5248\) Hz is less than \(10^{-10}\) kg, which is zero up to the rounding of the computation. The computation is in num-03.py.

At \(M_0 = 10\,m\) the error is \(9{,}2\) %, as predicted: \(M_0\) is only \(11{,}9\) times larger than \(|m_{\mathrm{d}}| = 0{,}84\,m\) (\(5000\) kg against \(420\) kg), and the requirement "\(M_0\) much larger than \(|m_{\mathrm{d}}|\)" is barely met. This is the first near miss of the method. Since \(m_{\mathrm{d}}\) is negative at \(4\) Hz, \(\varepsilon = |m_{\mathrm{d}}|/(M_0 - |m_{\mathrm{d}}|)\). An error of at most \(1\) % therefore requires \(M_0 - |m_{\mathrm{d}}| \ge 100\,|m_{\mathrm{d}}|\), so \(M_0 \ge 101\,|m_{\mathrm{d}}| = 42\,449\) kg \(= 84{,}9\,m\), and an error of at most \(0{,}1\) % requires \(M_0 \ge 1001\,|m_{\mathrm{d}}| = 841{,}4\,m\). The range given by GR is \(10^2\) to \(10^4\) times the norm of \(\mat M_{11}\) (PDF p. 129), for the frame \(100\,m\) to \(10\,000\,m\), and the error at \(4\) Hz is \(0{,}85\) % and \(0{,}0084\) % there.

The second near miss is the frequency. The theorem requires \(M_0 \gg |m_{\mathrm{d}}(\Omega)|\) at the frequency of the motion, and \(m_{\mathrm{d}}\) has a pole at every natural frequency of the frame with fixed support (lemma 21.13, item 3). At \(\Omega = 0{,}5\,\omega_1\), \(0{,}9\,\omega_1\), \(0{,}99\,\omega_1\) and \(0{,}999\,\omega_1\) (\(f = 1{,}1219\), \(2{,}0194\), \(2{,}2214\) and \(2{,}2416\) Hz) \(m_{\mathrm{d}} = 1961\), \(7359\), \(69\,046\) and \(686\,049\) kg (the two dots in figure 21.21 show the first two values, the last two are far above its upper edge), and the error at \(M_0 = 100\,m\) is \(3{,}77\) %, \(12{,}8\) %, \(58{,}0\) % and \(93{,}2\) %. At \(M_0 = 10^4\,m\) the errors are \(0{,}039\) %, \(0{,}147\) %, \(1{,}36\) % and \(12{,}1\) %. The cause is in sum (21.28): at \(0{,}99\,\omega_1\), \(\Omega^2/(\omega_1^2 - \Omega^2) = 49{,}251\) and the first term is \(1371{,}12 \cdot 49{,}251 = 67\,529\) kg. Physically: near resonance the structure responds with large displacements, its reaction \(R \approx m_{\mathrm{d}}\,\ddot u_{\mathrm{g}}\) becomes large and drags the heavy block, since \(R/M_0\) in (21.22) is large. Here the assumption of no damping enters. It is justified far from the natural frequencies, where damping hardly changes the response: at \(0{,}9\,\omega_1\) and \(M_0 = 100\,m\) the computation with modal damping of \(2\) % in all three modes gives the error \(12{,}7\) % instead of \(12{,}8\) %. Right at a natural frequency it does not hold, because damping cuts the pole off: \(|m_{\mathrm{d}}|\) stays below \(34\,322\) kg \(= 68{,}6\,m\), and the error at \(M_0 = 10^4\,m\) nowhere exceeds \(0{,}69\) %, while without damping it is \(12{,}1\) % at \(0{,}999\,\omega_1\). The numbers without damping are therefore an upper estimate near resonance. The computation with damping is a direct solution of the system with the added mass (num-03b.py), theorem 21.14 does not cover it. For an error of at most \(1\) % at \(0{,}99\,\omega_1\) we would need \(M_0 \ge 99\,m_{\mathrm{d}} = 6{,}84 \cdot 10^6\) kg \(= 1{,}4 \cdot 10^4\,m\) (here \(m_{\mathrm{d}}\) is positive and \(|\varepsilon| = m_{\mathrm{d}}/(M_0 + m_{\mathrm{d}})\), hence \(99\) instead of \(101\)), which is already outside the range of GR. Figure 21.22 shows the error against \(M_0\) at three of these frequencies.

In the figure there are two axes with logarithmic scales. Drawn are the blue curve at \(4\) Hz, the orange one at \(0{,}9\,\omega_1\) and the blackwhite one at \(0{,}99\,\omega_1\), and the dots are the four rows of the table. The grey band marks the range recommended by GR, and the lower part of the figure (conditioning) shows the price. The curves fall with slope \(-1\), except near small \(M_0\) and at frequencies near resonance, where \(m_{\mathrm{d}}\) holds them up.

The price of the large mass is in the matrix \(\mat M^0\). The condition number (definition 6.31) shows how many digits of the solution we lose in the computation, and it grows with \(M_0\) like in the penalty method (lemma 12.29).

Figure 21.23 shows the eigenvalues of the matrix \(\mat M^0\) of the frame at \(M_0 = 100\,m\). The logarithmic axis is drawn so that the values \(m\) and \(100\,m\) are far enough apart. On it lies \(\mu_1 = m\), the smallest eigenvalue of \(\mat M_{11}\), and the added mass \(M_0\). The smallest eigenvalue of \(\mat M^0\) lies in the band up to \(\mu_1\), the largest in the band from \(M_0\) onward, and the gap between them on the logarithmic axis is the condition number. The lemma says that this gap is at least \(M_0/\mu_1\).

Lemma 21.16 Growth of the condition number with the added mass (rast števila občutljivosti z dodano maso)

Let the hypotheses of definition 21.11 hold and \(\mu_1\) be the smallest eigenvalue of the matrix \(\mat M_{11}\). Then for every \(M_0 > 0\)

\[\kappa(\mat M^0) \ge \frac{M_0}{\mu_1} . \tag{21.31}\]
Proof

We must bound the largest eigenvalue from below and the smallest from above, both by the Rayleigh quotient (theorem 10.42 with \(\mat M = \mat I\)).

  1. The matrix \(\mat M^0\) is symmetric and positive definite (definition 21.11), so it has a condition number. The largest eigenvalue is at least the quotient at the column \(\vek e_2 = (\vek 0,\ 1)\): \(\vek e_2^\T\mat M^0\vek e_2 = M_{22} + M_0 \ge M_0\), because \(M_{22} \ge 0\) (a diagonal element of a positive semidefinite matrix).
  2. The smallest eigenvalue is at most the quotient at \((\vek v_1,\ 0)\), where \(\vek v_1\) is an eigencolumn of \(\mat M_{11}\) with eigenvalue \(\mu_1\): the quotient is \(\vek v_1^\T\mat M_{11}\vek v_1/|\vek v_1|^2 = \mu_1\), and does not depend on \(M_0\).
  3. The ratio of the two (definition 6.31) is at least \(M_0/\mu_1\) (for the frame the straight line in the lower part of figure 21.22).

Source: The proof is not from the sources. GR (PDF p. 129) limits \(\|\mat M^0_{22}\|\) to \(10^2\) to \(10^4\) times \(\|\mat M_{11}\|\), to keep the conditioning of the mass matrix.

For the frame \(\mu_1 = m\) and \(\mat M^0 = \mathrm{diag}(m, m, m, M_0)\), so for \(M_0 \ge m\) bound (21.31) is an equality: \(\kappa(\mat M^0) = M_0/m\), \(10\), \(10^2\), \(10^3\) and \(10^4\) in the table of example 21.15, the line in the lower part of figure 21.22. Rounding does not spoil the solution for this frame: the computed error of the relative displacements agrees with the formula of the theorem to three digits up to \(M_0 = 10^{12}\,m\) (num-03.out). The reason is the same as for the horizontal support in chapter 12: the large number stands on the diagonal only. For a mesh in which \(M_0\) takes part in off-diagonal terms we did not test this, and so the upper limit of GR remains a source and not a result of this section.

To sum up. The additional mass method replaces the prescribed motion of the support with a large mass and the force \(M_0\,\ddot u_{\mathrm{g}}\) on it (definition 21.11), and for harmonic ground motion the error of all relative displacements is the same factor \(\varepsilon = -m_{\mathrm{d}}/(M_0 + m_{\mathrm{d}})\) (theorem 21.14). The factor is small only when \(M_0\) is much larger than the dynamic mass at the frequency of the motion, which is large at frequencies near a natural frequency of the structure with fixed support (lemma 21.13). The price is a condition number that grows with \(M_0\) (lemma 21.16). What we proved is for harmonic motion and one support coordinate. For several support coordinates GR takes a matrix of added masses \(\mat M^0_{22}\) in place of a number (PDF p. 128), and for an arbitrary time dependence the theorem is not proved here. We do not use a Fourier series to split the frequencies. Sum (21.28) is the same as the support force per unit acceleration (21.17) of section 21.2, where we already shortened it to a few modes (approximations (21.18)), and the mode-acceleration correction is in section 21.1.

21.4 Guyan reduction (Guyanova redukcija)

So far in this chapter we have shortened the response: we kept the first few modes and, where needed, added a static correction to them (section 21.1). For that we must know the modes, that is, we must already have solved the eigenvalue problem of the whole structure, and for a large model this is exactly what we would like to save. This section starts at the other end. First we shrink the structure to a few coordinates, only then do we solve the eigenvalue problem, and that problem is small. How do we choose which coordinates to keep, and where do the others go? The simplest answer is equilibrium: the coordinates we do not keep are left to reach equilibrium by themselves, as if no force acted on them. After R. J. Guyan, one of the two authors who published it independently in \(1965\), the procedure is called Guyan reduction (Guyanova redukcija), in the literature also static condensation (statična kondenzacija): the coordinates we eliminate are, as it were, condensed into the kept ones, and it is static because only the equilibrium of forces in the stiffness matrix is taken into account, not inertia. The section proves three things. Static condensation is exact for loads on the kept coordinates (lemma 21.18). The Guyan approximation is a Ritz approximation (definition 10.58), so the upper bound of theorem 10.59 holds, and it is exact when the dependent coordinates have no mass (theorem 21.19). And the exact eigenvalue problem, of which Guyan's is only the first approximation, tells when it is good and when it is not (theorem 21.20). We test everything on two examples, a frame and a cantilever, and on both we also show a choice of coordinates for which the reduction fails.

21.4.1 A frame with one kept floor

Let us start with the smallest example where everything can be seen. The frame with three storeys from section 10.9 has floor displacements \(q_1, q_2, q_3\) (from the bottom up), each storey has stiffness \(k\) and each floor mass \(\bar m\). The model rests on two assumptions from chapter 10. First: the floors are rigid and do not rotate, so each floor has a single coordinate, its horizontal displacement, and a storey with two columns has stiffness \(k = 2 \cdot 12EI/h^3\). This holds when the floor is much stiffer than the columns. The top of a column is kept parallel to its initial position by the couple from the floor, and if the floor cannot supply it (the top of the column rotates freely), the stiffness of the column is \(3EI/h^3\), a quarter, and all eigenvalues are four times lower. Second: the columns have no mass, all the mass is in the floors. This holds when the columns are light next to the floors. If we add the mass of the columns, say a tenth of the mass of a floor, to the floor, all eigenvalues are divided by \(1{,}1\) and the frequencies drop by \(4{,}7\) %. We measure the eigenvalues in the unit \(k/\bar m\), and they are \(0{,}198062\), \(1{,}554958\) and \(3{,}246980\). The matrices are

\[\mat K = k\begin{pmatrix} 2 & -1 & 0 \\ -1 & 2 & -1 \\ 0 & -1 & 1 \end{pmatrix} , \qquad \mat M = \bar m\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} ,\]

and from here on we take \(k = \bar m = 1\). Only the lowest eigenvalue interests us, so of the three coordinates we keep one, the top floor \(q_3\), and ask where floors \(1\) and \(2\) should go.

First we draw the ground, the fixed base. On it we set up the columns, drawn dashed in the undeformed position, and above them the three floors, numbered from the bottom. Each piece of column between two floors (or between the ground and floor \(1\)) is a storey with horizontal stiffness \(k\). Now we move floor \(3\) by \(1\) to the right and hold it there with the force \(F\), which starts at the floor and points in the direction of the displacement. No external force acts on floors \(1\) and \(2\), and this is the requirement that the floors reach equilibrium by themselves. How do they move? Only the storey below and the storey above act on floor \(1\), and since no external force acts on it, the forces of the two storeys are equal by the law of equilibrium: \(k\,q_1 = k\,(q_2 - q_1)\) in magnitude. The same holds for floor \(2\): \(k\,(q_2 - q_1) = k\,(q_3 - q_2)\). The shear force is therefore the same in all three storeys, so the interstorey drifts (section 10.2.3), that is the displacements of a floor relative to the floor below it, are the same in all three storeys. Three equal drifts together give \(q_3 = 1\), so each is \(1/3\) and the floor displacements are \(q_1 = \tfrac13\), \(q_2 = \tfrac23\), \(q_3 = 1\), as the displacements in the figure show. The column \(\vek\psi = (\tfrac13,\ \tfrac23,\ 1)^\T\) is the static shape of the frame for a unit displacement of the top floor.

The force that holds the top floor is the shear force in the top storey, \(F = k\,(q_3 - q_2) = k/3\). At the same time this is the stiffness of the reduced system with one coordinate: a unit displacement needs the force \(k/3\). A second route, from energy, leads to the same stiffness and also gives the mass.

On the left of figure 21.25 the frame stands on the ground once more in the static shape. The stiffness \(\tilde K\) is twice the elastic energy at a unit displacement of the top floor: \(\tilde K = \vek\psi^\T\mat K\vek\psi = k\,(3 \cdot (1/3)^2) = k/3\), since each of the three storeys with drift \(1/3\) contributes \(k\,(1/3)^2\). The mass of the reduced system is twice the kinetic energy at unit velocity of the top floor, when all floors move according to \(\vek\psi\). Each floor contributes its mass times the square of its displacement, that is \(1/9\), \(4/9\) and \(1\): \(\tilde M = \vek\psi^\T\mat M\vek\psi = \bar m\,(\tfrac19 + \tfrac49 + 1) = \tfrac{14}{9}\bar m\). So the top floor carries \(9/14\) of the reduced mass, the bottom one only \(1/14\). The reduced eigenvalue is

\[\tilde\lambda = \frac{\tilde K}{\tilde M} = \frac{k/3}{14\bar m/9} = \frac{3}{14}\,\frac{k}{\bar m} = 0{,}214286\,\frac{k}{\bar m} , \tag{21.32}\]

which is \(8{,}19\) % above the true value \(0{,}198062\) (SymPy and NumPy), and \(4{,}01\) % in frequency (\(2{,}3339\) Hz instead of \(2{,}2438\) Hz for \(k = 501\,760\) N/m and \(\bar m = 500\) kg). That it is higher also follows from theorem 10.59: with one column \(\vek\psi\), \(\tilde\lambda\) is the Rayleigh quotient \(R(\vek\psi)\) of definition 10.58 and lies above \(\lambda_1\).

Why above, and by how much? On the right of figure 21.25 we lay the two shapes over each other, both with displacement \(1\) of the top floor. The static shape \((\tfrac13,\ \tfrac23,\ 1)^\T\) is grey dashed, the true first mode \((0{,}445,\ 0{,}802,\ 1)^\T\) (NumPy) orange. In the true mode floors \(1\) and \(2\) are further right by \(0{,}112\) and \(0{,}135\). Where does the difference come from? In vibration each floor carries the inertia force \(-\bar m\ddot q_{\mathrm{i}} = \lambda\bar m\,q_{\mathrm{i}}\), which points in the direction of the displacement. In the true mode these are the forces \(0{,}088\), \(0{,}159\) and \(0{,}198\) (in the unit \(k\), that is \(\lambda_1 = 0{,}198\) times the displacement of the floor). Floors \(1\) and \(2\) are therefore loaded and move more than they would without a force. The static shape knows only the force on the top floor and forgets the forces on the two lower ones. The reduced model holds the frame in the static shape, as if floors \(1\) and \(2\) were tied to the top one by two rods, and a constraint can only stiffen a structure, so \(\tilde\lambda\) lies above \(\lambda_1\). That is exactly the price of Guyan reduction, and theorem 21.20 measures it later.

21.4.2 Kept and dependent coordinates

We do the same for a system with many coordinates, which for the frame are the three floors. Let \(\mat K\) and \(\mat M\) be symmetric positive definite matrices of order \(n\) (theorem 10.21) and \(\lambda_1 \le \dots \le \lambda_{\mathrm{n}}\) their eigenvalues. We split the coordinates into two sets. The kept coordinates are labelled \(\mathrm{a}\), their number \(n_{\mathrm{a}}\), and we call them active (aktivne), because the shortened model keeps them as true unknowns. The others are labelled \(\text{d}\), their number is \(n_{\mathrm{d}} = n - n_{\mathrm{a}}\), and we call them dependent (odvisne), because equilibrium will determine their displacements from the displacements of the active ones. The labels \(\mathrm{a}\) and \(\text{d}\) are from CK (section 14.6, PDF p. 469), where the active ones are also called master and the dependent ones slave. We number the coordinates so that the active ones come first. Renumbering is a permutation of rows and columns, which changes neither symmetry nor positive definiteness, since \(\vek x^\T\mat P^\T\mat K\mat P\,\vek x = (\mat P\vek x)^\T\mat K\,(\mat P\vek x) > 0\) for \(\vek x \ne \vek 0\). In blocks the matrices are then

\[\mat K = \begin{pmatrix} \mat K_{\mathrm{aa}} & \mat K_{\mathrm{ad}} \\ \mat K_{\mathrm{da}} & \mat K_{\mathrm{dd}} \end{pmatrix} , \qquad \mat M = \begin{pmatrix} \mat M_{\mathrm{aa}} & \mat M_{\mathrm{ad}} \\ \mat M_{\mathrm{da}} & \mat M_{\mathrm{dd}} \end{pmatrix} , \tag{21.33}\]

with \(\mat K_{\mathrm{da}} = \mat K_{\mathrm{ad}}^\T\) and \(\mat M_{\mathrm{da}} = \mat M_{\mathrm{ad}}^\T\). For the frame \(\mathrm{a} = \{3\}\) and \(\text{d} = \{1, 2\}\). In chapter 12 we labelled the displacements and rotations of a beam \(\mathrm{t}\) and \(\mathrm{r}\) (lemma 12.45), which is a special case of this partition: \(\mathrm{a}\) are the displacements, \(\text{d}\) the rotations. In this chapter the bold \(\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}\) is a mode of vibration, and the rotation of a node is written out in words.

The block \(\mat K_{\mathrm{dd}}\) is positive definite: for a column \(\vek y \ne \vek 0\) the column \(\vek z = (\vek 0, \vek y)\) is nonzero and \(\vek z^\T\mat K\vek z = \vek y^\T\mat K_{\mathrm{dd}}\vek y > 0\) (as in step 2 of the proof of lemma 12.45). By theorem 6.29 it is therefore invertible, and \(\mat M_{\mathrm{dd}}\) is positive definite as well. What does invertibility say in words? If the active coordinates are held, the structure has exactly one equilibrium position for every load on the dependent coordinates, which holds for floors \(1\) and \(2\) of the frame when floor \(3\) is held.

From history

In the years from \(1960\) to \(1970\) computer technology grew fast, but the main obstacle in structural dynamics was the limit on the number of degrees of freedom a computer could still handle (GR, PDF p. 434). At the same time it was found that for accurate internal stresses the model must be divided finely enough, but that for the distribution of the inertia forces a large number of degrees of freedom is superfluous (GR, PDF p. 434). This led to the idea of dynamic reduction: we partition the coordinates and transfer the distribution of the inertia forces statically to a smaller set of coordinates (GR, PDF p. 434). The principle of static condensation for dynamic problems was published by Irons and Guyan in the same year \(1965\), independently of each other (GR, PDF p. 434). After both of them CK calls the method the Guyan-Irons reduction, often just Guyan reduction, and cites R. J. Guyan's article »Reduction of Stiffness and Mass Matrices« in the AIAA Journal of \(1965\) (CK, PDF pp. 469 and 481). At first the reduction was seen as a saver of degrees of freedom, but later it proved useful elsewhere too, for example in the exchange of large models between teams (GR, PDF p. 434). In \(1968\) Anderson, Irons and Zienkiewicz showed how the choice and the number of kept coordinates affect the accuracy of eigenvalues and modes in the vibration and stability of plates (CK, PDF pp. 469 and 481). Exactly this question, which coordinates we keep, will be our test on the cantilever.

Let us return to the partition (21.33): what should the columns of the Ritz basis be if we want the active coordinates to remain the coordinates of the shortened model? For the frame we found them from equilibrium (the static shape), and now we write the same in blocks.

Definition 21.17 Guyan basis (Guyanova baza)

Let \(\mat K\), \(\mat M\) and the partition \(\mathrm{a}\), \(\text{d}\) be as in equation (21.33). The matrix \(\mat\Psi_{\mathrm{d}} = -\mat K_{\mathrm{dd}}^{-1}\mat K_{\mathrm{da}}\) has \(n_{\mathrm{d}}\) rows and \(n_{\mathrm{a}}\) columns, and its column \(s\) holds the displacements of the dependent coordinates (for the frame the floor displacements) when the active coordinate \(s\) is displaced by \(1\), the other active ones are \(0\) and no external forces act on the dependent ones. The Guyan basis (Guyanova baza) is the matrix with \(n\) rows and \(n_{\mathrm{a}}\) columns

\[\mat\Psi_{\mathrm{G}} = \begin{pmatrix} \mat I \\ \mat\Psi_{\mathrm{d}} \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} \mat I \\ -\mat K_{\mathrm{dd}}^{-1}\mat K_{\mathrm{da}} \end{pmatrix} . \tag{21.34}\]

The Guyan approximation (Guyanov približek) is \(\vek q \approx \mat\Psi_{\mathrm{G}}\,\vek q_{\mathrm{a}}\), the reduced matrices \(\tilde{\mat K} = \mat\Psi_{\mathrm{G}}^\T\mat K\,\mat\Psi_{\mathrm{G}}\) and \(\tilde{\mat M} = \mat\Psi_{\mathrm{G}}^\T\mat M\,\mat\Psi_{\mathrm{G}}\) are of order \(n_{\mathrm{a}}\), and the Guyan values \(\tilde\lambda_1 \le \dots \le \tilde\lambda_{\mathrm{n}_{\mathrm{a}}}\) are the eigenvalues of the reduced problem \(\tilde{\mat K}\,\vek x = \tilde\lambda\,\tilde{\mat M}\,\vek x\). Guyan reduction is the Ritz approximation (definition 10.58) with the basis \(\mat\Psi = \mat\Psi_{\mathrm{G}}\), which has independent columns, because from \(\mat\Psi_{\mathrm{G}}\,\vek x = \vek 0\) the first block gives \(\vek x = \vek 0\) (definition 6.22).

Source: CK sections 14.6.2 and 14.6.3 (PDF pp. 466-467 and 469, equations 14.63 and 14.64): static condensation with the row \(\text{d}\) free of forces, and the Ritz matrix »the displacement patterns associated with unit displacement of the respective a-coordinates, while the d-coordinates are released«. GR section 6.9.1 (PDF pp. 499-500, equations 6.148 and 6.151): each column is the »static deformation of the structure when the jth retained degree of freedom is set to one, the others being set to zero«. The block notation and the labels \(\mat\Psi_{\mathrm{G}}\), \(\mat\Psi_{\mathrm{d}}\) are ours.

For the frame \(\mat K_{\mathrm{dd}} = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ -1 & 2\end{pmatrix}\), \(\mat K_{\mathrm{da}} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix}\) and \(\mat K_{\mathrm{dd}}^{-1} = \tfrac13\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{pmatrix}\), so \(\mat\Psi_{\mathrm{d}} = \tfrac13\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 2\end{pmatrix}\) and \(\mat\Psi_{\mathrm{G}} = (\tfrac13,\ \tfrac23,\ 1)^\T\), which is exactly the column of the figure. The row \(\text{d}\) of the product \(\mat K\mat\Psi_{\mathrm{G}}\) is \(\mat K_{\mathrm{da}} + \mat K_{\mathrm{dd}}\mat\Psi_{\mathrm{d}} = \mat 0\), so there are no forces on floors \(1\) and \(2\), and the row \(\mathrm{a}\) is exactly the force \(F\).

21.4.3 Static condensation

What does the reduced system \(\tilde{\mat K}\) say about statics? If no forces act on the dependent coordinates, it should give all displacements exactly, since the Guyan shape is then truly the equilibrium position, for the frame the static shape. Let us show this and also look at what happens when a force acts on a dependent coordinate.

Lemma 21.18 Static condensation (statična kondenzacija)

Let \(\mat K\) be symmetric positive definite with the partition (21.33) and \(\vek F = (\vek F_{\mathrm{a}}, \vek F_{\mathrm{d}})\) a column of forces (for the frame the force on the top floor). Then:

  1. The matrix \(\tilde{\mat K} = \mat\Psi_{\mathrm{G}}^\T\mat K\,\mat\Psi_{\mathrm{G}} = \mat K_{\mathrm{aa}} - \mat K_{\mathrm{ad}}\mat K_{\mathrm{dd}}^{-1}\mat K_{\mathrm{da}}\) is symmetric and positive definite, for the frame \(\tilde K = k/3\) for the force \(F\) on the top floor.
  2. The system \(\mat K\vek q = \vek F\) has exactly one solution. Its active coordinates solve \(\tilde{\mat K}\,\vek q_{\mathrm{a}} = \vek F_{\mathrm{a}} - \mat K_{\mathrm{ad}}\mat K_{\mathrm{dd}}^{-1}\vek F_{\mathrm{d}}\), and the dependent ones are \(\vek q_{\mathrm{d}} = \mat\Psi_{\mathrm{d}}\,\vek q_{\mathrm{a}} + \mat K_{\mathrm{dd}}^{-1}\vek F_{\mathrm{d}}\). For the frame this is the equilibrium of the floors.
  3. If \(\vek F_{\mathrm{d}} = \vek 0\), then \(\vek q = \mat\Psi_{\mathrm{G}}\,\vek q_{\mathrm{a}}\) and \(\tilde{\mat K}\,\vek q_{\mathrm{a}} = \vek F_{\mathrm{a}}\): the reduced system is exact for all coordinates, as for the static shape of the frame.
Proof

We must show that the reduced matrix has the properties of a true stiffness matrix, that all displacements follow from the reduced system, and that with force-free dependent coordinates what we saw for the frame happens.

  1. By the rule for the product of matrices in blocks (definition 1.99), \(\mat K\mat\Psi_{\mathrm{G}} = (\mat K_{\mathrm{aa}} + \mat K_{\mathrm{ad}}\mat\Psi_{\mathrm{d}},\ \mat K_{\mathrm{da}} + \mat K_{\mathrm{dd}}\mat\Psi_{\mathrm{d}})\) by rows, and the second block is \(\mat 0\) by definition 21.17, because \(\mat K_{\mathrm{dd}}\mat\Psi_{\mathrm{d}} = -\mat K_{\mathrm{da}}\). The first block is \(\mat K_{\mathrm{aa}} - \mat K_{\mathrm{ad}}\mat K_{\mathrm{dd}}^{-1}\mat K_{\mathrm{da}}\). With \(\mat\Psi_{\mathrm{G}}^\T = (\mat I,\ \mat\Psi_{\mathrm{d}}^\T)\) the product \(\mat\Psi_{\mathrm{G}}^\T\mat K\mat\Psi_{\mathrm{G}}\) is therefore the first block plus \(\mat\Psi_{\mathrm{d}}^\T\cdot\mat 0\), that is \(\tilde{\mat K}\). For the frame the second block is zero, because no forces act on the floors.
  2. Symmetry: \((\mat\Psi_{\mathrm{G}}^\T\mat K\mat\Psi_{\mathrm{G}})^\T = \mat\Psi_{\mathrm{G}}^\T\mat K^\T\mat\Psi_{\mathrm{G}}\) (lemma 1.102) and \(\mat K^\T = \mat K\). Positivity: for \(\vek x \ne \vek 0\) we have \(\mat\Psi_{\mathrm{G}}\vek x \ne \vek 0\) (the first block is \(\vek x\)), so \(\vek x^\T\tilde{\mat K}\vek x = (\mat\Psi_{\mathrm{G}}\vek x)^\T\mat K\,(\mat\Psi_{\mathrm{G}}\vek x) > 0\). This is point 1.
  3. The rows \(\text{d}\) of the system \(\mat K\vek q = \vek F\), for the frame the equilibria of floors \(1\) and \(2\), are \(\mat K_{\mathrm{da}}\vek q_{\mathrm{a}} + \mat K_{\mathrm{dd}}\vek q_{\mathrm{d}} = \vek F_{\mathrm{d}}\). Since \(\mat K_{\mathrm{dd}}\) is invertible, \(\vek q_{\mathrm{d}} = \mat\Psi_{\mathrm{d}}\vek q_{\mathrm{a}} + \mat K_{\mathrm{dd}}^{-1}\vek F_{\mathrm{d}}\) follows.
  4. The rows \(\mathrm{a}\) are \(\mat K_{\mathrm{aa}}\vek q_{\mathrm{a}} + \mat K_{\mathrm{ad}}\vek q_{\mathrm{d}} = \vek F_{\mathrm{a}}\). We insert \(\vek q_{\mathrm{d}}\) from step 3: \((\mat K_{\mathrm{aa}} + \mat K_{\mathrm{ad}}\mat\Psi_{\mathrm{d}})\,\vek q_{\mathrm{a}} = \vek F_{\mathrm{a}} - \mat K_{\mathrm{ad}}\mat K_{\mathrm{dd}}^{-1}\vek F_{\mathrm{d}}\), which is \(\tilde{\mat K}\,\vek q_{\mathrm{a}}\) on the left side (step 1).
  5. Uniqueness: \(\tilde{\mat K}\) is positive definite by step 2, hence invertible (theorem 6.29), and \(\vek q_{\mathrm{a}}\) is determined, and then \(\vek q_{\mathrm{d}}\) by step 3. Conversely: pairs \((\vek q_{\mathrm{a}}, \vek q_{\mathrm{d}})\) from these equations satisfy both block rows, since they were derived by equivalent transformations. For the frame the force at the top gives a single set of displacements. This is point 2.
  6. For \(\vek F_{\mathrm{d}} = \vek 0\) we have \(\vek q_{\mathrm{d}} = \mat\Psi_{\mathrm{d}}\vek q_{\mathrm{a}}\), so \(\vek q = \mat\Psi_{\mathrm{G}}\vek q_{\mathrm{a}}\), like the static shape of the frame, and the right side of step 4 is \(\vek F_{\mathrm{a}}\). This is point 3.

Source: CK section 14.6.2 (PDF pp. 466-467): equations 14.62 and 14.63 with the lower partition as the static constraint equation. GR section 6.9.1 (PDF p. 499, equations 6.147 and 6.148): separation of the static part. The general load in point 2 and the proof in steps are not from the sources.

Point 3 is the exact answer to the question we started the section with: for loads on the active coordinates the reduced system is exact, because equilibrium truly fixes the dependent coordinates. For the frame this holds for a force on the top floor: for the force \(F\) we have \(\tilde K\,q_3 = F\) with \(\tilde K = k/3\) and \(q_3 = 3F/k\), which is the true displacement of the top of the frame under this force.

Let us also test a case where the force is not only on the active coordinates.

On the same frame on the ground the force \(1\) acts on floor \(2\), and floor \(3\) is still active. The true response follows from \(\mat K\vek q = (0, 1, 0)^\T\): the equation of floor \(3\) is \(q_3 = q_2\), that of floor \(1\) is \(q_2 = 2q_1\), and that of floor \(2\) is \(-q_1 + 2q_2 - q_3 = -q_1 + q_2 = 1\), so \(\vek q = (1,\ 2,\ 2)^\T\), the orange shape. The storey above the force does not drift, because there is no force above it that it would have to carry. If we wrongly hold on to point 3, \(\vek F_{\mathrm{a}} = 0\), and \(\tilde K\,q_3 = 0\) gives \(q_3 = 0\), a displacement that is not there. Point 2, however, correctly accounts for the force on the dependent coordinate: the right side is \(F_{\mathrm{a}} - \mat K_{\mathrm{ad}}\mat K_{\mathrm{dd}}^{-1}\vek F_{\mathrm{d}} = 0 - (0,\ -1)\cdot\tfrac13(1,\ 2)^\T = \tfrac23\), so \(q_3 = (2/3)/(1/3) = 2\), and \(\vek q_{\mathrm{d}} = \tfrac13(1,\ 2)^\T\cdot 2 + \mat K_{\mathrm{dd}}^{-1}(0,\ 1)^\T = (\tfrac23 + \tfrac13,\ \tfrac43 + \tfrac23)^\T = (1,\ 2)^\T\), which is the true answer. The static shape \(\mat\Psi_{\mathrm{G}}\,q_3\) alone would give \((\tfrac23,\ \tfrac43,\ 2)^\T\) for a force on the dependent coordinate, the grey dashed shape, which misses \(\vek q_{\mathrm{d}}\) by the term \(\mat K_{\mathrm{dd}}^{-1}\vek F_{\mathrm{d}} = (\tfrac13,\ \tfrac23)^\T\), the blue differences in the figure.

In dynamics the inertia forces \(-\mat M\ddot{\vek q}\) are exactly such a load on the dependent coordinates, for the frame the forces on floors \(1\) and \(2\). The right side of point 2 is \(\vek F_{\mathrm{a}} + \mat\Psi_{\mathrm{d}}^\T\vek F_{\mathrm{d}}\), because \(\mat\Psi_{\mathrm{d}}^\T = -\mat K_{\mathrm{ad}}\mat K_{\mathrm{dd}}^{-1}\): the inertia force of the dependent coordinates is transferred statically to the active ones by the same matrix we used for the displacements.
