The columns of the middle storey carry two forces and the second floor drifts by \(2\) relative to the first, those of the top storey only one and the third floor goes \(1\) further. The floor displacements are the sums of the drifts, \(3\), \(3 + 2 = 5\) and \(5 + 1 = 6\), and the shape \((3, 5, 6)\) is no longer \((1, 1, 1)\): the starting shape is not a mode. Normalize it with the top floor, \(\vek x_1 = (0{,}5,\ 0{,}8333,\ 1)^\T\). The Rayleigh quotient (definition 10.41) of the starting shape is \(R(\vek x_0) = 1/3\), of the new one \(R(\vek x_1) = 0{,}200000\), which is already only \(1{,}0\) % above the true value \(0{,}198062\) (by theorem 10.42 never below it). Repeat the step five more times and every time the shape comes nearer to the first mode: after the sixth step \(\vek x_6 = (0{,}445044,\ 0{,}801939,\ 1)^\T\) and \(R = 0{,}19806226\). Let us write down what we did.

Definition 21.26 Inverse iteration (inverzna iteracija)

Let \(\mat K\) and \(\mat M\) be symmetric positive definite matrices of order \(n\) and \(\vek x_0 \ne \vek 0\) a starting column. Inverse iteration is the sequence of columns \(\vek x_{\mathrm{k}}\) obtained by solving, in step \(k+1\), the system

\[\mat K\,\vek y_{\mathrm{k}+1} = \mat M\,\vek x_{\mathrm{k}} \tag{21.44}\]

where the right side is the force on the floors and the solution is the static response, and setting \(\vek x_{\mathrm{k}+1} = \vek y_{\mathrm{k}+1}/t_{\mathrm{k}+1}\) with a nonzero number \(t_{\mathrm{k}+1}\), for example such that the last component equals \(1\). The estimate of the eigenvalue after \(k\) steps is the Rayleigh quotient \(R(\vek x_{\mathrm{k}})\).

Source: CK section 15.2.1 (PDF pp. 489-490, equations 15.7 to 15.10): an equation of the form \(\vek u_{\mathrm{s}+1} = \mat D\,\vek u_{\mathrm{s}}\) with the dynamical matrix \(\mat D = \mat K^{-1}\mat M\) and a "scaling factor" that makes the largest element equal to \(1\). The estimate by the Rayleigh quotient is in CK example 15.1 (PDF pp. 491-492).

The number \(t_{\mathrm{k}+1}\) changes neither the shape of the column (in figure 21.45 every iterate is scaled to \(1\) at the top floor, another scaling would only stretch the profile) nor the quotient, since \(R(t\,\vek x) = R(\vek x)\) for every \(t \ne 0\) (numerator and denominator are multiplied by \(t^2\)). So in the proofs we write simply \(\vek x_{\mathrm{k}} = (\mat K^{-1}\mat M)^k\vek x_0\) up to a number.

21.6.2 Why the shape converges

What does the frame actually do during the iteration? The expansion theorem (corollary 10.22) writes every column by modes, \(\vek x_0 = \sum_{\mathrm{r}} c_{\mathrm{r}}\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}\) with \(c_{\mathrm{r}} = \vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}^\T\mat M\,\vek x_0\), so it is enough to see what one step does to one mode. From \(\mat K\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}} = \lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\mat M\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}\) follows \(\mat K^{-1}\mat M\,\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}} = \vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}/\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\). In every step mode \(r\) is multiplied by \(1/\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\), so the mode with the smallest eigenvalue grows most. Figure 21.44 shows this on the numbers of the frame.

The horizontal axis of all three groups is the mode number \(r\). The grey bars are the shares of the modes in the starting shape \((1,1,1)\) relative to the first: the coefficients are \(c_{\mathrm{r}} = 1{,}655971,\ 0{,}473952,\ 0{,}182018\) and the shares \(c_{\mathrm{r}}/c_1\) are \(1\), \(0{,}286\) and \(0{,}110\). The orange bars are the factors by which the step multiplies each mode, \(1/\lambda_{\mathrm{r}} = 5{,}05\), \(0{,}64\) and \(0{,}31\): the first mode grows five times, the other two shrink. When we divide the new shape by the coefficient of the first mode, we get the blue bars: the first is \(1\) again, the second is \(0{,}286\cdot0{,}643/5{,}049 = 0{,}036\) and the third \(0{,}110\cdot0{,}308/5{,}049 = 0{,}0067\). The share of mode \(r\) was multiplied by \(\lambda_1/\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\), that is by \(0{,}127\) and \(0{,}061\). Every further step does the same once more. Figure 21.45 shows what this means for the shape of the frame and for the shares over several steps.

On the axes of the left picture the floor number is vertical and the displacement horizontal, and every shape is scaled so that the displacement of the top floor is \(1\). We see how the starting shape, vertical above the first floor, goes over into the first and second iterate, which cling to the exact first mode (orange). The right picture has on its axes the steps \(k\) horizontally and, vertically on a logarithmic scale, the ratio \(c_{\mathrm{r},\mathrm{k}}/c_{1,\mathrm{k}}\), where \(c_{\mathrm{r},\mathrm{k}}\) is the coefficient of mode \(r\) in the iterate \(\vek x_{\mathrm{k}}\). On it the second mode and the third mode fall along a straight line, which means the content of each decreases by a constant ratio in every step. The first two points of each line are the grey and the blue bar of figure 21.44: \(0{,}2862\) and \(0{,}0365\) for the second mode, \(0{,}1099\) and \(0{,}0067\) for the third. The ratios by steps are computed by the theorem.

Theorem 21.27 Convergence of inverse iteration (konvergenca inverzne iteracije)

Let \(\mat K\), \(\mat M\) be symmetric positive definite, \(\lambda_1 < \lambda_2 \le \dots \le \lambda_{\mathrm{n}}\) the eigenvalues of the pair \((\mat K, \mat M)\) with \(\mat M\)-orthonormal columns \(\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}\) (theorem 10.21) and \(\vek x_{\mathrm{k}} = t_{\mathrm{k}}(\mat K^{-1}\mat M)^k\vek x_0\) with nonzero numbers \(t_{\mathrm{k}}\). Let the start \(\vek x_0 = \sum_{\mathrm{r}} c_{\mathrm{r}}\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}\) have a part of the first mode, \(c_1 \ne 0\). Denote \(d_{\mathrm{r}}^{(k)} = (c_{\mathrm{r}}/c_1)(\lambda_1/\lambda_{\mathrm{r}})^k\) for \(r \ge 2\) (blue bars for \(k = 1\)) and the shape error by \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{k}} = \bigl(\sum_{\mathrm{r}\ge 2}(d_{\mathrm{r}}^{(k)})^2\bigr)^{1/2}\). Then:

  1. The column \(\vek x_{\mathrm{k}}\) equals, up to a number, \(\vek\varphi_1 + \sum_{\mathrm{r}\ge2}d_{\mathrm{r}}^{(k)}\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}\), and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{k}} \le (\lambda_1/\lambda_2)^k\,\varepsilon_0\). The shape converges to the first mode: the iterate clings to the first mode and the content of the second and third modes falls.
  2. \(0 \le R(\vek x_{\mathrm{k}}) - \lambda_1 \le (\lambda_1/\lambda_2)^{2k}\sum_{\mathrm{r}\ge2}(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}} - \lambda_1)(c_{\mathrm{r}}/c_1)^2\). The quotient approaches \(\lambda_1\) from above.
Proof

We must show how the coefficients of the modes change with the steps (point 1) and where this leads for the quotient (point 2).

  1. By the expansion theorem \((\mat K^{-1}\mat M)\sum_{\mathrm{r}} c_{\mathrm{r}}\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}} = \sum_{\mathrm{r}} (c_{\mathrm{r}}/\lambda_{\mathrm{r}})\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}\), because \(\mat K^{-1}\mat M\,\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}} = \vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}/\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\) (multiply \(\mat K\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}} = \lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\mat M\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}\) by \(\mat K^{-1}\)). After \(k\) steps the coefficient of mode \(r\) is \(c_{\mathrm{r}}/\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}^k\). In figure 21.44 this is the multiplication of the grey bars by the orange ones, \(k\) times in a row.
  2. Divide by the coefficient of the first mode \(c_1/\lambda_1^k \ne 0\). The coefficient of mode \(r\) becomes \((c_{\mathrm{r}}/c_1)(\lambda_1/\lambda_{\mathrm{r}})^k = d_{\mathrm{r}}^{(k)}\) and that of the first becomes \(1\). This is the first claim of point 1. For \(k = 1\) these are the blue bars.
  3. Since \(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}} \ge \lambda_2\) for \(r \ge 2\), we have \(\lambda_1/\lambda_{\mathrm{r}} \le \lambda_1/\lambda_2 < 1\) and \(|d_{\mathrm{r}}^{(k)}| \le (\lambda_1/\lambda_2)^k|c_{\mathrm{r}}/c_1|\). Squaring and summing over \(r \ge 2\) gives \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{k}} \le (\lambda_1/\lambda_2)^k\varepsilon_0\). The right side falls toward zero, so the shape approaches \(\vek\varphi_1\): the lines of the second and the third mode fall, the third more steeply, because \(\lambda_1/\lambda_3 < \lambda_1/\lambda_2\).
  4. The Rayleigh quotient is independent of scale, so we compute it with the shares \(1, d_2, \dots, d_{\mathrm{n}}\). By equation (10.59), \(R(\vek x_{\mathrm{k}}) = (\lambda_1 + \sum_{\mathrm{r}\ge2}\lambda_{\mathrm{r}} d_{\mathrm{r}}^2)/(1 + \sum_{\mathrm{r}\ge2}d_{\mathrm{r}}^2)\) and
    \[R(\vek x_{\mathrm{k}}) - \lambda_1 = \frac{\sum_{\mathrm{r}\ge2}(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}} - \lambda_1)\,d_{\mathrm{r}}^2}{1 + \sum_{\mathrm{r}\ge2}d_{\mathrm{r}}^2} .\]
    The numerator is nonnegative because \(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}} \ge \lambda_1\), so the difference is \(\ge 0\).
  5. The denominator is \(\ge 1\), so the difference is at most \(\sum_{\mathrm{r}\ge2}(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}} - \lambda_1)d_{\mathrm{r}}^2\). By step 3, \(d_{\mathrm{r}}^2 \le (\lambda_1/\lambda_2)^{2k}(c_{\mathrm{r}}/c_1)^2\), which gives the upper bound of point 2.

Source: CK section 15.2.2 (PDF pp. 493-494): proof of convergence by expansion in modes, the speed depends on the ratios \(\lambda_1/\lambda_{\mathrm{i}}\), especially \(\lambda_1/\lambda_2\), and on the content of the starting column. The bound for the shape error and the quotient in this notation was added by the book.

Test the bounds on the frame. For \(\vek x_0 = (1,1,1)^\T\) we have \(\lambda_1/\lambda_2 = 0{,}12737\) and its square \(0{,}01622\), the sum in point 2 with the starting shares \(c_2/c_1 = 0{,}2862\) and \(c_3/c_1 = 0{,}1099\) is \(0{,}2862^2\cdot1{,}3569 + 0{,}1099^2\cdot3{,}0489 = 0{,}148\) (in the unit \(k/\bar m\)). The computation by steps (NumPy):

\(k\) \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{k}}\) ratio \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{k}}/\varepsilon_{\mathrm{k}-1}\) \(R(\vek x_{\mathrm{k}}) - \lambda_1\) ratio
0 \(3{,}0659\cdot10^{-1}\) \(1{,}3527\cdot10^{-1}\)
1 \(3{,}7067\cdot10^{-2}\) \(0{,}1209\) \(1{,}9377\cdot10^{-3}\) \(0{,}0143\)
2 \(4{,}6615\cdot10^{-3}\) \(0{,}1258\) \(2{,}9767\cdot10^{-5}\) \(0{,}0154\)
3 \(5{,}9199\cdot10^{-4}\) \(0{,}1270\) \(4{,}7659\cdot10^{-7}\) \(0{,}0160\)
4 \(7{,}5353\cdot10^{-5}\) \(0{,}1273\) \(7{,}7086\cdot10^{-9}\) \(0{,}0162\)
5 \(9{,}5966\cdot10^{-6}\) \(0{,}1274\) \(1{,}2498\cdot10^{-10}\) \(0{,}0162\)
6 \(1{,}2223\cdot10^{-6}\) \(0{,}1274\) \(2{,}0275\cdot10^{-12}\) \(0{,}0162\)

The ratios of the shape error approach \(\lambda_1/\lambda_2 = 0{,}12737\), which is the drop of the blue straight line on the right of the figure in one step, the ratios of the quotient approach its square \(0{,}01622\), as the theorem predicts, and the bound of point 2 at \(k = 6\) is \(0{,}148\cdot0{,}01622^6 = 2{,}7\cdot10^{-12}\), the actual value \(2{,}0\cdot10^{-12}\), so below the bound. The meaning is that the quotient gains twice as many digits as the shape: \(-\log_{10}0{,}12737 = 0{,}895\) digits of shape and \(1{,}790\) digits of quotient per step. The frequency from the quotient by steps \(k = 0\) to \(3\) is \(18{,}2895\), \(14{,}1670\), \(14{,}0993\), \(14{,}0982\) 1/s, the exact one is \(\omega_1 = \sqrt{0{,}198062 \cdot 1003{,}52\ \text{1/s}^2} = 14{,}0982\) 1/s (\(f_1 = 2{,}2438\) Hz). After two steps the frequency is right to four digits (relative error \(7{,}5\cdot10^{-5}\)), while the shape still has the error \(\varepsilon_2 = 4{,}7\cdot10^{-3}\).

This quotient is a Ritz one (definition 10.58): every iterate is one Ritz shape \(\mat\Psi = (\vek x_{\mathrm{k}})\) of order \(m = 1\) and theorem 10.59 guarantees \(R(\vek x_{\mathrm{k}}) \ge \lambda_1\) in every step, which is the left part of point 2: the quotient lies above \(\lambda_1\).

When is the speed bad? At \(\lambda_1/\lambda_2 = 0{,}99\) we need \(229{,}1\) steps for one digit of shape error, for the frame \(1{,}12\) steps. The smallness of the ratio is therefore essential. On the frame every step reduces the shape error to about \(0{,}13\) of the previous one, like the falling line of the second mode, while with a dense spectrum, where the first two eigenvalues are nearly equal, the iteration stalls: the factors of the first two modes are nearly equal, so their share hardly changes. This is why the theorem requires \(\lambda_1 < \lambda_2\). At \(\lambda_1 = \lambda_2\) the ratio is \(1\) and the bound does not fall: the step multiplies both modes by the same factor (two orange bars of equal height), so their share relative to each other stays as it was at the start. The quotient still reaches \(\lambda_1\), but the shape stops at the combination of the two modes that the start had, and this is an eigenshape as well.

On bar \(C\) of section 10.10.5 (steel, \(16\) elements, the start is the static shape under the force at the end) \(\lambda_1/\lambda_2 = 0{,}11040\) and its square \(0{,}012188\). On the axes of the right picture the steps \(k\) run horizontally and the relative error of the frequency vertically, against \(f_1 = 1253{,}70\) Hz of the model with \(16\) elements, on a logarithmic scale. The points are the errors by steps \(0\) to \(3\), \(1{,}02\cdot10^{-1}\), \(6{,}41\cdot10^{-4}\), \(7{,}44\cdot10^{-6}\), \(9{,}01\cdot10^{-8}\), and their ratios \(0{,}0063\), \(0{,}0116\), \(0{,}0121\) approach the square \(0{,}0122\), which the dashed line shows. The start from the static shape is sensible because the first mode already dominates it: the left bar, with its share on the left axis, shows that its \(c_1^2\) is \(98{,}55\) % of the sum \(\sum_{\mathrm{r}} c_{\mathrm{r}}^2\), all the other modes together have \(1{,}45\) %, and the static shape gives \(81{,}12\) % of the displacement of the end (section 10.10.5). So the first step already hits well.

From history

The procedure in this form is older than computers. Vianello used it in 1898 for the buckling of a strut and Stodola in 1904 for the vibration of a rotating shaft (CK, PDF p. 489). CK writes that it is perhaps the most effective procedure for hand computation of a few eigenvalues and modes of a small system, for example with \(N \le 5\) degrees of freedom (CK, PDF p. 489). History is here because it shows that the procedure computes one lowest value and shape without the characteristic polynomial, as hand computation needed: the repeated step leads to the first mode. The rotating shaft comes in chapter 24.

21.6.3 The cost of one step

Step (21.44) means solving a system with the matrix \(\mat K\), which in finite elements is banded (definition 7.40), with only zeros outside the band. The factorization \(\mat K = \mat L\mat D\mat L^\T\) (lemma 7.47) is done only once, then every step needs only two substitutions, forward with \(\mat L\) and backward with \(\mat L^\T\) (and division by \(\mat D\)), and the product \(\mat M\vek x_{\mathrm{k}}\). Each substitution has at most \(b\) terms in every row, where \(b\) is the half bandwidth. For order \(n = 10\,000\) and half bandwidth \(b = 100\) the costs in multiplications are:

job expression multiplications in factorizations of the banded matrix
factorization of a full matrix (equation (7.43)) \(n^3/6\) \(1{,}67\cdot10^{11}\) \(3300\)
factorization of the banded matrix, once (equation (7.44)) at most \(b(b+1)(3n - 2b - 1)/6\) \(5{,}02\cdot10^7\) \(1\)
two substitutions about \(2nb\) \(2{,}0\cdot10^6\) \(1/25\)
the product \(\mat M\vek x_{\mathrm{k}}\) with a banded \(\mat M\) about \(2nb\) \(2{,}0\cdot10^6\) \(1/25\)
one step (the two rows above) about \(4nb\) \(4{,}0\cdot10^6\) \(1/12{,}5\)
\(11\) steps \(11\cdot4nb\) \(4{,}4\cdot10^7\) \(0{,}88\)

Read the table and the figure from the top down, with the multiplications on the logarithmic axis. The factorization of the full matrix is by far the longest row, and the banded factorization saves a factor of \(3300\). The two substitutions and the product with \(\mat M\) cost \(2{,}0\cdot10^6\) each, so less than the banded factorization. One step costs \(12{,}5\) times less than the factorization, so we factorize once and repeat only the substitutions. Why \(11\) steps? At speed \(0{,}13\) per step, as on the frame, ten digits of the shape need \(10/0{,}895 = 11{,}2\) steps. These \(11\) steps cost somewhat less than the factorization itself. The whole iteration, the factorization and the steps together \(9{,}4\cdot10^7\) multiplications, therefore (the whole iteration) costs less than two factorizations, about \(1800\) times less than the factorization of the full matrix.

21.6.4 What does not work: a start without the first mode

The theorem requires \(c_1 \ne 0\). What happens if \(c_1 = 0\)? Take \(\vek x_0 = \vek\varphi_2 + \vek\varphi_3\), which is \(\mat M\)-orthogonal to \(\vek\varphi_1\) up to \(8{,}3\cdot10^{-17}\), that is, up to rounding. Then by step 1 of the proof of the theorem the coefficient of the first mode is zero in all steps, and the iterate stays in the plane of modes \(2\) and \(3\). Its quotient goes toward \(\lambda_2 = 1{,}554958\), since the third mode decreases in the ratio \(\lambda_2/\lambda_3 = 0{,}4789\) per step.

In the figure the horizontal axis counts the steps \(k\) and the vertical one shows the quotient \(R(\vek x_{\mathrm{k}})\). The grey dashed lines are the eigenvalues. No curve reaches the highest, \(\lambda_3\), because the quotient is a weighted mean of the eigenvalues (equation (10.59)) and the share of the third mode falls in every step. The ordinary start is the blue curve, which hits \(\lambda_1\) after a few steps. The start without the first mode (orange) first goes toward \(\lambda_2\): \(R = 2{,}400969\) at \(k = 0\), \(1{,}870613\) at \(k = 1\), \(1{,}556031\) at \(k = 5\), \(1{,}554959\) at \(k = 10\) and \(1{,}554947\) at \(k = 15\). Then it falls: \(1{,}512998\) at \(k = 17\), \(0{,}655418\) at \(k = 18\), \(0{,}209164\) at \(k = 19\), \(0{,}198244\) at \(k = 20\) and \(0{,}198062 = \lambda_1\) from \(k = 22\) on. Why? Rounding in every step returns a small part of the first mode into the iterate, and this part is multiplied in a step against the second by the ratio \(\lambda_2/\lambda_1 = 7{,}851\). From \(8{,}3\cdot10^{-17}\) to a size of order \(1\) it needs \(\ln(1/8{,}3\cdot10^{-17})/\ln 7{,}851 = 17{,}97\) steps, and indeed the orange curve breaks at \(k = 17\) to \(19\). Computing the second mode is therefore impossible with a good start alone: the first mode must be removed in every step, not only at the beginning.

21.6.5 Higher modes: removing those already found

How do we remove the first mode? Once \(\vek\varphi_1\) is known, we subtract from any column \(\vek x\) its parallel component. Figure 21.50 shows this in the plane of the first two modes of the frame.

The axes \(\eta_1\) and \(\eta_2\) are the coefficients of the column at the first and second mode, \(\eta_{\mathrm{r}} = \vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}^\T\mat M\,\vek x\) (corollary 10.22). Divide the column \(\vek x\) into the part along the first mode and the remainder, which is perpendicular to it, as the parallel line to the axis shows. We write this in general.

Lemma 21.28 Removing the found modes and iteration of a higher mode (\(\mat M\)-Gram-Schmidt sweeping, \(\mat M\)-Gram-Schmidtova ortogonalizacija)

Let \(\vek\varphi_1, \dots, \vek\varphi_{\mathrm{p}}\) be the first \(\mat M\)-orthonormal eigencolumns (theorem 10.21) and

\[\mat S_{\mathrm{p}} = \mat I - \sum_{\mathrm{s}=1}^p\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{s}}\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{s}}^\T\mat M . \tag{21.45}\]

The matrix \(\mat S_{\mathrm{p}}\) takes from a column the parts along the first \(p\) modes and leaves the remainder. Then:

  1. For \(\vek x = \sum_{\mathrm{r}} c_{\mathrm{r}}\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}\) we have \(\mat S_{\mathrm{p}}\vek x = \sum_{\mathrm{r}>\mathrm{p}}c_{\mathrm{r}}\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}\), and \(\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{s}}^\T\mat M\,\mat S_{\mathrm{p}}\vek x = 0\) for \(s \le p\). In figure 21.50 this is the remainder, which the parallel line separates from the axis of the first mode.
  2. If \(\lambda_{\mathrm{p}+1} < \lambda_{\mathrm{p}+2}\) and \(c_{\mathrm{p}+1} \ne 0\), the iteration \(\vek x_{\mathrm{k}+1} = t\,\mat S_{\mathrm{p}}\mat K^{-1}\mat M\,\vek x_{\mathrm{k}}\) with the start \(\mat S_{\mathrm{p}}\vek x_0\) (and nonzero numbers \(t\)) satisfies theorem 21.27 with \(\lambda_{\mathrm{p}+1}\) in place of \(\lambda_1\) and \(\lambda_{\mathrm{p}+2}\) in place of \(\lambda_2\): the shape of \(\vek x_{\mathrm{k}}\) converges to \(\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{p}+1}\) with the ratio \(\lambda_{\mathrm{p}+1}/\lambda_{\mathrm{p}+2}\) per step and the quotient to \(\lambda_{\mathrm{p}+1}\) with its square. For \(p = 1\) on the frame this is the line of the quotient error in figure 21.51.
Proof

We must show what the matrix \(\mat S_{\mathrm{p}}\) does to the expansion, and then that the steps of the iteration keep the zeros.

  1. By the expansion theorem \(c_{\mathrm{s}} = \vek\varphi_{\mathrm{s}}^\T\mat M\,\vek x\). So \(\mat S_{\mathrm{p}}\vek x = \vek x - \sum_{\mathrm{s}\le \mathrm{p}}c_{\mathrm{s}}\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{s}} = \sum_{\mathrm{r}>\mathrm{p}}c_{\mathrm{r}}\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}\).
  2. The coefficient of mode \(s \le p\) in \(\mat S_{\mathrm{p}}\vek x\) is zero, so \(\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{s}}^\T\mat M\,\mat S_{\mathrm{p}}\vek x = 0\). This is the first point.
  3. The step \(\mat K^{-1}\mat M\) divides the coefficients by \(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\) (step 1 of theorem 21.27), and \(\mat S_{\mathrm{p}}\) sets those with \(r \le p\) to zero again. After \(k\) steps mode \(r > p\) has \(c_{\mathrm{r}}/\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}^k\) up to a number.
  4. The proof of theorem 21.27 from step 2 on (division by the coefficient of mode \(p+1\), estimates with \(\lambda_{\mathrm{p}+1}/\lambda_{\mathrm{r}} \le \lambda_{\mathrm{p}+1}/\lambda_{\mathrm{p}+2}\)) stays the same, because the sum runs only over \(r \ge p+2\).

Source: CK section 15.2.3 (PDF pp. 494-496, equations 15.16 to 15.22): removal by Gram-Schmidt, the "sweeping matrix" \(\mat S_1\) in example 15.2, removal in every step because rounding reintroduces the first mode. The notation with \(\mat M\)-orthonormal columns and the bounds are ours.

On the frame with the start \((1,1,1)\) and removal of \(\vek\varphi_1\) in every step the quotient by steps \(k = 0\) to \(7\) is \(1{,}772437\), \(1{,}610318\), \(1{,}567983\), \(1{,}557963\), \(1{,}555648\), \(1{,}555116\), \(1{,}554994\), \(1{,}554966\) and the errors against \(\lambda_2 = 1{,}554958\) on the logarithmic axis are \(2{,}175\cdot10^{-1}\), \(5{,}536\cdot10^{-2}\), \(1{,}302\cdot10^{-2}\), \(3{,}005\cdot10^{-3}\), \(6{,}901\cdot10^{-4}\), \(1{,}583\cdot10^{-4}\), \(3{,}631\cdot10^{-5}\), \(8{,}327\cdot10^{-6}\). The ratios of successive errors \(0{,}2546\), \(0{,}2353\), \(0{,}2307\), \(0{,}2297\), \(0{,}2294\), \(0{,}2294\), \(0{,}2293\) approach the square of the ratio, \((\lambda_2/\lambda_3)^2 = 0{,}22934\) (the dashed line), as the lemma says. The speed here is worse than for the first mode (\(0{,}016\)), because the ratio \(\lambda_2/\lambda_3 = 0{,}479\) is closer to \(1\) than \(\lambda_1/\lambda_2 = 0{,}127\).

21.6.6 What does not work: removal only at the start

The lemma says we must remove the mode in every step. What if we remove it only at the start? In practice \(\vek\varphi_1\) is only approximate. Take \(\vek\varphi_1\) from four steps of inverse iteration with the start \((1,1,1)\), which has a shape error \(7{,}5\cdot10^{-5}\), and remove the first mode with it. The remainder then still has \(|c_1| = 7{,}1\cdot10^{-5}\). If we remove only at the start, this part is multiplied by \(\lambda_2/\lambda_1 = 7{,}851\) per step, and by steps \(k = 0, 2, 4, 6\) we have \(|c_1| = 7{,}1\cdot10^{-5}\), \(4{,}7\cdot10^{-3}\), \(2{,}8\cdot10^{-1}\), \(1{,}0\). The quotient by steps \(k = 0, 2, \dots, 12\) is \(1{,}772531\), \(1{,}567959\), \(1{,}451422\), \(0{,}202342\), \(0{,}198063\), \(0{,}198062\), \(0{,}198062\) and the iteration ends at the first mode, as with the start without the first mode. If we remove in every step, \(|c_1| = 7{,}5\cdot10^{-5}\) stays for all steps and the quotient goes toward \(1{,}554958\) (\(1{,}554994\) at \(k = 6\), \(1{,}554960\) at \(k = 8\) and \(1{,}554958\) from \(k = 10\) on). Removal in every step therefore holds even when \(\vek\varphi_1\) is only approximate.

21.6.7 The shift: other modes with the same method

Removal needs all the lower modes. Is it possible to reach the mode we need without them? Instead of the matrix \(\mat K\) take a matrix that has its smallest eigenvalue where we search. Figure 21.52 shows this on the frame.

At the top, without a shift, the highest bar is at \(\lambda_1\) (amplification \(5{,}049\) against \(0{,}643\) and \(0{,}308\)). Below, with a shift \(\lambda_0 = 1{,}4\), the highest bar is at \(\lambda_2\) (\(6{,}453\) against \(0{,}832\) and \(0{,}541\)), because the distance \(|\lambda_2 - \lambda_0| = 0{,}155\) is the smallest. The amplification of mode \(r\) is the reciprocal of this distance.

Definition 21.29 Spectrum shift (premik spektra)

Let \(\mat K\), \(\mat M\) be as in definition 21.26 and \(\lambda_0\) a real number that is not an eigenvalue of the pair \((\mat K, \mat M)\). Inverse iteration with the shift \(\lambda_0\), which in figure 21.52 is the lower row, solves in every step

\[(\mat K - \lambda_0\mat M)\,\vek y_{\mathrm{k}+1} = \mat M\,\vek x_{\mathrm{k}} . \tag{21.46}\]

Source: CK section 15.2.4 (PDF p. 497, equations 15.23 to 15.25): "let \(\mu\) be a number in the vicinity of the frequency of interest", in this book written \(\lambda_0\) because \(\mu\) means the absorber ratio.

The name is because all eigenvalues are shifted by \(\lambda_0\): \((\mat K - \lambda_0\mat M)\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}} = (\lambda_{\mathrm{r}} - \lambda_0)\mat M\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}\), the spectrum moves along the axis downward by \(\lambda_0\). The eigenvalues of the shifted pair are \(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}} - \lambda_0\), and their absolute values are the distances below the lower axis of the figure. The matrix \(\mat K - \lambda_0\mat M\) is invertible: if \((\mat K - \lambda_0\mat M)\vek v = \vek 0\) for \(\vek v \ne \vek 0\), then \(\mat K\vek v = \lambda_0\mat M\vek v\) and by corollary 10.22 \(\lambda_0\) would be an eigenvalue. For \(\lambda_0 > \lambda_1\) it is no longer positive definite, so lemma 7.47 does not hold for it and the factorization may need adapting (row exchange), which we do not prove here.

Corollary 21.30 Inverse iteration with a shift (inverzna iteracija s premikom)

Let \(\lambda_0\) be as in definition 21.29 and let \(\lambda_{\mathrm{j}}\) be the only eigenvalue nearest to \(\lambda_0\) (the shortest distance): \(|\lambda_{\mathrm{j}} - \lambda_0| < |\lambda_{\mathrm{r}} - \lambda_0|\) for every \(r \ne j\). Let \(c_{\mathrm{j}} \ne 0\) and \(\rho = |\lambda_{\mathrm{j}} - \lambda_0|/\min_{\mathrm{r}\ne \mathrm{j}}|\lambda_{\mathrm{r}} - \lambda_0| < 1\). Then the shape of the iterates converges to \(\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{j}}\), because the amplification of mode \(j\) is the largest, the shape error \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{k}}\), defined as in theorem 21.27 with mode \(j\) in place of the first, satisfies \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{k}} \le \rho^k\varepsilon_0\), and

\[|R(\vek x_{\mathrm{k}}) - \lambda_{\mathrm{j}}| \le \rho^{2k}\sum_{\mathrm{r}\ne \mathrm{j}}|\lambda_{\mathrm{r}} - \lambda_{\mathrm{j}}|\,(c_{\mathrm{r}}/c_{\mathrm{j}})^2 .\]
Proof

We must show that the proof of theorem 21.27 stayed the same with another number in the denominator.

  1. Denote \(\mu_{\mathrm{r}} = \lambda_{\mathrm{r}} - \lambda_0\). From \((\mat K - \lambda_0\mat M)\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}} = \mu_{\mathrm{r}}\mat M\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}\) follows \((\mat K - \lambda_0\mat M)^{-1}\mat M\,\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}} = \vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}/\mu_{\mathrm{r}}\) (equation (21.46), \(\mu_{\mathrm{r}} \ne 0\)).
  2. After \(k\) steps the coefficient of mode \(r\) is \(c_{\mathrm{r}}/\mu_{\mathrm{r}}^k\) up to a number. Divide by the coefficient of mode \(j\) and obtain \(d_{\mathrm{r}}^{(k)} = (c_{\mathrm{r}}/c_{\mathrm{j}})(\mu_{\mathrm{j}}/\mu_{\mathrm{r}})^k\) for \(r \ne j\), with \(|\mu_{\mathrm{j}}/\mu_{\mathrm{r}}| \le \rho < 1\). As in step 3 of theorem 21.27, \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{k}} \le \rho^k\varepsilon_0\).
  3. By equation (10.59), \(R(\vek x_{\mathrm{k}}) - \lambda_{\mathrm{j}} = \sum_{\mathrm{r}\ne \mathrm{j}}(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}} - \lambda_{\mathrm{j}})d_{\mathrm{r}}^2/(1 + \sum_{\mathrm{r}\ne \mathrm{j}}d_{\mathrm{r}}^2)\). The denominator is \(\ge 1\) and \(d_{\mathrm{r}}^2 \le \rho^{2k}(c_{\mathrm{r}}/c_{\mathrm{j}})^2\), which gives the bound. The sign of the difference is now not determined, because \(\lambda_{\mathrm{j}}\) is no longer the lowest, so the bound is for the absolute value.

Source: CK section 15.2.4 (PDF p. 497): "a proof similar to that in Eqs. 15.11 through 15.15 can be used to show that inverse iteration applied to the shifted eigenproblem [...] produces convergence to the \(\lambda_{\mathrm{i}}\) closest to the shift value". The derivation of the bounds is ours.

Test on the frame. At \(\lambda_0 = 1{,}4\) the distances are \(|\mu_{\mathrm{r}}| = 1{,}201938,\ 0{,}154958,\ 1{,}84698\), the nearest is \(\lambda_2\), and \(\rho = 0{,}154958/1{,}201938 = 0{,}12892\). The quotients by steps \(1\) to \(5\) are \(1{,}32773\), \(1{,}55041\), \(1{,}55488\), \(1{,}55496\), \(1{,}55496\) and the errors \(2{,}27\cdot10^{-1}\), \(4{,}55\cdot10^{-3}\), \(7{,}60\cdot10^{-5}\), \(1{,}26\cdot10^{-6}\), \(2{,}10\cdot10^{-8}\) with the ratios \(0{,}0200\), \(0{,}0167\), \(0{,}0166\), \(0{,}0166\) against \(\rho^2 = 0{,}01662\). The shift therefore reaches the second mode without removing the first, and the speed is nearly that for the first mode without a shift (\(0{,}0166\) against \(0{,}0162\)), because the ratio of distances \(\rho = 0{,}1289\) is nearly the ratio \(\lambda_1/\lambda_2 = 0{,}1274\). At \(\lambda_0 = 3{,}0\) the distances are \(2{,}802,\ 1{,}445,\ 0{,}247\) and the iteration goes to \(\lambda_3 = 3{,}246980\) with \(\rho = 0{,}17092\) (\(\rho^2 = 0{,}02921\)): quotients \(2{,}0\), \(3{,}22222\), \(3{,}24658\), \(3{,}24697\). The shift is near \(\lambda_3\) against the spacing of the eigenvalues: the distance \(0{,}247\) is \(0{,}17\) of the distance to the second nearest. A good choice of shift therefore has \(\rho \ll 1\), which means \(|\lambda_{\mathrm{j}} - \lambda_0|\) must be several times smaller than every other distance.

The condition of a unique nearest eigenvalue is essential. Take the shift \(\lambda_0 = 0{,}876510\), the midpoint between \(\lambda_1\) and \(\lambda_2\), where both distances are \(0{,}678448\). On the top axis \(\lambda_0\) lies between the first two eigenvalues. Then modes \(1\) and \(2\) are amplified equally, the third less, and the iteration converges to neither: the coefficients of the first two modes in the normalized iterate are, bottom left, by steps, \((-0{,}961, 0{,}275)\), \((0{,}961, 0{,}275)\), \((-0{,}961, 0{,}275)\), ... (the third decays), the sign of the first oscillates, the second stays, and the quotient goes toward \(0{,}300797\) (bottom right). This is not an eigenvalue but the weighted mean \((\lambda_1c_1^2 + \lambda_2c_2^2)/(c_1^2 + c_2^2)\) for \(c = (0{,}961398,\ 0{,}27516)\), which are the coefficients \(c_1 = 1{,}655971\) and \(c_2 = 0{,}473952\) of the start divided by \(\sqrt{c_1^2 + c_2^2}\). The corollary does not apply here, because the nearest eigenvalue is not unique: the ratio is \(\rho = 1\), so the bound \(\rho^{2k}\sum_{\mathrm{r}\ne \mathrm{j}}|\lambda_{\mathrm{r}} - \lambda_{\mathrm{j}}|(c_{\mathrm{r}}/c_{\mathrm{j}})^2\) does not decrease with the steps.

On the axis the illustrative eigenvalues are \(0\), \(0{,}6\) and \(1{,}4\). For a system with rigid-body modes \(\mat K\) is singular and the inverse does not exist, the amplification \(1/|\lambda_{\mathrm{r}} - \lambda_0|\) is infinite at \(\lambda_0 = 0\). A small shift removes the singularity (CK, PDF p. 497), because \(\mat K - \lambda_0\mat M\) becomes invertible and the amplification is finite. For other procedures for such systems CK refers to another source (PDF p. 497), we do not treat them.

The section showed that one eigenvalue and its mode can be found with one factorization and the repetition of a static computation, and that the speed is determined by the ratio \(\lambda_1/\lambda_2\) (or with removal \(\lambda_{\mathrm{p}+1}/\lambda_{\mathrm{p}+2}\), with a shift the ratio of distances). The speed may be good or bad, and it leads us to the question of whether we should not improve several columns at once and in every step take the best combinations by a Ritz step. This is done by subspace iteration in the next section.

We do not treat the QR method, Householder, Jacobi, Sturm sequences and the determinant search: they are in CK sections 15.1 and 15.4 (PDF pp. 487-489 and 501-506) and are not proved in this book.

21.7 Subspace iteration (iteracija podprostora)

Inverse iteration from section 21.6 finds one mode. For the first \(p\) modes we must repeat it \(p\) times and in every step remove the modes already found from the column (lemma 21.28). The speed depends on the ratio of the wanted eigenvalue to the next one, and if the two are close it is slow. Could we iterate several columns at once and leave the orthogonality to someone else? The Ritz approximation of chapter 10 already does this job: from any independent columns it makes \(\mat M\)-orthonormal Ritz shapes (lemma 10.57). This section therefore takes \(q\) columns, makes one step of inverse iteration on each, and then a Ritz step, which orthonormalizes the columns and sorts them by eigenvalue. The procedure is called subspace iteration (iteracija podprostora) because no single column converges, but the space the columns span: in every step this space comes closer to the space of the first \(q\) modes. The section fixes what the procedure does, proves how fast the Ritz values approach the eigenvalues, and shows on the cantilever of chapter 12 which \(q\) pays off and when the procedure fails. The path is the same as for all earlier reduced models: every step is a Ritz approximation (definition 10.58), so the upper bound of theorem 10.59 holds, the only difference being that the basis \(\mat\Psi\) improves itself (CK section 15.3, PDF p. 498).

We read the figure by rows. Every graph has the clamp on the left, the beam axis and the exact mode \(\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}\) as a grey dashed line: the first has one bend, the second one zero, the third two. In the row \(k = 0\) the start column, taken from the first three columns of the start block, is a random curve that resembles anything more than a mode. After one step the three blue curves are already close to the grey dashed ones, and after two they nearly cover them in the figure. This section tells why this happens and how fast.

21.7.1 The procedure

A step of inverse iteration is a static problem: from a column of shape \(\vek x\) we form the inertia forces \(\mat M\,\vek x\) and find the displacements \(\vek y\) these forces cause, \(\mat K\,\vek y = \mat M\,\vek x\) (CK, step 6 in table 15.1, PDF p. 500 and remark 4, PDF p. 501). For \(q\) columns we solve \(q\) such static problems with the same matrix \(\mat K\), which we factorize once (lemma 7.47), and every further static problem is only forward and back substitution. Instead of normalizing the columns one by one, we now send them together into a Ritz step.

We build the figure from left to right. The block \(\mat X_{\mathrm{k}-1}\) is \(q\) columns at the start of the step. From each one comes an inertia force, a column of \(\mat M\,\mat X_{\mathrm{k}-1}\). Each force goes through a static problem with the same matrix \(\mat K\) and gives a column of \(\mat Y_{\mathrm{k}}\). We squeeze the columns \(\mat Y_{\mathrm{k}}\) into the reduced matrices of order \(q\), their eigenproblem gives the matrix \(\mat A_{\mathrm{k}}\) and the estimates \(\tilde\lambda\), and the new block \(\mat X_{\mathrm{k}} = \mat Y_{\mathrm{k}}\,\mat A_{\mathrm{k}}\) goes into the next step.

Definition 21.31 Subspace iteration (iteracija podprostora)

Let \(\mat K\) and \(\mat M\) be symmetric positive definite matrices of order \(n\) (definition 6.27), \(1 \le q \le n\) and \(\mat X_0\) a matrix with \(n\) rows and \(q\) linearly independent columns (definition 6.22), the start block (začetni blok). Subspace iteration (iteracija podprostora) is the sequence of matrices \(\mat X_{\mathrm{k}}\), \(k = 1, 2, \dots\), obtained by doing the following in step \(k\):

  1. Solve \(q\) static problems, \(\mat K\,\mat Y_{\mathrm{k}} = \mat M\,\mat X_{\mathrm{k}-1}\).
  2. Form the reduced matrices \(\tilde{\mat K}_{\mathrm{k}} = \mat Y_{\mathrm{k}}^\T\mat K\,\mat Y_{\mathrm{k}}\) and \(\tilde{\mat M}_{\mathrm{k}} = \mat Y_{\mathrm{k}}^\T\mat M\,\mat Y_{\mathrm{k}}\) of order \(q\).
  3. Solve the reduced eigenproblem \(\tilde{\mat K}_{\mathrm{k}}\,\mat A_{\mathrm{k}} = \tilde{\mat M}_{\mathrm{k}}\,\mat A_{\mathrm{k}}\,\tilde{\mat\Lambda}_{\mathrm{k}}\) with \(\mat A_{\mathrm{k}}^\T\tilde{\mat M}_{\mathrm{k}}\,\mat A_{\mathrm{k}} = \mat I\) and \(\tilde{\mat\Lambda}_{\mathrm{k}} = \mathrm{diag}\big(\tilde\lambda^{(k)}_1, \dots, \tilde\lambda^{(k)}_{\mathrm{q}}\big)\), \(\tilde\lambda^{(k)}_1 \le \dots \le \tilde\lambda^{(k)}_{\mathrm{q}}\) (the columns of the matrix \(\mat A_{\mathrm{k}}\) are \(\vek a_1, \dots, \vek a_{\mathrm{q}}\) of lemma 10.57).
  4. Set \(\mat X_{\mathrm{k}} = \mat Y_{\mathrm{k}}\,\mat A_{\mathrm{k}}\).

The numbers \(\tilde\lambda^{(k)}_{\mathrm{r}}\) are the estimates of the eigenvalues, the columns of the matrix \(\mat X_{\mathrm{k}}\) the estimates of the modes after \(k\) steps.

Source: CK section 15.3 (PDF pp. 498-501, table 15.1 on p. 500): the table has steps 0 to 7 with the choice of the start loads, the static problem, the reduced matrices, the reduced eigenproblem, the estimates of the modes and the improved loads. The symbols \(\mat Y_{\mathrm{k}}\), \(\mat A_{\mathrm{k}}\), \(\tilde{\mat\Lambda}_{\mathrm{k}}\) are ours. GR section 6.8.1 (PDF pp. 482-484, (6.112) to (6.116)) has the same steps with normalized \(\mat Z_{\mathrm{k}}\) and other symbols. BATHE section 11.6.2 (PDF pp. 975-976, (11.151) to (11.155)).

The Ritz step is always the same here: the reduced basis \(\mat\Psi = \mat Y_{\mathrm{k}}\) has \(q\) columns, and the estimates are Ritz values (definition 10.58). Whether the start is enough for \(\mat Y_{\mathrm{k}}\) to stay independent and for the estimates to be really Ritz values, we check in the lemma.

We build this figure part by part too. The previous space \(\mathcal S_{\mathrm{k}-1}\) is the plane of the columns \(\mat X_{\mathrm{k}-1}\). The step \(\mat K^{-1}\mat M\) maps it to the space \(\mathcal S_{\mathrm{k}}\). In it the columns \(\mat Y_{\mathrm{k}}\) are slanted, because a static problem does not keep orthogonality, the columns \(\mat X_{\mathrm{k}}\) span the same plane but are \(\mat M\)-orthonormal, and any other basis \(\mat Y_{\mathrm{k}}\mat T\) is just one more window onto the same plane.

Lemma 21.32 Steps of subspace iteration are Ritz steps (koraki iteracije podprostora so Ritzovi koraki)

Let \(\mat K\), \(\mat M\), \(q\), \(\mat X_0\), \(\mat Y_{\mathrm{k}}\), \(\mat X_{\mathrm{k}}\), \(\tilde\lambda^{(k)}_{\mathrm{r}}\) be as in definition 21.31 and \(\lambda_1 \le \dots \le \lambda_{\mathrm{n}}\) the eigenvalues of the pair \((\mat K, \mat M)\). Let \(\mathcal S_{\mathrm{k}}\) be the column space of the matrix \(\mat X_{\mathrm{k}}\) (the set of all linear combinations). Then for every \(k \ge 1\):

  1. The columns of the matrix \(\mat Y_{\mathrm{k}}\) are independent, so step 3 is well defined and \(\mat A_{\mathrm{k}}\) is invertible.
  2. \(\mat X_{\mathrm{k}}^\T\mat M\,\mat X_{\mathrm{k}} = \mat I\) and \(\mat X_{\mathrm{k}}^\T\mat K\,\mat X_{\mathrm{k}} = \tilde{\mat\Lambda}_{\mathrm{k}}\). The columns are \(\mat M\)-orthonormal, hence independent.
  3. \(\mathcal S_{\mathrm{k}} = (\mat K^{-1}\mat M)\,\mathcal S_{\mathrm{k}-1}\), so \(\mathcal S_{\mathrm{k}}\) is the column space of the matrix \((\mat K^{-1}\mat M)^k\mat X_0\).
  4. The numbers \(\tilde\lambda^{(k)}_{\mathrm{r}}\) are the Ritz values of the basis \(\mat Y_{\mathrm{k}}\) and stay the same for every other basis of the space \(\mathcal S_{\mathrm{k}}\). They satisfy \(\tilde\lambda^{(k)}_{\mathrm{r}} \ge \lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\) for \(r = 1, \dots, q\), and \(\tilde{\mat K}_{\mathrm{k}} = \mat Y_{\mathrm{k}}^\T\mat M\,\mat X_{\mathrm{k}-1}\).
Proof

We must show that lemma 10.57 really applies to the basis \(\mat Y_{\mathrm{k}}\), then read off the orthonormality and the space from it, and finally show that \(\tilde\lambda\) depends only on the space.

  1. By induction on \(k\) let \(\mat X_{\mathrm{k}-1}\) have independent columns (for \(k = 1\) this is the assumption). If \(\mat Y_{\mathrm{k}}\,\vek b = \vek 0\), then \(\mat M\,\mat X_{\mathrm{k}-1}\vek b = \mat K\,\mat Y_{\mathrm{k}}\vek b = \vek 0\). For \(\vek w = \mat X_{\mathrm{k}-1}\vek b\) we get \(\vek w^\T\mat M\,\vek w = 0\), hence \(\vek w = \vek 0\) (definition 6.27), and since the columns of \(\mat X_{\mathrm{k}-1}\) are independent, \(\vek b = \vek 0\). The columns of the matrix \(\mat Y_{\mathrm{k}}\) are independent. By lemma 10.57 \(\tilde{\mat M}_{\mathrm{k}}\) is positive definite and \(\mat A_{\mathrm{k}}\) with the required properties exists.
  2. By lemma 10.57, point 2, \(\mat X_{\mathrm{k}}^\T\mat M\,\mat X_{\mathrm{k}} = \mat A_{\mathrm{k}}^\T\tilde{\mat M}_{\mathrm{k}}\mat A_{\mathrm{k}} = \mat I\) and \(\mat X_{\mathrm{k}}^\T\mat K\,\mat X_{\mathrm{k}} = \mat A_{\mathrm{k}}^\T\tilde{\mat K}_{\mathrm{k}}\mat A_{\mathrm{k}} = \tilde{\mat\Lambda}_{\mathrm{k}}\), because \(\tilde{\mat K}_{\mathrm{k}}\mat A_{\mathrm{k}} = \tilde{\mat M}_{\mathrm{k}}\mat A_{\mathrm{k}}\tilde{\mat\Lambda}_{\mathrm{k}}\) and \(\mat A_{\mathrm{k}}^\T\tilde{\mat M}_{\mathrm{k}}\mat A_{\mathrm{k}} = \mat I\). If \(\mat X_{\mathrm{k}}\vek b = \vek 0\), we multiply by \(\mat X_{\mathrm{k}}^\T\mat M\) and get \(\vek b = \vek 0\). So the columns of \(\mat X_{\mathrm{k}}\) are independent, which completes the induction of step 1.
  3. If \(\mat A_{\mathrm{k}}\vek b = \vek 0\), then \(\vek b = \mat A_{\mathrm{k}}^\T\tilde{\mat M}_{\mathrm{k}}\mat A_{\mathrm{k}}\vek b = \vek 0\). By lemma 8.22 \(\mat A_{\mathrm{k}}\) is invertible, so \(\mat Y_{\mathrm{k}} = \mat X_{\mathrm{k}}\mat A_{\mathrm{k}}^{-1}\) and \(\mat X_{\mathrm{k}} = \mat Y_{\mathrm{k}}\mat A_{\mathrm{k}}\) have the same column space. Since \(\mat Y_{\mathrm{k}} = \mat K^{-1}\mat M\,\mat X_{\mathrm{k}-1}\), we have \(\mathcal S_{\mathrm{k}} = (\mat K^{-1}\mat M)\,\mathcal S_{\mathrm{k}-1}\), and by induction \(\mathcal S_{\mathrm{k}}\) is the column space of the matrix \((\mat K^{-1}\mat M)^k\mat X_0\).
  4. The Ritz values of the basis \(\mat Y_{\mathrm{k}}\) are \(\tilde\lambda^{(k)}_{\mathrm{r}}\) by definition 10.58, and \(\tilde\lambda^{(k)}_{\mathrm{r}} \ge \lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\) by theorem 10.59, point 1. Let \(\mat\Psi' = \mat Y_{\mathrm{k}}\mat T\) be another basis of the space \(\mathcal S_{\mathrm{k}}\) (\(q\) independent columns, each a combination of the columns of \(\mat Y_{\mathrm{k}}\), and \(\mat T\) square). From \(\mat T\vek b = \vek 0\) it follows that \(\mat\Psi'\vek b = \vek 0\) and \(\vek b = \vek 0\), so \(\mat T\) is invertible (lemma 8.22). The reduced matrices of the basis \(\mat\Psi'\) are \(\mat T^\T\tilde{\mat K}_{\mathrm{k}}\mat T\) and \(\mat T^\T\tilde{\mat M}_{\mathrm{k}}\mat T\), and \(\mat T^\T(\tilde{\mat K}_{\mathrm{k}} - \lambda\tilde{\mat M}_{\mathrm{k}})\mat T\,\vek a = \vek 0\) exactly when \((\tilde{\mat K}_{\mathrm{k}} - \lambda\tilde{\mat M}_{\mathrm{k}})\,\mat T\vek a = \vek 0\) (\(\mat T^\T\) is invertible). The map \(\vek a \mapsto \mat T\vek a\) therefore takes eigencolumns of one problem to eigencolumns of the other with the same eigenvalue, and independent ones to independent ones, so the ordered lists of eigenvalues are equal (as in step 8 of the proof of theorem 10.59). Finally, by step 1 of definition 21.31, \(\tilde{\mat K}_{\mathrm{k}} = \mat Y_{\mathrm{k}}^\T(\mat K\,\mat Y_{\mathrm{k}}) = \mat Y_{\mathrm{k}}^\T\mat M\,\mat X_{\mathrm{k}-1}\).

Source: The proof is not from a source. CK (PDF p. 499) says that the step \(\tilde{\mat K}\), \(\tilde{\mat M}\) is a "Ritz approximation", and BATHE (PDF p. 977) that "one subspace iteration ... in fact, a Ritz analysis", so the estimates are upper bounds.

The last point gives two things. Every step has all the advantages of a Ritz approximation: the estimates are upper bounds (definition 10.58 and theorem 10.59), and the space \(\mathcal S_{\mathrm{k}}\) is what counts, the basis in it does not change the values. And \(\tilde{\mat K}_{\mathrm{k}}\) needs no new multiplication by \(\mat K\): we get it from the columns already computed, it costs only \(q^2\) scalar products and saves multiplying a large matrix by \(q\) columns.

21.7.2 Why the space converges

Look at the space \(\mathcal S_{\mathrm{k}}\) in modal coordinates. If \(\vek x = \sum_{\mathrm{s}} c_{\mathrm{s}}\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{s}}\) (corollary 10.22), then \(\mat K^{-1}\mat M\,\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{s}} = \vek\varphi_{\mathrm{s}}/\lambda_{\mathrm{s}}\) (from \(\mat K\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{s}} = \lambda_{\mathrm{s}}\mat M\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{s}}\), where \(\lambda_{\mathrm{s}} = R(\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{s}}) > 0\) because \(\mat K\) is positive definite), so \((\mat K^{-1}\mat M)^k\vek x = \sum_{\mathrm{s}}\lambda_{\mathrm{s}}^{-k}c_{\mathrm{s}}\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{s}}\). Every step multiplies the mode \(s\) by \(1/\lambda_{\mathrm{s}}\), so the low modes grow relative to the high ones. This is already so in inverse iteration (theorem 21.27), but now all \(q\) columns would grow towards the first mode and become more and more parallel, were it not for the Ritz step that sorts them again every time. The speed with which the space approaches the first \(q\) modes is set by the ratio of the largest eigenvalue we want to the smallest one we must suppress. We draw this first, then the theorem writes the same for Ritz values.

Take the smallest case we can draw: the frame with three floors of chapter 10 (\(n = 3\), \(\lambda_1 = 0{,}198062\), \(\lambda_2 = 1{,}554958\), \(\lambda_3 = 3{,}246980\) in the unit \(k/\bar m\)) and \(q = 2\). A column of three numbers is a point in the space with three axes, on which we mark its modal coordinates \(c_1\), \(c_2\), \(c_3\). The space of two columns is a plane through the origin. The target is the horizontal plane of the modes \(\vek\varphi_1\) and \(\vek\varphi_2\), the third mode points up. The starting plane is tilted. In it we pick the columns that stand exactly above \(\vek\varphi_1\) and \(\vek\varphi_2\): \(\vek\psi_1 = \vek\varphi_1 + 0{,}8\,\vek\varphi_3\) and \(\vek\psi_2 = \vek\varphi_2 + 0{,}6\,\vek\varphi_3\). The heights \(0{,}8\) and \(0{,}6\) are the shares of the third mode, which we do not want. The step \(\mat K^{-1}\mat M\) multiplies the coordinate \(c_{\mathrm{s}}\) by \(1/\lambda_{\mathrm{s}}\), so \(\vek\psi_2\) goes to \(\vek\varphi_2/\lambda_2 + 0{,}6\,\vek\varphi_3/\lambda_3\). We multiply it by \(\lambda_2\), which does not change the space, and it stands above \(\vek\varphi_2\) again, while its height is \(0{,}6\cdot\lambda_2/\lambda_3 = 0{,}6\cdot0{,}479 = 0{,}287\). In the same way the height of the first column is multiplied by \(\lambda_1/\lambda_3 = 0{,}061\) and falls from \(0{,}8\) to \(0{,}049\). The plane after one step therefore almost lies flat along \(\vek\varphi_1\) and is still tilted along \(\vek\varphi_2\), and after the second step the height of the second column is \(0{,}138\). The picture adds to the algebra the meaning of the words "the space converges": no single column moves, the plane lies down onto the target plane, along every mode with its own factor \(\lambda_{\mathrm{j}}/\lambda_{\mathrm{q}+1}\), slowest along the one whose eigenvalue is closest to the first one left out.

What this means for a Ritz value is shown by the computation for the second value of this start (NumPy). The row of heights \((0{,}8,\ 0{,}6)\) is the matrix \(\mat G\) of the theorem that follows, and \(B_2 = \lambda_3\,(0{,}8^2 + 0{,}6^2) = 3{,}25\) is its constant.

\(k\) height of \(\vek\psi_2\) \(\tilde\lambda^{(k)}_2 - \lambda_2\) bound \(B_2(\lambda_2/\lambda_3)^{2k}\)
0 \(0{,}600\) \(0{,}606\) \(3{,}25\)
1 \(0{,}287\) \(0{,}129\) \(0{,}745\)
2 \(0{,}138\) \(0{,}0314\) \(0{,}171\)
3 \(0{,}0659\) \(0{,}00732\) \(0{,}0392\)

The height falls by the factor \(0{,}479\) every time, the error of the value by \(0{,}21\), \(0{,}24\) and \(0{,}23\), so roughly by \(0{,}479^2 = 0{,}229\). Why the square? The Rayleigh quotient is a ratio of two sums of squares of the coordinates. For the column \(\vek\psi_2\) with the height \(h\) it is \(R = (\lambda_2 + \lambda_3h^2)/(1 + h^2)\), so \(R - \lambda_2 = (\lambda_3 - \lambda_2)\,h^2/(1 + h^2)\): the height enters the error of the value squared. At \(h = 0{,}287\) this is \(1{,}692\cdot0{,}0826/1{,}0826 = 0{,}129\), which is the error of the table to three places.

Theorem 21.33 Convergence of subspace iteration (konvergenca iteracije podprostora)

Let \(\mat K\), \(\mat M\) be symmetric positive definite of order \(n\), \(\lambda_1 \le \dots \le \lambda_{\mathrm{n}}\) the eigenvalues of the pair \((\mat K, \mat M)\) with \(\mat M\)-orthonormal columns \(\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{s}}\) (theorem 10.21) and \(q < n\) with \(\lambda_{\mathrm{q}} < \lambda_{\mathrm{q}+1}\). Let \(\mat\Phi_1\) be the matrix of the first \(q\) columns \(\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{s}}\), \(\mat\Phi_2\) the matrix of the others, \(\mat X_0\) a start block with independent columns, \(\mat C_1 = \mat\Phi_1^\T\mat M\,\mat X_0\), \(\mat C_2 = \mat\Phi_2^\T\mat M\,\mat X_0\) and \(\mat C_1\) invertible (the start has an invertible part on the first \(q\) modes). Let \(\mat G = \mat C_2\mat C_1^{-1}\) and \(\tilde\lambda^{(k)}_{\mathrm{r}}\) as in definition 21.31. Then for every \(r = 1, \dots, q\) and \(k \ge 1\)

\[0 \le \tilde\lambda^{(k)}_{\mathrm{r}} - \lambda_{\mathrm{r}} \le B_{\mathrm{r}}\left(\frac{\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}}{\lambda_{\mathrm{q}+1}}\right)^{2k} , \qquad B_{\mathrm{r}} = \sum_{\mathrm{s}=\mathrm{q}+1}^n\lambda_{\mathrm{s}}\sum_{\mathrm{j}=1}^r G_{\mathrm{sj}}^2 , \tag{21.47}\]

where \(G_{\mathrm{sj}}\) is the element \((s - q, j)\) of the matrix \(\mat G\) (we number the rows of \(\mat G\) with \(s = q+1, \dots, n\)).

Proof

We must show that the same space \(\mathcal S_{\mathrm{k}}\) contains a basis that is ever closer to the first \(q\) modes, and then find how large the error of the Ritz value is on this basis.

  1. Let \(\mat\Phi = [\mat\Phi_1\ \mat\Phi_2]\), and \(\mat\Lambda_1\) and \(\mat\Lambda_2\) the diagonal matrices of the eigenvalues \(\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_{\mathrm{q}}\) and \(\lambda_{\mathrm{q}+1}, \dots, \lambda_{\mathrm{n}}\), and \(\mat\Lambda\) the diagonal matrix of all \(n\) eigenvalues. By corollary 10.22, point 1, \(\mat X_0 = \mat\Phi\,\mat C\) with \(\mat C = \mat\Phi^\T\mat M\,\mat X_0 = \begin{pmatrix}\mat C_1 \\ \mat C_2\end{pmatrix}\). From \(\mat K^{-1}\mat M\,\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{s}} = \vek\varphi_{\mathrm{s}}/\lambda_{\mathrm{s}}\) it follows that \(\mat Z_{\mathrm{k}} := (\mat K^{-1}\mat M)^k\mat X_0 = \mat\Phi\,\mat\Lambda^{-k}\mat C\), and by lemma 21.32, point 3, \(\mathcal S_{\mathrm{k}}\) is the column space of the matrix \(\mat Z_{\mathrm{k}}\).
  2. Let \(\mat T_{\mathrm{k}} = \mat C_1^{-1}\mat\Lambda_1^k\), an invertible matrix of order \(q\). Then \(\mat Z_{\mathrm{k}}\mat T_{\mathrm{k}} = \mat\Phi_1\mat\Lambda_1^{-k}\mat C_1\mat C_1^{-1}\mat\Lambda_1^k + \mat\Phi_2\mat\Lambda_2^{-k}\mat C_2\mat C_1^{-1}\mat\Lambda_1^k = \mat\Phi_1 + \mat\Phi_2\mat E_{\mathrm{k}} =: \mat\Psi_{\mathrm{k}}\) with \(\mat E_{\mathrm{k}} = \mat\Lambda_2^{-k}\mat G\,\mat\Lambda_1^k\) and elements \((\mat E_{\mathrm{k}})_{\mathrm{sj}} = G_{\mathrm{sj}}(\lambda_{\mathrm{j}}/\lambda_{\mathrm{s}})^k\). The columns of \(\mat\Psi_{\mathrm{k}}\) are combinations of the columns of \(\mat Z_{\mathrm{k}}\) with an invertible matrix, so \(\mat\Psi_{\mathrm{k}}\) has the same column space \(\mathcal S_{\mathrm{k}}\) and \(q\) independent columns. By lemma 21.32, point 4, the \(\tilde\lambda^{(k)}_{\mathrm{r}}\) are the Ritz values of the basis \(\mat\Psi_{\mathrm{k}}\), and \(\tilde\lambda^{(k)}_{\mathrm{r}} \ge \lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\). This is the left estimate. In figure 21.58 \(\mat\Phi_1\) is the horizontal pair and \(\mat\Psi_{\mathrm{k}}\) the pair of columns above it with the heights \((\mat E_{\mathrm{k}})_{3\mathrm{j}} = G_{3\mathrm{j}}(\lambda_{\mathrm{j}}/\lambda_3)^k\), which every step multiplies by the factors \(\lambda_1/\lambda_3\) and \(\lambda_2/\lambda_3\).
  3. Let \(\vek t \ne \vek 0\) be a column of \(q\) numbers with \(t_{\mathrm{j}} = 0\) for \(j > r\) and \(\vek v = \mat\Psi_{\mathrm{k}}\vek t\). Write \(e_{\mathrm{s}} = \sum_{\mathrm{j} \le \mathrm{r}}(\mat E_{\mathrm{k}})_{\mathrm{sj}}\,t_{\mathrm{j}}\) for \(s > q\). Then \(\vek v = \sum_{\mathrm{j}\le \mathrm{r}}t_{\mathrm{j}}\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{j}} + \sum_{\mathrm{s}>\mathrm{q}}e_{\mathrm{s}}\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{s}}\), and by \(\mat M\)-orthonormality and \(\mat K\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{s}} = \lambda_{\mathrm{s}}\mat M\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{s}}\) we have \(\vek v^\T\mat M\,\vek v = \sum t_{\mathrm{j}}^2 + \sum e_{\mathrm{s}}^2\) and \(\vek v^\T\mat K\,\vek v = \sum_{\mathrm{j}\le \mathrm{r}}\lambda_{\mathrm{j}}t_{\mathrm{j}}^2 + \sum_{\mathrm{s}>\mathrm{q}}\lambda_{\mathrm{s}}e_{\mathrm{s}}^2\). In figure 21.58 \(\vek v\) is any column of the tilted plane, the \(t_{\mathrm{j}}\) are its horizontal coordinates and \(e_3\) its height above the target plane. Both sums are sums of squares of the coordinates, so the height enters them squared.
  4. Write \(a = \sum_{\mathrm{j}\le \mathrm{r}}t_{\mathrm{j}}^2 > 0\). Since \(\lambda_{\mathrm{j}} \le \lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\) for \(j \le r\), the numerator of the quotient \(R(\vek v)\) is at most \(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\,a + \sum_{\mathrm{s}}\lambda_{\mathrm{s}}e_{\mathrm{s}}^2\), the denominator is at least \(a\) and the numerator is not negative, so \(R(\vek v) \le \lambda_{\mathrm{r}} + \sum_{\mathrm{s}>\mathrm{q}}\lambda_{\mathrm{s}}e_{\mathrm{s}}^2/a\). By the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality (lemma 8.24, point 1) for the sum \(e_{\mathrm{s}} = \sum_{\mathrm{j}\le \mathrm{r}}(\mat E_{\mathrm{k}})_{\mathrm{sj}}t_{\mathrm{j}}\) we have \(e_{\mathrm{s}}^2 \le a\sum_{\mathrm{j}\le \mathrm{r}}(\mat E_{\mathrm{k}})_{\mathrm{sj}}^2\), so \(R(\vek v) \le \lambda_{\mathrm{r}} + \sum_{\mathrm{s}>\mathrm{q}}\lambda_{\mathrm{s}}\sum_{\mathrm{j}\le \mathrm{r}}(\mat E_{\mathrm{k}})_{\mathrm{sj}}^2\).
  5. For \(j \le r \le q < s\) we have \(0 < \lambda_{\mathrm{j}}/\lambda_{\mathrm{s}} \le \lambda_{\mathrm{r}}/\lambda_{\mathrm{q}+1}\), so \((\mat E_{\mathrm{k}})_{\mathrm{sj}}^2 \le G_{\mathrm{sj}}^2(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}/\lambda_{\mathrm{q}+1})^{2k}\) and \(R(\vek v) \le \lambda_{\mathrm{r}} + B_{\mathrm{r}}(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}/\lambda_{\mathrm{q}+1})^{2k}\) for every such \(\vek v\). In figure 21.58 this is the slower of the two factors, \(\lambda_2/\lambda_3 = 0{,}479\) at \(r = q = 2\), and it enters the bound as the square \(0{,}229\).
  6. The reduced pair \((\tilde{\mat K}, \tilde{\mat M})\) of the basis \(\mat\Psi_{\mathrm{k}}\) has a symmetric matrix \(\tilde{\mat K}\) and a symmetric positive definite matrix \(\tilde{\mat M}\) (lemma 10.57, point 1), as theorem 10.44 requires. Its eigenvalues are \(\tilde\lambda^{(k)}_{\mathrm{r}}\), and the quotient of the pair is \(R(\mat\Psi_{\mathrm{k}}\vek t)\) (lemma 10.57, point 3). By theorem 10.44, point 2, for the pair \((\tilde{\mat K}, \tilde{\mat M})\) and the columns \(\vek e_1, \dots, \vek e_{\mathrm{r}}\) (the first \(r\) columns of the identity matrix of order \(q\)) we have \(\tilde\lambda^{(k)}_{\mathrm{r}} \le \max R(\mat\Psi_{\mathrm{k}}\vek t)\) over all \(\vek t \ne \vek 0\) with \(t_{\mathrm{j}} = 0\) for \(j > r\). By step 5 this largest quotient is at most \(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}} + B_{\mathrm{r}}(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}/\lambda_{\mathrm{q}+1})^{2k}\). This is the right estimate.

Source: The proof is not from a source. BATHE (PDF p. 976) says that "the \(i\)th column ... converges linearly to \(\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{i}}\) and the convergence rate is \(\lambda_{\mathrm{i}}/\lambda_{\mathrm{p}+1}\)" and that more vectors raise the speed, GR (PDF p. 485, (6.117)) has the same ratio with the mode \(p + 1\), CK (PDF pp. 500-501) does not analyse the speed. The theorem proves the speed of the square of this ratio for the eigenvalues, and the constant \(B_{\mathrm{r}}\), which is not in the sources.

The proof gave three things. The Ritz values of subspace iteration are upper bounds, and their error falls at least as fast as \(B_{\mathrm{r}}(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}/\lambda_{\mathrm{q}+1})^{2k}\), so with the square of the ratio of one value already in the subspace to the first one that is not (step 5). The ratio depends on \(q + 1\), not on \(r + 1\): with a larger \(q\) we raise the denominator \(\lambda_{\mathrm{q}+1}\), the ratio gets smaller and for the same \(r\) the speed is greater (these are the "buffer vectors" of GR, PDF p. 485). And the constant \(B_{\mathrm{r}}\) depends on the start through \(\mat G = \mat C_2\mat C_1^{-1}\): if \(\mat C_1\) is nearly singular, \(\mat G\) is usually large and so is the bound, and the error can stay large for several steps (the frame at the end of the section). If \(\mat C_1\) is singular, the condition of the theorem is not met. The speed for the shape, \(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}/\lambda_{\mathrm{q}+1}\), as stated by BATHE and GR, is not proved here. On the frame figure 21.58 shows it, on the cantilever figure 21.59.

The theorem has three assumptions, and each enters at its own place. The first is that the matrix \(\mat K\) is positive definite. We need it in step 1 of definition 21.31, so that every static problem has exactly one solution, and in the proof, so that all \(\lambda_{\mathrm{s}} > 0\) and we may divide by them. It holds for a supported structure such as the cantilever and the frame. For a free structure \(\lambda_1 = 0\) and \(\mat K\) is not invertible, and then a spectrum shift helps (definition 21.29). The second is \(\lambda_{\mathrm{q}} < \lambda_{\mathrm{q}+1}\). The steps of the proof do not use it, it is needed so that the bound falls for \(r = q\) too: with \(\lambda_{\mathrm{q}} = \lambda_{\mathrm{q}+1}\) the factor is \((\lambda_{\mathrm{q}}/\lambda_{\mathrm{q}+1})^2 = 1\) and the bound for \(r = q\) stays \(B_{\mathrm{q}}\) for all \(k\). This happens at a double eigenvalue when the block cuts the pair, for example for a bar with a square cross-section, which bends in both planes with the same frequency. Values that are merely close already cost: for the cantilever of the next subsection the factor is \((\lambda_3/\lambda_4)^2 = 0{,}0678\) at \(q = 3\) and \((\lambda_3/\lambda_7)^2 = 4{,}76\cdot10^{-4}\) at \(q = 6\). The remedy is a larger \(q\). The third is that the matrix \(\mat C_1\) is invertible. It enters in step 2 of the proof, where \(\mat C_1^{-1}\) puts the columns above the modes. In figure 21.58 it means that the starting plane has a column of its own above each of the modes \(\vek\varphi_1\), \(\vek\varphi_2\). It fails when the plane stands upright, for example when \(\vek\varphi_1\) and \(\vek\varphi_3\) span it: then nothing is above \(\vek\varphi_2\) and the steps do not lay it down. An almost upright plane has large heights in \(\mat G\) and with them a large constant \(B_{\mathrm{r}}\), which costs steps at the start. Both cases with numbers are in subsection 21.7.4.

21.7.3 The cantilever with six columns

Take the cantilever of chapter 12 with \(16\) elements, which has \(32\) free coordinates (deflection and rotation at \(16\) nodes, clamped on the left), in units \(EI = \rho A = L = 1\). We want the first three modes, \(p = 3\). The eigenvalues from NumPy are \(\lambda_1 = 12{,}3624\), \(\lambda_2 = 485{,}524\), \(\lambda_3 = 3806{,}85\), \(\lambda_4 = 14\,621{,}7\), \(\lambda_7 = 174\,481\), the angular frequencies \(\omega_1, \omega_2, \omega_3 = 3{,}51602\), \(22{,}0346\), \(61{,}6997\) and \(\omega_4 = 120{,}920\). The start is random: \(q = 6\) columns from the normal distribution (the NumPy generator with seed \(1\)). The matrix \(\mat C_1 = \mat\Phi_1^\T\mat M\,\mat X_0\) has \(|\det\mat C_1| = 4{,}3\cdot10^{-3}\) (the sign depends on the signs of the modes) and the matrix \(\mat G\) has elements of absolute value at most \(2{,}60\). So the start has an invertible part on the first six modes, as the theorem requires. In the basis \(\mat\Phi_1 + \mat\Phi_2\mat G\) of the same space (step 2 of the proof at \(k = 0\)) every column has the share \(1\) of its own low mode and at most \(2{,}6\) of every higher one.

Example 21.34 Subspace iteration on the cantilever, \(p = 3\), \(q = 6\)

We make the steps of definition 21.31 for \(q = 6\) and read \(\tilde\lambda^{(k)}_1\), \(\tilde\lambda^{(k)}_2\) and \(\tilde\lambda^{(k)}_3\) from the diagonal of the matrix \(\tilde{\mat\Lambda}_{\mathrm{k}}\). The table gives the relative error \(\tilde\lambda^{(k)}_{\mathrm{r}}/\lambda_{\mathrm{r}} - 1\), which by lemma 21.32, point 4, is nowhere negative (up to rounding):

\(k\) \(r = 1\) \(r = 2\) \(r = 3\)
1 \(1{,}12\cdot10^{-5}\) \(5{,}90\cdot10^{-3}\) \(5{,}78\cdot10^{-2}\)
2 \(< 10^{-11}\) \(4{,}20\cdot10^{-8}\) \(1{,}45\cdot10^{-5}\)
3 \(< 10^{-11}\) \(< 10^{-11}\) \(2{,}93\cdot10^{-9}\)
4 \(< 10^{-11}\) \(< 10^{-11}\) \(7{,}9\cdot10^{-13}\)

The column \(r = 3\) of the table is the blue curve in figure 21.60. An entry \(< 10^{-11}\) means an error we can no longer tell from rounding. The computer rounds every number by about \(10^{-16}\) relative (double precision, chapter 12). At \(q = 6\) the iterated values differ from values computed to \(40\) digits (mpmath) by at most \(5\cdot10^{-11}\), with both signs, which at \(\lambda_1 = 12{,}4\) is \(4\cdot10^{-12}\) relative. The exact \(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\) for the table are therefore computed to \(40\) digits. The usual computation with NumPy already misses \(\lambda_1\) by \(5{,}4\cdot10^{-11}\) relative, and with such a comparison the column \(r = 1\) would show only this error from \(k = 2\) on (we do not analyse rounding further). The ratios of successive errors of the third value are \(2{,}5\cdot10^{-4}\), \(2{,}0\cdot10^{-4}\) and \(2{,}7\cdot10^{-4}\). In the bound of the theorem the factor per step is \((\lambda_3/\lambda_7)^2 = 0{,}02182^2 = 4{,}76\cdot10^{-4}\). The actual ratios are of the same order of magnitude, for this start smaller by a factor of \(1{,}8\) to \(2{,}4\), so the bound catches the speed. The theorem does not bound the ratio of two successive errors, though: with other seeds of the generator we also got \(5{,}2\cdot10^{-4}\) and \(5{,}9\cdot10^{-4}\). The constant is \(B_3 = 1{,}34\cdot10^8\), and \(B_3/\lambda_3 = 35\,088\). The bound of the relative error is therefore \(16{,}7\), \(7{,}95\cdot10^{-3}\) and \(3{,}78\cdot10^{-6}\) at \(k = 1, 2, 3\), which is \(290\) times, \(550\) times and \(1290\) times more than the measured values. In the first step the bound allows \(\tilde\lambda_3\) up to \(17{,}7\,\lambda_3\) and tells nothing of practical use, and from the second step on it tells how large the error is at most.

The first test of the theorem therefore succeeds: the error falls by a factor of \(3700\) to \(4900\) per step, and the order of magnitude of this factor is set by \(\lambda_3\) and \(\lambda_7\), not by the random start (with four other seeds of the generator it was between \(1700\) and \(4700\)). What happens to the shape in the process is shown by the next figure.

We expand the third Ritz shape in the modes \(\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{s}}\) (corollary 10.22) and read in the figure how much of each it contains. The open circle is the third mode, which takes up \(1\). The vertical line separates the first six modes, present in the space \(\mathcal S_{\mathrm{k}}\) by design, from the modes \(7\) to \(12\), which the iteration must suppress. The vertical axis is logarithmic. After the first step the share of the modes \(7\) to \(12\) is from \(6\cdot10^{-4}\) to \(1{,}4\cdot10^{-2}\), after the second from \(4{,}5\cdot10^{-6}\) to \(3{,}7\cdot10^{-4}\) and after the third from \(1{,}5\cdot10^{-8}\) to \(4{,}9\cdot10^{-6}\). The share of mode \(7\) at \(k = 1, 2, 3\) is \(5{,}1\cdot10^{-3}\), \(2{,}2\cdot10^{-4}\) and \(4{,}9\cdot10^{-6}\). We divide it by \((\lambda_3/\lambda_7)^k = 0{,}0218^k\) and get \(0{,}234\), \(0{,}465\) and \(0{,}468\). The last two values match the element \(|G_{73}| = 0{,}468\) of step 2 of the proof of the theorem: the third column of the basis \(\mat\Psi_{\mathrm{k}}\) has at mode \(7\) the share \((\mat E_{\mathrm{k}})_{73} = G_{73}(\lambda_3/\lambda_7)^k\). In this share the third Ritz shape is already nearly equal to the third column of the basis \(\mat\Psi_{\mathrm{k}}\) after two steps. So the share of mode \(7\) in the shape falls here by the factor \(\lambda_3/\lambda_7\) per step, as BATHE and GR state the speed of the shape, and the square of this factor holds for the eigenvalue, which the theorem proves.

Let us also compare three sizes of the block, \(q = 3\), \(6\) and \(11\), for the third eigenvalue. The ratio \(\lambda_3/\lambda_{\mathrm{q}+1}\) is in the second column of the table, the relative error after the first three steps in the last.

\(q\) \(\lambda_3/\lambda_{\mathrm{q}+1}\) \((\lambda_3/\lambda_{\mathrm{q}+1})^2\) error after \(k = 1, 2, 3\)
3 \(0{,}2604\) \(0{,}0678\) \(3{,}44\), \(1{,}84\), \(0{,}291\)
6 \(0{,}02182\) \(4{,}76\cdot10^{-4}\) \(5{,}8\cdot10^{-2}\), \(1{,}4\cdot10^{-5}\), \(2{,}9\cdot10^{-9}\)
11 \(0{,}002170\) \(4{,}71\cdot10^{-6}\) \(1{,}9\cdot10^{-3}\), \(1{,}9\cdot10^{-8}\), \(8\cdot10^{-14}\)

The figure puts the table on the axis with the step \(k\) horizontal and the logarithmic error vertical. The orange curve (\(q = 3\)) falls more slowly in the first steps and from \(k = 4\) on it meets the prediction with the slope \(0{,}0678\) per step (a factor of \(15\)). The blue curve (\(q = 6\)) falls by about \(3{,}6\) orders of magnitude per step and lies below the prediction, because its ratios of successive errors, \(2{,}0\) to \(2{,}7\cdot10^{-4}\), are smaller than \(\rho = 4{,}76\cdot10^{-4}\). The blackwhite curve (\(q = 11\)) is steeper still, but it has only two points, because the third value is at the rounding limit. Its second point lies a factor of \(2{,}2\) above the prediction: the error fell by the factor \(1{,}0\cdot10^{-5}\) and not \(\rho = 4{,}7\cdot10^{-6}\). This does not contradict the theorem, because it bounds the error, not the ratio of two successive errors. Its bound \(B_3\rho^k/\lambda_3\) at \(q = 11\) and \(k = 2\) is \(5{,}1\cdot10^{-3}\), far above the measured \(1{,}9\cdot10^{-8}\). At \(q = 6\) the error after \(3\) steps and \(18\) static problems is \(2{,}9\cdot10^{-9}\), at \(q = 11\) after \(2\) steps and \(22\) static problems \(1{,}9\cdot10^{-8}\), at \(q = 3\) after \(8\) steps and \(24\) static problems still \(4{,}6\cdot10^{-7}\).

At about \(20\) static problems the most accurate is therefore the middle choice \(q = 6\). The static problems are only part of the cost: every step needs also \(q^2\) scalar products for the matrices \(\tilde{\mat K}\), \(\tilde{\mat M}\) and a reduced eigenproblem of order \(q\) with full matrices, which grows as \(q^3\). For a large \(n\) the static problems dominate, for a large \(q\) the reduced problem. CK (PDF p. 501) recommends for \(N_{\mathrm{d}}\) wanted modes \(N_{\mathrm{s}} = \min\{2N_{\mathrm{d}},\ N_{\mathrm{d}} + 8\}\) vectors, GR the same (PDF p. 485, citing Bathe and Wilson): at \(p = 3\) we have \(q = \min\{6,\ 11\} = 6\), which we took. The rule means that we add \(p\) spare vectors as long as \(p \le 8\), and \(8\) for a larger \(p\). BATHE (section 11.6.2, PDF p. 977) writes \(\max\{2p,\ p + 8\}\) in the text, but its cost table (PDF p. 982) has \(\min\{2p,\ p + 8\}\). The books disagree, we follow the \(\min\) of three places, because \(\max\) at \(p = 100\) would give \(q = 200\) and not \(108\). The recommendation comes from experience and is not proved. Only the speed at a given \(q\) is proved.

21.7.4 Near miss: a start without the second mode

The theorem requires \(\mat C_1\) to be invertible. What happens if it is not? We try the frame of chapter 10 with three floors, units \(k/\bar m\), eigenvalues \(\lambda_1 = 0{,}198062\), \(\lambda_2 = 1{,}554958\), \(\lambda_3 = 3{,}246980\). We take \(q = 2\), so we want \(\lambda_1\) and \(\lambda_2\), and three starts.

Example 21.35 The frame, \(q = 2\), a start without the second mode

The first start (the blue curve in figure 21.61) has the columns \((1, 1, 1)^\T\) and \((0, 1, 3)^\T\). Its matrix \(\mat C_1\) (the rows are \(\vek\varphi_1^\T\mat M\,\mat X_0\) and \(\vek\varphi_2^\T\mat M\,\mat X_0\)) has \(|\det\mat C_1| = 3{,}72\), so it is invertible, and the second Ritz value after \(k = 1, 2, 3, 4\) steps is \(1{,}55524\), \(1{,}55502\), \(1{,}55497\) and \(1{,}55496\) in turn: it approaches \(\lambda_2 = 1{,}554958\) from above.

The second start (the blackwhite line) has the columns \(\vek\varphi_1 + \vek\varphi_3\) and \(\vek\varphi_1 + 2\vek\varphi_3\). Both are combinations of the first and third mode only, so the second row of the matrix \(\mat C_1\) is zero, only the first one is nonzero, and the condition of the theorem is not met. The space of all combinations of the modes \(\vek\varphi_1\) and \(\vek\varphi_3\) is invariant in this case: because \(\mat K^{-1}\mat M\,\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{s}} = \vek\varphi_{\mathrm{s}}/\lambda_{\mathrm{s}}\), every step stays in it, and we never get the second mode. The Ritz values are for all \(k\) exactly \(0{,}198062\) and \(3{,}246980\), that is \(\lambda_1\) and \(\lambda_3\), and \(\lambda_2\) is nowhere. This holds in a computation without rounding, what rounding does is told by the paragraph after figure 21.61.

The third start (the orange curve) has the columns \(\vek\varphi_1 + \vek\varphi_3\) and \(\vek\varphi_1 + 2\vek\varphi_3 + 10^{-3}\vek\varphi_2\): a small share of the second mode. Now \(\mat C_1\) is invertible (\(\det\mat C_1 = 10^{-3}\)), but \(\mat G = (1,\ 1000)\) and the constant is \(B_2 = 3{,}2\cdot10^6\). The second Ritz value is \(3{,}24697\) at \(k = 1\), \(3{,}24637\) at \(k = 4\), \(3{,}0514\) at \(k = 8\), \(2{,}0406\) at \(k = 10\), \(1{,}5900\) at \(k = 12\), \(1{,}55684\) at \(k = 14\), \(1{,}55506\) at \(k = 16\) and \(1{,}554958\) with the relative error \(1{,}8\cdot10^{-7}\) at \(k = 20\) and \(1{,}1\cdot10^{-10}\) at \(k = 25\).

The figure collects all three starts. The step \(k\) is horizontal, \(\tilde\lambda_2\) vertical. The blue curve lies on \(\lambda_2\) from the first step. The blackwhite line stays at \(\lambda_3\) for all \(30\) steps: the space is two-dimensional and invariant, and the reduced problem in it has only \(\lambda_1\) and \(\lambda_3\). The orange curve starts at \(\lambda_3\) and falls towards \(\lambda_2\) only after \(k \approx 10\). Why just there? The difference of the two columns is \(\vek\varphi_3 + \varepsilon\,\vek\varphi_2\) and lies in the space of the start. The share of the second mode in it is \(\varepsilon = 10^{-3}\), the share of the third is \(1\), and every step multiplies them by \(1/\lambda_2\) and \(1/\lambda_3\), so the ratio of the parts changes by \(\lambda_3/\lambda_2 = 2{,}088\) per step. The second mode becomes equal to the third at \(\varepsilon\,(2{,}088)^k = 1\), that is at \(k = \ln 10^3/\ln 2{,}088 = 9{,}4\), and so it is in the figure. Later the curve falls at the predicted speed: the mean ratio of successive errors between \(k = 20\) and \(25\) is \((1{,}119\cdot10^{-10}/1{,}763\cdot10^{-7})^{1/5} = 0{,}229\), which is the \((\lambda_2/\lambda_3)^2 = 0{,}229\) of the theorem. The slow start does not contradict the theorem, which puts it down to the constant \(B_2 = 3{,}2\cdot10^6\): the bound of the relative error is \(0{,}84\) at \(k = 10\) and \(3{,}4\cdot10^{-7}\) at \(k = 20\), above the measured \(0{,}31\) and \(1{,}8\cdot10^{-7}\). The same computation explains what happens to the blackwhite line in the computer. Rounding creates in the columns a share of the second mode of the order \(10^{-16}\), which becomes equal to the third at \(k = \ln 10^{16}/\ln 2{,}088 = 50\). The second Ritz value of the second start is still \(3{,}24698\) at \(k = 40\), it is \(1{,}794\) at \(k = 50\) and already \(1{,}55496\) at \(k = 60\). CK (PDF p. 500, remark 1) requires that the initial loads excite all the low modes we are interested in. In our notation this is the invertibility of the matrix \(\mat C_1\), and by CK choosing such loads needs experience.

21.7.5 Summary

Subspace iteration makes a step of inverse iteration on \(q\) columns and then a Ritz step (definition 21.31). Every step is a Ritz approximation (lemma 21.32), so the estimates of the eigenvalues are upper bounds, while the column space lies down onto the space of the first \(q\) modes (figure 21.58), as for the Guyan and Craig-Bampton bases, the only difference being that we improve the basis ourselves each time. By theorem 21.33 the bound of the error of the \(r\)th estimate shrinks by the factor \((\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}/\lambda_{\mathrm{q}+1})^2\) per step, when the start has an invertible part on the first \(q\) modes. For the cantilever at \(q = 6\) and \(r = 3\) the factor is \(4{,}8\cdot10^{-4}\), at \(q = 3\) it is \(0{,}068\), and six columns give the error \(3\cdot10^{-9}\) after three steps, three columns \(5\cdot10^{-7}\) after eight. Without a share of the second mode in the start the procedure stays, in a computation without rounding, in the wrong subspace and does not find \(\lambda_2\) (the blackwhite line in figure 21.61). In the computer it finds it only after about \(50\) steps, when rounding creates this share and the steps enlarge it.

The cost is \(q\) static problems and a reduced problem of order \(q\) in every step. The Lanczos procedure in the next section builds the subspace from a single column and gets every further vector with one static problem. The Ritz steps and the upper bounds remain.

21.8 The Lanczos method (Lanczosov postopek)

In section 21.6 we obtained the first mode from one column by repeatedly solving \(\mat K\vek x_{\mathrm{k}+1} = \mat M\vek x_{\mathrm{k}}\), and in section 21.7 the first \(q\) modes from \(q\) columns. In both we threw away the intermediate columns \(\vek x_0, \vek x_1, \dots\) and kept only the last one or the last block. Yet each of them cost one solution with the factorized matrix \(\mat K\) (lemma 7.47), so the discarded work is lost. In this section we keep everything. If the \(m\) columns that we obtained with \(m\) solutions are independent, they span a space, and by theorem 10.59 the Ritz values from any such space are upper bounds of the eigenvalues. The question is how much more work we need to obtain from these columns a small problem that we can solve. The answer is surprising: if we \(\mat M\)-orthogonalize the columns as we go, each new column needs only the two previous ones, and the reduced matrix is tridiagonal. In the figure the discarded columns of inverse iteration are grey and the kept ones blue. The rows from the top are inverse iteration, subspace iteration and Lanczos, and the dots mean that the vectors go on up to \(\vek x_{\mathrm{m}}\). Each is the result of one solve, and in the Lanczos method each new vector needs only two previous ones.

The procedure is called the Lanczos method (Lanczosov postopek) after the author who introduced it. It was introduced in 1950 (CK, PDF p. 507). The source also says something that determines how we treat the method in this section. In rounding arithmetic the recurrence is unstable because of the loss of orthogonality, which at first held the method back, and so for some time the Householder method was the method of choice. With various ways of reorthogonalization, that is, of correcting the vectors as we go so that they stay orthogonal, however, the Lanczos method again became a competitor for large sparse problems of the kind that arise in structural dynamics. We therefore first prove the theorem for computation without rounding, and then on the cantilever of example 21.40 we measure what happens if we run the recurrence without reorthogonalization.

After this section we will be able to build an \(\mat M\)-orthonormal basis from one starting shape with a three-term recurrence (theorem 21.37), to say why the Ritz values from it are upper bounds and never worse than those of inverse iteration with the same starting shape (lemma 21.38), to see that a start at the static solution \(\mat K^{-1}\vek F\) gives a basis that contains this solution (corollary 21.41, a continuation of section 21.1), and to measure when and why the method without reorthogonalization goes wrong.

21.8.1 Krylov vectors

Let \(\mat A = \mat K^{-1}\mat M\). The matrix \(\mat K\) is positive definite, hence invertible (lemma 8.22), and \(\mat A\vek x\) is exactly the result of one step of inverse iteration: one multiplication by \(\mat M\) and one solution with the factorization \(\mat L\mat D\mat L^\T\). An eigenpair \((\lambda, \vek\varphi)\) of the pair \((\mat K, \mat M)\) has \(\mat A\vek\varphi = \vek\varphi/\lambda\), since we multiply \(\mat K\vek\varphi = \lambda\mat M\vek\varphi\) by \(\lambda^{-1}\mat K^{-1}\). The eigenvalues of the matrix \(\mat A\) are therefore \(\theta_{\mathrm{r}} = 1/\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\) with the same modes \(\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}\), and the lowest eigenvalue \(\lambda_1\) belongs to the largest \(\theta_1\). This explains why repeated multiplication by \(\mat A\) emphasizes the first mode. In the figure the eigenvalues \(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\) are mapped by inversion to the values \(\theta_{\mathrm{r}} = 1/\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\), and the smallest \(\lambda_1\) belongs to the largest \(\theta_1\).

Definition 21.36 Krylov subspace (Krilov podprostor)

Let \(\mat K\) and \(\mat M\) be symmetric positive definite matrices of order \(n\), \(\mat A = \mat K^{-1}\mat M\) and \(\vek r \ne \vek 0\) a column with \(n\) entries. The Krylov vectors (Krilovi vektorji) are \(\vek v_{\mathrm{i}} = \mat A^i\vek r\) for \(i = 0, 1, 2, \dots\), that is \(\vek v_0 = \vek r\) and \(\vek v_{\mathrm{i}+1} = \mat A\vek v_{\mathrm{i}}\). The Krylov subspace (Krilov podprostor) of order \(m\) is the set of all linear combinations of the first \(m\) Krylov vectors,

\[\mathcal K_{\mathrm{m}}(\mat A, \vek r) = L(\vek v_0, \vek v_1, \dots, \vek v_{\mathrm{m}-1}) = \Big\{ \sum_{\mathrm{i}=0}^{m-1}c_{\mathrm{i}}\mat A^i\vek r \Big\} . \tag{21.48}\]

In the figure the Krylov vectors form a chain in which \(\mat A\) maps each vector to the next, and the Krylov subspace is the space that they span.

Source: CK section 15.5.1 (PDF p. 508), where the \(j\)-th Krylov subspace is \(\mathcal K_{\mathrm{j}}(\vek r)\) with the Krylov vectors \(\vek v_{\mathrm{i}} = \mat A^i\vek r\). The name Krylov is from the source. The notation with \(\mat A = \mat K^{-1}\mat M\) is ours, because it matches inverse iteration from section 21.6.

Since \(\vek r = \sum_{\mathrm{s}} c_{\mathrm{s}}\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{s}}\) is the expansion in modes (corollary 10.22) and \(\mat A^i\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{s}} = \theta_{\mathrm{s}}^i\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{s}}\), we have \(\mat A^i\vek r = \sum_{\mathrm{s}} c_{\mathrm{s}}\theta_{\mathrm{s}}^i\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{s}}\). The elements of the Krylov subspace are therefore \(\sum_{\mathrm{s}} c_{\mathrm{s}}\,p(\theta_{\mathrm{s}})\,\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{s}}\) for any polynomial \(p\) of degree less than \(m\).
